papers.abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.
authors: Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Botong Zhang, Boning Shao, Jing Wang, Ruijie Zheng, Yuvan Sharma, Runyu Lu, Jiaming Liu, Renrui Zhang, Roei Herzig, Yutong Bai, Ken Goldberg, Danfei Xu, Yuke Zhu, Guanzhi Wang, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Trevor Darrell
bullets: Addresses the gap between predictive world action models and agentic systems with reusable, code-based skills.
Uses a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture with coupled code, video, and action generation streams.
Represents skills as parameterized programs while using code to structure multi-step prediction and control.
Introduces automated trajectory curation that aligns robot and human videos with programs and builds reusable skill libraries.
Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual tasks report improved task performance, language following, semantic reasoning, and robustness over VLA and WAM baselines.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose $\textbf{LongZero}$, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.
bullets: Addresses the scarcity, cost, and difficulty of obtaining long, diverse, challenging, verifiable RL training data.
Generates compact multi-hop questions, answers, and evidence first, then expands the evidence into long multi-document contexts.
Combines self-generated multi-hop reasoning and multi-round retrieval tasks, trained with GRPO.
Evaluated on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks; it generalizes to real tasks and outperforms the stated baselines.
Scope: the approach is designed for long-context reasoning and relies on self-generated tasks with verifiable evidence.

papers.abstract: Video world models predict future frames from past frames and actions. They serve as simulators in which agents train, plan or are evaluated, and that humans can control interactively. They generate in the latent space of a video autoencoder, whose compression sets their cost per frame and how long each action waits to take effect. Yet world models often reuse the autoencoders of text-to-video generators, built for offline generation with no agent waiting and, without their training data and code, not retrainable at another compression. We therefore ask how, where and how much a world model should compress. We build CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders spanning multiple spatio-temporal compressions. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features and share a diffusion decoder self-distilled to one or a few steps. We train the same world model on each autoencoder in two domains, manipulation and navigation, with two environments each. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera. Our study also leads to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality. Code, models and a live demo are at https://kyutai.org/blog/2026-10-21-cadre
authors: Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Yutong Bai, Nicolas Dufour, Patrick P\'erez, David Picard
bullets: World-model autoencoders determine both per-frame computation and how quickly actions affect predictions.
CADRE is a family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders covering multiple spatial and temporal compression levels.
The same world model was evaluated across manipulation and navigation domains with multiple environments per domain.
CADRE achieves most of the latency–quality frontier, particularly in moving-camera settings.
Findings include sharper reconstruction from diffusion decoding under strong compression and different optimal compression choices for manipulation versus navigation.

papers.selection_reason: Rethinks video autoencoders for interactive world models with causal diffusion representation autoencoders; directly relevant to video and interactive world models.
papers.title: Rethinking Video Autoencoders for Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: CADRE shows that video-autoencoder compression should be tailored to interactive world-model latency and environment dynamics, rather than inherited from offline video generators.

papers.abstract: Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per-item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed-depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec's learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: lower-frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.
authors: Zhanshuo Cao, Jiakai Tang, Yuqi Zhou, Sunhao Dai, Jun Xu
bullets: Items in an interaction history have highly variable computational needs, making uniform processing inefficient.
LoopRec uses a weight-shared recursive block with a lightweight per-item gate that decides whether each item exits or continues.
The method learns per-item computation depth without auxiliary depth labels and can adapt to different backbone architectures.
Experiments across four backbone families and public benchmarks show consistent gains over matched fixed-depth models.
The learned allocation gives deeper processing to patterns such as lower-frequency items and more recent interactions.

papers.abstract: Language models' abilities to interpret tasks and generate programs offer a promising basis for 3D spatial reasoning. Yet following spatial instructions in 3D scenes requires programs to construct geometric references that language leaves implicit. In this work, we introduce VoxProg, which formulates 3D object placement through voxel programming: a language model translates task interpretations into executable programs over local voxel views of scene surfaces. Because these views index surface geometry on regular grids with explicit coordinates and neighborhood relations, an evidence program can isolate task-relevant regions and boundaries directly from scene meshes, and a downstream pose program can measure the resulting geometry to compute a target $SE(3)$ pose. Visual and numerical feedback from execution lets the model inspect intermediate selections and candidate placements to iteratively revise its code. To evaluate open-ended placement across functional use, geometric fit, and contextual arrangements, we introduce the 71-task VoxProg-Bench benchmark along with an evaluation suite pairing perceptual Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity. Across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks, VoxProg consistently outperforms relation-based, keypoint-based, and mesh-based baselines.
authors: Zhichao Zhai, Menglei Zhao, Guikun Chen, Zihao Yan, Kanzhi Wu, Wenguan Wang, Jun Xiao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating implicit spatial instructions into explicit geometric references for 3D placement.
Uses a language model to generate executable evidence and pose programs over local voxel views with coordinates and neighborhood relations.
Computes target SE(3) poses from selected scene geometry and revises programs using visual and numerical execution feedback.
Introduces the 71-task VoxProg-Bench and evaluation metrics for Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity.
Outperforms relation-, keypoint-, and mesh-based baselines across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.
authors: Yunhao Luo, Wentao He, Yinpei Dai, Hyelin Nam, Hongze Fu, Joyce Chai, Nima Fazeli, Jeong Joon Park
bullets: Addresses physics ambiguity—such as mass distribution, damping, and friction—that causes prediction drift in novel scenes.
Encodes an exploratory interaction clip into a compact physics descriptor token for in-context conditioning.
Trains end-to-end using only latent prediction loss, without analytical physics modeling or physics annotations.
Reuses the descriptor across rollouts with negligible inference overhead.
Across four environments, improves rollout accuracy and visual planning success; descriptors generalize beyond training physics ranges.

papers.abstract: World models turn visual representations into predictions and actions. We argue that their visual foundation should combine physical-state information, native language alignment, and pixel reconstruction, so that a single representation can support prediction, instruction, and inspection. However, existing encoders typically specialize in only one or two of these capabilities; we therefore introduce ALPS, a pretrained visual state encoder that unifies all three in a single set of patch tokens. Using only still images and text, we pretrain a ViT-B/16 from scratch with language, reconstruction, and spatial correspondence objectives, and then refine it via cross-view self-distillation. In a unified evaluation across fifteen public encoders, ALPS achieves the lowest aggregate LIBERO state-probe error among ViT-B models (matching the 3.5x larger V-JEPA 2-L) while maintaining strong language alignment and accurate pixel reconstruction. Downstream, frozen ALPS tokens reach the highest mean policy success on LIBERO (85.5%) when paired with our native text tower, match or exceed leading encoders on world-model planning across PushT, Wall, and Granular, and allow predicted future tokens to be decoded directly into pixels for visual inspection. We hope this work helps establish visual pretraining as a shared foundation for understanding, prediction, and action in world models.

Uses a single set of patch tokens for prediction, instruction following, and visual inspection.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.
authors: Yanzhe Chen, Ziyi Yang, Jifeng Zhu, Qiming Huang, Ruihe An, Peiyao Xu, Hesen Yang, Runda Liu, Chang Gong, Zhijun Cao, Zechen Bai, Wenzheng Zeng, Yiqi Lin, Guoqiang Liang, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Mike Zheng Shou

Uses a capability-centric framework to compare embodied agents with multimodal agents and robotic systems, independent of architecture.
Highlights five physical constraints, including partial observability and difficult-to-verify outcomes, that reduce reversibility and require stronger action reasoning.

papers.abstract: Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively. Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student--teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration. Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and the privileged expert provides action labels conditioned on that context. By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student's on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed. This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning. Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves ~2x higher returns under fixed exploration budgets, uses ~100x fewer interactions than RL baselines, and outperforms frontier models at exploration. Finally, our method transfers policies trained in simulation to vision-denied real-world robot manipulation, exhibiting efficient exploration and increasing success by +40% over standard distillation. Overall, it provides a simple yet surprisingly effective framework to learn efficient test-time exploration.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.

papers.abstract: Vietnamese pre-trained encoders have improved rapidly, but the strongest ones are large, multilingual-vocabulary models or depend on external word segmentation, which makes them costly to deploy. We present GoiBERT, a family of two compact Vietnamese encoders with 26M and 49M parameters that operate directly on raw text. GoiBERT learns from two complementary teachers. A same-tokenizer Vietnamese encoder first teaches general-purpose representations. A much larger teacher then provides task-level guidance through soft labels that are generated without ever labeling its own training data. Across eight benchmarks covering text classification, aspect-based sentiment analysis, natural language inference, and named entity recognition, GoiBERT-large achieves the highest average score among non-teacher models. It does so with fewer than half the parameters of the strongest compact baseline and twice its throughput. GoiBERT-base retains 99% of that baseline's performance at a quarter of its size. Our analysis shows that compression is nearly lossless for sentiment and classification tasks but remains costly for inference and entity recognition, which points to clear directions for future work. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/Nhantran65/GoiBERT.git

papers.abstract: Uniform diffusion language models (UDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising sequences of ordinary vocabulary tokens, any of which may be corrupted and subsequently revised. During training, UDLMs must denoise from a context that may itself be unreliable, whereas masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) always condition on a clean context. This challenging training objective makes UDLMs more FLOP-intensive to train than MDLMs, but it yields stronger downstream reasoning performance. Recently, selective looping, which recursively applies a few early Transformer layers within each denoising step, has been shown to improve training efficiency in MDLMs under an iso-FLOP budget. We investigate looping in UDLMs while keeping the training objective and sampler unchanged. We find that looping significantly improves training efficiency: looped UDLMs reach the validation NLL of a non-looped UDLM trained on about 0.5 trillion tokens with up to 2.8x fewer training FLOPs on OpenWebText and 3.3x fewer on FineWeb-Edu. We also find that, at a matched NFE budget, looped UDLMs reach up to 9.8% lower generation perplexity than the non-looped UDLM, with most gains achieved at moderate loop counts. Finally, we study different loop-count distributions and find that sampling smaller loop counts more frequently during training improves inference efficiency: on downstream tasks, this strategy uses 12% fewer loops than uniform loop-count sampling without degrading accuracy.
authors: Saiteja Utpala, Chieh-Hsin Lai, Yuki Mitsufuji, Praneeth Vepakomma

At matched function-evaluation budgets, looping improves generation perplexity by up to 9.8%.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in frontier AI models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use, raising the possibility of using general-purpose AI models for robot manipulation without task-specific training. However, their manipulation capabilities have not been systematically evaluated on standardized robotics benchmarks. In this report, we present a unified closed-loop manipulation framework for evaluating frontier AI models on the LIBERO-10 benchmark. Our framework enables models to control a robot directly through visual observations, robot proprioception, and structured tool calls, primarily by specifying target end-effector poses and gripper commands, without task-specific fine-tuning or pretrained manipulation skills. We evaluate six frontier AI models, including GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini-4 Argon, across three reasoning effort levels, resulting in 18 configurations and 1,800 evaluation episodes. Our results show that GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest success rate of 44%, followed by Gemini-4 Argon at 43%. Increasing reasoning effort generally improves manipulation performance, but the benefits vary across models and come at additional inference cost. We also observe substantial differences across tasks, with models performing relatively well on object placement tasks but struggling with precise spatial arrangements and complex multi-step interactions. These findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of frontier AI models for robot manipulation, highlighting the challenges of translating reasoning capabilities into reliable physical actions. We release our evaluation framework and experimental results to support reproducible benchmarking and future research on reasoning-based robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires an effective interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole-body coordination. This may burden the high-level policy or leave one aspect underspecified. We present SP-HLM, a framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. The interface combines five task-critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms. SP-VLA, a vision-language-action model, first predicts task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action-chunk inference. Given these sparse targets, SP-MGM, a motion generation model trained through two-stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full-body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation. SP-GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole-body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole-body coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches. Additional results and videos are available on our \href{https://sp-hlm.github.io/}{\textcolor{blue}{project page}}.

papers.abstract: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

papers.abstract: Increasing the attention context length significantly improves streaming video generation quality, while incurring prohibitive memory and computational costs as the context grows. Existing methods attempt to capture this contextual information through attention selection or compression, but remain limited by bounded representations and lack explicit attention-level supervision to retain historical contributions to current queries. To address this, we introduce Attn-Forcing, a novel framework that preserves full-context attention contributions for streaming video generation under bounded memory and computation. We achieve this by introducing attention proxies that continuously approximate the attention responses induced by the historical context. Specifically, we implement the proxies as learnable visual latents and employ a Proxy Update Module to incorporate visual context from historical latents. Moreover, we propose an Attention Matching Loss to explicitly constrain the attention behavior of the learned proxies using full-context attention supervision. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate that Attn-Forcing consistently improves streaming video generation quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance over existing baseline methods.
authors: Junyao Gao, Sibo Liu, Jiaxing Li, Yanan Sun, Hanxin Zhu, Weidong Zhang, Jun Zhang, Cairong Zhao
bullets: Longer attention contexts improve quality but create prohibitive memory and computational costs.
The method uses learnable visual latents as attention proxies for historical context.
A Proxy Update Module continuously incorporates context from historical latents.
An Attention Matching Loss provides explicit supervision from full-context attention behavior.
Experiments report consistent quality improvements and state-of-the-art performance over existing baselines.

papers.abstract: A patient who has lost part of the skull vault needs an implant that fits the defect exactly, and such implants are still drawn by hand in CAD by specialists, which makes each case slow and expensive. The task can be considered as a shape completion problem, so pretrained completion models, and now the first shape completion foundation models, look like a way to remove that manual step. We audited three publicly released pretrained shape completion models, two of them foundation models, applied zero-shot to 239 cranial defects, some carved from public skull datasets and some real post-craniectomy cases. Each output was compared with simply returning the patient's own remaining bone, and tested for whether the predicted material could be placed without intersecting the bone that is still there. On the 210 carved defects none of the three improved on doing nothing, and on the 29 real cases only one did so beyond chance. Yet not one output, from any model in any configuration, was implantable: none managed both to stay clear of the bone the patient still has and to place more material than doing nothing, where a task-specific volumetric model, trained for this task and selected on these cases, was implantable on all but one. The output that most convincingly resembles a skull is no more placeable than the rest, and at these point densities implant thickness cannot be read off the emitted points at all, which is a property of the output representation rather than of any one model. On this evidence the shape completion foundation models we could obtain cannot be trusted and, used as released, are not usable in clinical practice. Substantial research towards trustworthy foundation models for shape completion is still needed.
authors: Marek Wodzinski, Kamil Kwarciak, Daria Hemmerling, Mateusz Daniol
bullets: Evaluated three pretrained models on 239 cranial defects, including carved synthetic defects and real post-craniectomy cases.
None outperformed simply using the patient’s remaining bone on 210 carved defects; only one improved beyond chance on 29 real cases.
No model output was implantable because predictions failed to both avoid existing bone and add useful material.
A task-specific volumetric model was implantable on all but one case, indicating the limitation is not inherent to the task.
At the tested point densities, emitted points cannot reliably determine implant thickness, highlighting a representation-level limitation.

(a) advantage over a no-op at 2 mm; (b) deepest penetration into retained bone, log scale, implantable count above each box. In (b): dotted rule, the 1 mm tolerance; dashed line, the task-specific reference, which is ours and test-selected (Sec. 3); shaded band, the instrument’s floor.

Fig. 2: Case B0001 of MUG500+, from outside (top) and in section (bottom). The patient’s own bone is grey, what each method adds is in colour, black marks material inside bone that is there. MSN-FM’s addition is granular; AdaPoinTr’s and MGPC’s read as solid caps, though only AdaPoinTr’s points lie on a surface. All three run into bone the patient still has. On this case two of them exceed the no-op; the medians in Tab. 1 do not.

No budget the audited models emit or receive reaches 3 mm, so thickness is lost before a model is asked to recover it. That 3 mm is a design target rather than a law, and the clinical data break it: 11 of the 29 real MUG500+ implants (38 %) are thinner than 3 mm, the 29 having median 3.05 mm and mean 3.30 ± 1.41 mm. The dashed box is AdaPoinTr’s other checkpoint (Sec. 4).

Every synthetic result is significant at p < 10−24 under both. MUG500+ ships a manufactured implant, so its columns measure whether material went where the device goes.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low-resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi-view reconstruction methods can produce high-quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-resolution (2K), 4D-consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout-aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to the multi-view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi-view relationships, leading to more 4D-consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency-domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA-Rendering benchmark and our self-captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.
authors: Chenxu Zhou, Zhiyuan Yu, Yudong Jin, Yinji Shentu, Yu Zhang, Jiaming Sun, Xiaowei Zhou
bullets: Targets costly dense multi-view capture requirements and the limited resolution and 4D consistency of prior generative methods.
Builds auxiliary data from capture videos and combines latent representations with layout-aware positional embeddings.
Adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to model relationships across viewpoints and time.
Uses latent frequency-domain supervision to reduce the gap between generated videos and real captures.
Experiments on DNA-Rendering and the self-captured RealVV dataset show improved visual fidelity and 4D consistency over existing methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our framework. These auxiliary videos are fed into a high-resolution video diffusion model to produce enhanced videos, which are then used together with the input captures to optimize the 4DGS representation for volumetric video reconstruction. The detailed model architecture is illustrated in Fig. 3.

Fig. 3. Model architecture.Weuse a ControlNet [Zhang et al. 2023] branch to inject control signals from condition latents and text features. DiT blocks use these signals with layout-aware positional embeddings to denoise noisy latents via factorized spatio-temporal attention.

papers.abstract: LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM-harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.

papers.abstract: Language 3D Gaussian Splatting enables open-vocabulary scene understanding by associating Gaussian primitives with language features. These semantic attributes increase model storage, while most existing 3DGS compression methods are designed mainly to preserve RGB rendering quality. One straightforward approach is to apply sparsification and quantization sequentially. However, pruning based only on rendering quality can remove Gaussians that have small RGB contributions but are important for semantic prediction. Once removed, their semantic information cannot be recovered by later quantization. We propose ClunoGS, a compact framework for Language 3DGS that combines semantics-aware Gaussian sparsification and vector quantization in a unified constrained objective. Semantic supervision is used during sparsification, and the objective jointly considers rendering quality, semantic accuracy, and compactness. We optimize the unified objective with alternating primal, sparsification, quantization, and dual updates. We evaluate ClunoGS on open-vocabulary localization and segmentation using the LERF and ScanNet-10 benchmarks. Under aggressive compression, our unified, semantics-aware formulation substantially alleviates the degradation of semantic representations caused by sequential compression and semantics-agnostic Gaussian sparsification. Ablations further show that jointly coordinating sparsification and quantization better preserves semantic accuracy than applying them independently.
authors: Jian Xu, Yi Li, Ying Huang, Siyi Wu, Bingzhe Li, Yuede Ji, Miao Yin
bullets: Addresses the loss of important semantic information when RGB-focused Gaussian pruning is followed by quantization.
Combines semantics-aware Gaussian sparsification and vector quantization in one constrained objective.
Balances rendering quality, semantic accuracy, and compactness using alternating primal, sparsification, quantization, and dual updates.
Evaluated on open-vocabulary localization and segmentation with LERF and ScanNet-10.
Under aggressive compression, better preserves semantic representations than sequential or independently applied compression.

papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed. The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging. Therefore, we present 1) DONIC, the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with 2) BiHOI, a multi-view dataset of 1,575 sequences spanning 229 objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references. DONIC combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role. Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references. Without finetuning, a single checkpoint achieves 86.79% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32% on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by 77.36 and 45.73 percentage points.
authors: Mingze Sun, Ziang Cao, Yuan Fei, Qiankuan Tao, Zihan Wang, Tianqi Liu, Junhao Chen, Haiwen Diao, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Ziwei Liu

Combines proximal policy optimization, behavioral cloning, and verified-execution data recycling in a feedback loop.
Uses object-centered per-hand rewards and Clip-Centered Advantages to preserve contact roles and stabilize learning across references.
A single checkpoint reaches 86.79% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32% on held-out objects.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging, as it must preserve fine-grained visual evidence while tracking entity evolution across sessions. Existing abstraction-based memories compress images into text, often discarding visually discriminative details, whereas pixel-preserving memories retain raw observations but struggle to reliably associate diverse observations with persistent entity identities and track their evolving states. To address these limitations, we propose MHG-Mem, a multimodal hypergraph memory that jointly organizes entity identity, state evolution, and provenance to visual evidence. Specifically, MHG-Mem represents distinct entity mentions and their observed facts as individual nodes, grouping identity-consistent mentions and facts through occurrence hyperedges. It then synthesizes aspect-specific evolution states from these grouped observations and links them to supporting entities, facts, and source evidence through evolutionary and evidential hyperedges. To navigate this structured memory, we introduce hypergraph-based agentic search, which adaptively selects an entry layer, traverses typed hyperedges across memory levels, and inspects source observations when fine-grained verification is required. These designs support both detailed visual verification and reasoning over cross-session state changes. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MHG-Mem, improving performance by 8.20-9.98% over the strongest baseline.
authors: Jielong Tang, Ling-An Zeng, Xujie Yuan, Xiao Dong, Zhiqian Xia, Qingfeng Li, Shixiong Kai, Kaichao Liang, Rong Yao, Jian Yin
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between text-based memories that lose visual detail and pixel-based memories that struggle with persistent entity tracking.
Represents entity mentions and observed facts as nodes, connecting identity-consistent observations with occurrence hyperedges.
Builds aspect-specific evolution states linked to supporting entities, facts, and source visual evidence.
Uses agentic hypergraph search to navigate memory hierarchies and retrieve fine-grained evidence for verification.
Across three benchmarks, improves performance by 8.20–9.98% over the strongest baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MHG-Mem. (a) Memory construction proceeds through three steps. (b) The three-layer MHG-Mem architecture and three types of hyperedges enable cross-layer traversal and provenance tracing. (c) Hypergraph-based agentic search employs four types of tools to adaptively construct query-aware evidence chains.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve. Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution. We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher-forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context. Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged. Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution. Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.
authors: Ruopeng Gao, Yukun Huang, Jiarui Hu, Shuai Wang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Limin Wang
bullets: Teacher forcing can exploit temporal redundancy, favoring local continuity over genuine modeling of visual evolution.

It improves physical plausibility while using less overall training compute than standard teacher-forced training.
Visualizations suggest FCP produces a more structured representation space, potentially benefiting autoregressive world models.

papers.abstract: Adaptive experiments use bandit algorithms to favor interventions with higher expected rewards. However, decision-makers also require reliable inference on current treatment effects: differences between intervention and reference-arm mean rewards at the present time, rather than historical averages. These objectives conflict: reward maximization favors better interventions, whereas current-effect inference requires continued exploration of potentially suboptimal interventions as outcomes change over time. We characterize this tradeoff for $K$-arm bandits with H\"older-smooth mean rewards of exponent $\beta\in(0,1]$ and constant $L$. Requiring high-probability simultaneous coverage of all current effects by confidence intervals of width at most $w$, we establish matching minimax bounds, up to logarithmic factors, on expected dynamic regret. Over horizon $T$, our algorithm TRACE (Tracking Rewards and Current Effects) achieves regret of order $\widetilde{O}_{\beta}\left(\sqrt{KT}+K^{\beta/(2\beta+1)}L^{1/(2\beta+1)}T^{(\beta+1)/(2\beta+1)}+Kw^{-2}(1+L^{1/\beta}w^{-1/\beta})\right)$, where the notation hides logarithms and constants depending only on $\beta$. This regret--precision tradeoff separates reward-learning regret from the cost of refreshing current-effect estimates, which remains unavoidable even when one arm is uniformly optimal. An empirical-Bernstein e-process extension adapts exploration to realized prediction errors while preserving worst-case guarantees. When within-block drift is negligible relative to sampling error, all observations, including reward-learning observations, can be reused for asymptotically normal pointwise inference and stronger local stationarity yields local asymptotic efficiency. Finally, we show that regret constraints can prevent honest adaptation to unknown smoothness and support our theory with extensive numerical experiments.
bullets: Current-effect inference requires continued exploration of possibly suboptimal arms, conflicting with reward maximization.
For Hölder-smooth mean rewards, the authors derive matching minimax dynamic-regret bounds for simultaneous confidence intervals of width at most $w$.
TRACE separates regret from learning which arms are best from the additional cost of refreshing current-effect estimates.
An empirical-Bernstein e-process extension adapts exploration to observed prediction errors while retaining worst-case guarantees.
Regret constraints can prevent honest adaptation to unknown smoothness; favorable local-stationarity conditions enable efficient pointwise inference.

Inference in block Bj , j ≥ 2, uses estimates constructed from the preceding block, allowing the procedure to maintain up-to-date confidence intervals while continuing to optimize reward.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based models achieve strong performance on blind compressed image restoration (CIR) under unknown compression settings, but their densely stacked projection operators make deployment costly. We study training-free acceleration for such models through an empirical, operator-level analysis. Specifically, we profile where computation is concentrated, characterize channel-wise activation distributions under compressed inputs, and examine the singular-value decay of representative projection weights. These measurements identify the recurring projections in the attention, feed-forward, convolutional, and prompt-conditioning pathways as effective low-rank replacement targets that preserve the original inference graph. They further establish truncated SVD (TSVD) as a principled training-free baseline for blind CIR and reveal why a uniform low-rank objective is mismatched to the channel-imbalanced feature distributions of compressed images. Accordingly, we formulate Activation-Calibrated Singular Value Decomposition (ASVD) for this restoration setting, deriving low-rank factors entirely offline from pretrained weights and lightweight activation statistics gathered from only a few compressed calibration images. By weighting the decomposition with channel-wise activation magnitudes, our ASVD assigns larger penalties to errors on more active channels, requiring neither retraining nor online calibration and leaving the restoration pipeline intact. When instantiated on PromptCIR at rank 64, ASVD consistently improves PSNR-B over TSVD across four standard benchmarks under identical parameter and MAC budgets. At this operating point, the factorized model cuts parameters by 59% (34.75M to 14.34M) and computation by 16.1% (258.79 to 217.16 GMACs for a 256 x 256 input), enabling acceleration without retraining.

On PromptCIR at rank 64, ASVD improves PSNR-B over TSVD across four benchmarks under equal parameter and MAC budgets.
Reduces parameters by 59% and computation by 16.1% for 256×256 inputs, without retraining or changing the inference pipeline.

papers.abstract: Recovering metric world-space hand motion from egocentric video supports understanding human interactions and transferring them to embodied agents. Three challenges complicate this task: multi-stage pipelines propagate errors from independently estimated hand and camera motion; monocular observations leave physical scale ambiguous; and occlusion and out-of-view hands admit multiple plausible motion trajectories. We present DewHand, a unified model for direct joint reconstruction of world-space hand and camera motion. To avoid compounding errors from multi-stage estimation, DewHand jointly predicts hand and camera motion in a shared world coordinate system within a single-stage pipeline. To resolve metric-scale ambiguity, it combines scene-level geometric features from VGGT-$\Omega$ with metric-space supervision, while hand-specific features preserve fine-grained articulation. To handle occlusion and out-of-view hands, we formulate reconstruction as conditional motion generation with flow matching. Under the same architecture, this generative formulation outperforms direct regression in both accuracy and temporal smoothness with only two sampling steps. Experiments on HOT3D and ARCTIC demonstrate improved world-space accuracy and temporal consistency over state-of-the-art methods. DewHand reduces rigid-aligned world-space error relative to StableHand from 32.9 to 28.4 mm on HOT3D and from 76.2 to 36.2 mm on ARCTIC. It also recovers camera scale within 10% on two thirds of HOT3D clips, versus about a quarter for SLAM. Moreover, in zero-shot evaluations on HoloAssist, H2O, and TACO, captured with different devices, DewHand achieves the lowest rigid-aligned world-space error (WA-MPJPE) on each dataset.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.
authors: Yufeng Li, Zaijing Li, Fuchen Zhang, Zongzong Wu, Ming Zhao, Fengxiao Tang
bullets: Addresses semantic loss from converting text into discrete graph symbols and modality mismatch between graphs and LLM-pretrained text.
Uses a Semantic Topology Mapper to create context-intact semantic nodes connected by narrative, semantic, and lexical edges.
Applies Energy-Driven Pathfinding to identify query-relevant subgraphs and deterministically linearize them into textual evidence paths.
Outperforms strong baselines across three multi-hop QA benchmarks, including 14.4% EM improvement on HotpotQA and 5.8% on 2WikiMultihop.
Reduces token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline; evaluation focuses on multi-hop QA benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) can produce visually plausible videos, yet their camera ego-motion often drifts over long horizons. Camera ego-motion determines how the viewpoint changes between frames and is essential for maintaining consistent geometry and trajectories. To address this problem, we propose CausalAlign, a causal alignment framework with two components. First, we diagnose how precise ego motion is represented, used, and retained within VGMs using linear probes and causal interventions, revealing a rise-and-fall pattern during denoising. Second, we strengthen ego-motion state in VGM by aligning the representations at the identified layers to a 3D foundation model through delta-token space. This space encodes the changes between consecutive frames, allowing the alignment to focus on ego-motion dynamics rather than static scene content. With Wan2.2 fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, CausalAlign can largely improve motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness, while preserving visual quality. For example, it improves geometric consistency by more than 20% relative to the base model. Moreover, with the fine-tuned VGM, CausalAlign improves the success rate of world action models (WAMs) by 10 points on mobile manipulation tasks of RoboCasa365 benchmark. Overall, CausalAlign improves ego-motion consistency in diffusion-based VGMs and yields noticeable gains in embodied models.
authors: Kai Zhu, Yintianrun Zhang, Shuwei Jiang, Ruolin Zuo, Yixin Chen, Duomin Wang, Miao Liu, Yin Li, Daquan Zhou, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Targets ego-motion drift, which harms geometric and trajectory consistency in generated videos.
Uses linear probes and causal interventions to locate where ego-motion is represented, used, and retained during denoising.
Aligns representations at identified layers in delta-token space, emphasizing frame-to-frame motion changes over static scene content.
Fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K with Wan2.2, it improves motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness while preserving visual quality.
The improved video model also raises world action model success rates on RoboCasa365 mobile-manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CausalAlign. Left: Existing approaches rely on external 3D caches that may propagate errors, optimize output-level preferences without directly supervising ego-motion states, or align 3D features at randomly selected layers. Middle: Our CausalAlign first identifies the targeted layers through causal diagnosis and then strengthens ego-motion states through delta-token alignment. Right: CausalAlign consistently improves camera ego-motion consistency in video generation and largely boosts downstream mobile manipulation performance.

Figure 3: Ego-motion diagnosis and retention. We compare base model Wan2.2 and our method CausalAlign through probe decodability and causal intervention effects across layers (sub-figure (a) & (b): results are averaged over timesteps) and across denoising timesteps (sub-figure (c) & (d): results are averaged over layers). Dashed vertical lines represent the selected alignment locations and shading shows the 10th–90th percentiles over the averaged dimension. Our method CausalAlign can raise both signals from rise-and-fall to rise-and-maintain pattern, indicating improved ego-motion retention.

Figure 2: Three stages of CausalAlign training. CausalAlign transfers ego-motion knowledge from a 3D teacher to the VGM through three-stage training. In Stage 1, consecutive features from a streaming 3D foundation model are encoded into a teacher delta-token space that captures inter-frame geometric transitions. In Stage 2, a projector maps VGM DiT features into the same delta-token space and is frozen after training, using a small subset of the training split. In Stage 3, with full training split, LoRA adapters are optimized only at the identified VGM layers using delta tokens, while the projector remains frozen.

Figure 5: Additional evidence for geometric state forgetting. (a) Linear and MLP probes both show a rise-and-fall pattern in ego-motion decodability. (b) Motion-only interventions produce substantially larger causal effects than norm-matched content-only controls. (c) Geometry commitment K(s) rises early and remains high, while the decodability D(s) and motion-specific causal effect C(s) reused from (a) and (b), respectively, decline during late denoising. Both probes and causal effects decline at later stages, while geometry commitment remains high, supporting the existence of geometric state forgetting.

Figure 6: Successful mobile manipulation rollouts. We visualize two policy rollouts on RoboCasa365, showing a robot placing a bowl into a refrigerator and moving a bread basket to a counter. Both examples demonstrate successful execution of mobile manipulation tasks.

Table 1: Camera ego-motion consistency. We evaluate videos generated from the DL3DV and RealEstate10K evaluation splits with the same estimators and generation settings. Methods without camera control receive the first frame and text prompt; methods that require control also receive camera trajectories and 3D caches. Bold indicates the best result for each metric. CausalAlign improves all seven metrics over Wan2.2 and leads on six of seven metrics.

Table 4: Delta-token ablations. We compare (a) semantic regions with matched-width PCA projections of equally supervised unpartitioned encoders and (b) 128D delta tokens with original 8192D/4096D LingBotMap features. Best values within each panel are bold. Delta tokens lead all six metrics in both panels.

Table 11: Effects of adapter updates and weight averaging. We evaluate different update configurations and weight averaging strategies on the 5B backbone, reporting improvements over the original model. Scaling the update at layer 22 to 0.25 achieves the highest mean gain of 0.769% among the compared configurations.

Table 3: Transfer to world action models. We report success rates (%) on the three RoboCasa365 Target100 task groups. Bold marks the best value in each column, including ties. CausalAlign improves Fast-WAM across all three groups, increasing average success from 43.5% to 54.2% and Atomic-Seen success by 19.0 percentage points.

Table 10: Effects of auxiliary motion objectives. We compare supervision using relative poses, motion dynamics, and their combination on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B under identical training settings. Relative pose supervision achieves the largest trajectory gain of 3.525%, while combining both objectives provides better geometric and temporal preservation.

Table 9: Effects of alignment placement and temporal modulation. We compare LoRA updates at different layer groups and strategies for temporal modulation on Wan2.2-14B, reporting composite gains with 95% confidence intervals. The layers selected by causal diagnosis achieve the largest gain of 3.109%, while the temporal modulation comparisons have confidence intervals that include zero.

Table 12: Effects of training objectives and configurations. We compare different objectives for motion, geometry, and appearance under various training configurations on the 5B backbone. Relative pose alignment at step 72 achieves the highest mean gain of 0.982% among the compared configurations.

Table 13: Training and evaluation settings for Fast-WAM. We summarize the training configuration and evaluation protocol for mobile manipulation on RoboCasa365 Target100. The protocol evaluates the policy on 18 Atomic-Seen tasks with 50 rollouts per task, providing the settings used to assess downstream performance.

Table 2: Visual quality preservation. We evaluate Wan2.2 and CausalAlign using VBench-I2V (quality, I2V score, and smoothness) together with FVD, CLIP, SSIM, and LPIPS. Bold indicates the best result for each metric, including ties. CausalAlign preserves visual quality comparable to Wan2.2.

Table 7: Camera trajectory accuracy under explicit conditioning. We compare CausalAlign with the native Wan2.2 camera control model and FantasyWorld using identical camera trajectories, initial frames, and text prompts. CausalAlign achieves the best results on six of seven metrics, while FantasyWorld has the lowest relative translation error.

Table 6: Ego-motion consistency in text-to-video generation. We evaluate Wan2.2-14B-T2V and CausalAlign using the same text prompts and geometric estimators. CausalAlign improves all seven metrics across motion magnitude, geometric consistency, and temporal dynamics.

Table 5: Visual quality in text-to-video generation. We compare Wan2.2-14B-T2V and CausalAlign using VBench and complementary visual metrics. CausalAlign improves quality, semantic score, FVD, and LPIPS while preserving smoothness, with slightly lower CLIP and SSIM scores.

Table 8: Specialization of delta-token regions. We evaluate the ego-motion, geometry, and visual regions using probes with a common dimension of 24 on 256 scenes across three seeds. Each region performs best on its corresponding task, demonstrating the effectiveness of semantic partitioning.

papers.abstract: Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438 staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects' falls (67% over all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at 160x120 with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the 9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt ("a person who goes out of view ... is not a fall") accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from 4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at 8x6 pixels (34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the model called a fall, its explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.
authors: Marcos Junca (Senecta Inc.), Mauro Junca (Senecta Inc.)
bullets: Evaluated Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.7 Flash as deployed decision stages using one request per short thermal clip, with audio when available.
On staged laboratory data, Gemini 3.8 Flash detected 69% of held-out-subject falls and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying down and rising.
In 76 hours of occupied-home footage, it produced no false calls and detected 4 of 9 visible staged falls; the reported upper bound was 1.2 false alarms per day.
Removing a prompt warning about people leaving view substantially increased sensitivity, but caused deliberate lie-downs to be labeled as falls.
Performance fell to 34% sensitivity at 8×6 pixels; identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows, while detected falls were temporally localized accurately.

Fig. 4: One staged fall (a slow backward faint) from the public laboratory data [6] (CC BY 4.0), in the colour map the model saw, seconds from the landing, at the sensor’s 32 × 24 and block-averaged to 16 × 12 and 8 × 6. The performer is back on their feet within six seconds.

Fig. 6: Each screener as one point: laboratory falls called (held-out subjects, Wilson 95% interval) against false fall calls per 24 h of ordinary living in the home (exact Poisson 95% interval). The conventional detectors were built on the laboratory data and run at 32 × 24.

Fig. 5: Effect of sensor resolution (block averaging, same field of view, same display size). (a) Laboratory falls and non-falls called a fall, held-out subjects, Wilson 95% intervals. (b) Home: visible staged falls called (of 9) and false calls on sampled ordinary-living clips.

Fig. 3: Laboratory falls called a fall, by fall type (all six subjects): Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.7 Flash with the deployed prompt (v8), and 3.7 Flash with v8 without its out-of-view sentence. Bed falls are shown but excluded from the other laboratory numbers.

Fig. 1: The prototype. A thermal camera and a microphone stream continuously; a wake gate combines sound and thermal movement; each wake becomes one short clip (3 s before, 15 s after, extended by further wakes); the clip is rendered as a video with its sound track and reviewed once by a multimodal LLM, which answers with a fixed JSON form. This paper evaluates the last two boxes.
TABLE II: The model’s answers, verbatim (deployed request; the laboratory answers’ opening “Audio is unavailable” is omitted). Chosen to illustrate each situation, not sampled.

TABLE I: Conditions, each changing one factor of the deployed request, and what each was run on: laboratory windows (all 1,001, or the 360 of the two held-out subjects) and home clips (the 395 ordinary-living clips, or the fixed sample of 73 of them, together with the 48 staged clips; or the staged clips alone). “–”: not run, or not finished when the paper was built. Gemini 3.5 Flash was run with the base request on 360 laboratory windows.

TABLE IV: The occupied home (160 × 120 with sound). False calls: ordinary-living clips called a fall, all of them false alarms, out of the clips reviewed (every clip for the deployed request on Gemini 3.8 Flash; a fixed 20% sample otherwise; “–” for the conditions run on the staged clips only). Visible: staged falls the camera saw, called. Occluded: staged falls whose landing the camera did not see, called. Clips that began with a person already on the floor, and deliberate lie-downs, are reported in the text.

TABLE III: Laboratory windows (eHomeSeniors, 32 × 24, no sound), 14 fall types (bed falls apart, Section VI-A). Falls called (%) for the two held-out subjects (n = 140) and for all six subjects (n = 414; “–” where a condition was run on the held-out subjects only), and non-fall windows called a fall (upright, recovery and rest windows together; all subjects, or held-out where only those were run).

TABLE V: The zero-shot model and two conventional detectors. Laboratory: held-out subjects, 14 fall types, falls and non-falls called (%). Home: visible staged falls called, ordinary-living clips called a fall (all false alarms), and occluded staged falls called. The detectors run at 32 × 24 and were built on the laboratory data.
TABLE VI: Test–retest at temperature 0: the deployed request sent twice to the same model. Agreement (%), Cohen’s κ and the number of windows or clips whose verdict flipped.

papers.title: Asking a Multimodal LLM Whether Someone Fell: Zero-Shot Screening of Low-Resolution Thermal Video in a Laboratory and an Occupied Home
papers.tldr: A zero-shot multimodal LLM screened low-resolution thermal clips with no false alarms in tested ordinary home activity, but its fall sensitivity depended strongly on prompt wording, resolution, and whether falls went out of view.

papers.abstract: Learning across medical imaging modalities requires making use of images without paired text and accommodating new domains while retaining existing representations. We propose a medical vision-language technique built around an expandable bank of modality experts. Its Multiway Transformer combines shared visual computation with deterministically routed feed-forward experts and a separate text pathway. A modality-aware visual tokenizer supplies targets for masked pretraining on 19.4 million unpaired image rows across seven modalities; contrastive alignment then uses 3.23 million image-text pairs. Additional fundus and optical coherence tomography experts learn from paired data while the original image and text embedding paths remain frozen. With a ViT-Large backbone, the proposed technique achieves the best or tied-best result in 24 of 25 benchmark settings across nine modalities: 10 of 11 zero-shot classification benchmarks, all 10 linear probes, and all four retrieval benchmarks. Mean balanced accuracy is 0.674 for zero-shot classification and 0.856 for linear probing, and mean bidirectional retrieval recall is 20.70%. A separate three-seed sequential experiment with matched adaptation data yields fundus and OCT retrieval gains of 14.95 and 9.31 percentage points, with no measured loss on preceding fundus or pathology tasks. The preservation argument requires unchanged existing computation paths and inference conditions, and feature-identity checks verify retention on evaluated inputs. The proposed technique provides a modular approach to learning and expanding medical vision-language representations.
authors: DM BAPPY, Eunsu Kim, Hanjoo Lee, Sung Hak Lee, Sangjeong Ahn
bullets: Addresses unpaired multimodal medical images and continual adaptation to new domains without disrupting prior capabilities.
Uses a Multiway Transformer with shared visual computation, deterministically routed modality experts, a separate text pathway, and a modality-aware visual tokenizer.
Pretrains on 19.4M unpaired image rows across seven modalities, then aligns vision and language using 3.23M image-text pairs.
Achieves the best or tied-best performance in 24 of 25 benchmarks across nine modalities, including zero-shot classification, linear probing, and retrieval.
Sequential fundus and OCT adaptation improves retrieval by 14.95 and 9.31 percentage points, with no measured loss on preceding evaluated tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Proposed technique: pipeline, training data, and evaluation breadth. (a) A modality-aware tokenizer supplies discrete targets for masked pretraining; contrastive alignment then connects the separate image and text pathways. New modalities use paired data to train new routed experts while existing paths remain frozen. (b) Each spoke is a source dataset grouped by modality. On a shared log10 scale, wide bars show Stage-1 image rows and narrow bars show Stage-2 pairs; fundus and OCT use paired data only. The core pair count is approximately 17% of the masked-pretraining image-row count. (c) Raw mean performance by modality across applicable task families, with retrieval percentages divided by 100. Each axis uses its own range; markers are data and curves are visual guides.

Figure 2: Learning new modalities while retaining existing capabilities. Models use 20,000 fundus pairs followed by 16,000 OCT pairs. Left: fundus learning and retention. Middle: OCT learning. Right: retention on Derm7pt. Points show mean bidirectional recall and error bars show standard deviation across three training seeds. Baselines use LoRA; the proposed technique trains new experts with existing pathways frozen. This experiment uses training subsets, not the full training corpus.

Figure 3: PathGen retention through fundus–OCT adaptation. Mean bidirectional Recall@{1, 10, 50} at the base checkpoint, after fundus, and after OCT. Baseline error bars show standard deviation over three seeds. The proposed technique’s independently trained experts leave the pathology pathway unchanged. Training history, data exposure, and adaptation capacity differ between the proposed technique and the sequentialLoRA baselines.

Figure 8: Additional CT-Kidney qualitative example. This is a zero-shot classification example, not a retrieval example, and it is not included in Table 13. We show the top three predictions among four classes (kidney cyst, stone, tumor, and normal kidney) for the same query before and after integration. Baseline results use seed 0. Green marks the ground-truth class (cyst). Its rank is: the proposed technique 1 → 1; BMC 1→ 3; BMCA 1→ 3; ConceptCLIP 1→ 2; UniMed-CLIP 1→ 4. At the original checkpoint, every model ranks the ground-truth class first. After adaptation, the rank decreases for every baseline on this query. However, on the full CT-Kidney benchmark, BMCA’s mean balanced accuracy improves after adaptation. CT-Kidney is a separate zero-shot evaluation and is not the ROCO-CT retrieval benchmark in Table 13. This difference shows why a single example should not be used to infer aggregate performance.

Figure 11: Qualitative saliency across nine modalities. Similarity-gradient Grad-CAM through each modality’s routed expert; top row original, bottom row saliency. Left to right: pneumonia, renal tumour, thyroid nodule, glioma on FLAIR with the ground-truth box, macular scar, colorectal polyp, macular edema on OCT, melanocytic lesion, and malignant gland on H&E. Fundus and OCT use experts added to a frozen model.
