papers.abstract: Geometric structure is essential for robotic manipulation and understanding the 3D world. Most VLA models rely on 2D representations of current observations, while geometry-aware approaches often require additional 3D information. However, geometry inferred independently from individual observations is often discarded rather than accumulated into a persistent task representation. Our key insight is that action generation needs a compact, task-relevant geometric abstraction that can be continuously updated, rather than a complete, renderable 3D reconstruction at every step. We introduce GeoMem-VLA, a VLA framework that internalizes explicit 3D supervision into dedicated geometric tokens and maintains them as temporal memory for action generation, without directly aligning the VLM's native visual embeddings with the teacher feature space. During training, a frozen geometry foundation model supervises learnable GeoPlan tokens through a geometric flow-matching objective over the current scene point map and future end-effector tracks. These tokens are integrated with the memory of observation representations, where historical information is retrieved, adaptively fused with current observations, and consolidated to retain event frames as the task progresses. At inference, the policy retrieves historical representations and fuses them with the current working representation to predict actions, without invoking the 3D teacher or explicitly reconstructing the scene. After benchmark-specific downstream adaptation, GeoMem-VLA achieves 98.9% average success on LIBERO and 91.10% / 91.24% on RoboTwin's clean/randomized settings. Across five real-world tasks, GeoMem-VLA achieves 78.0% average success. These results suggest that internalizing and remembering 3D scene understanding is a promising approach to robot control.
authors: Qinfan Zhang, Yifan Luo, Haoyuan Shi, Guanlin Liu, Han Dong, Haozhe Shan, Yong Dai, Xiangcong Ren, Xiaozhu Ju
bullets: Addresses the loss of accumulated geometric information in VLA models that primarily use current 2D observations.
Learns dedicated GeoPlan tokens from frozen geometry-model supervision over scene point maps and future end-effector tracks.
Retrieves, fuses, and consolidates geometric and visual memories across time without requiring 3D reconstruction or the teacher model at inference.
Reports 98.9% average success on LIBERO, 91.10%/91.24% on RoboTwin clean/randomized settings, and 78.0% across five real-world tasks.
Scope: performance depends on benchmark-specific downstream adaptation and is evaluated on the reported simulation and real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: How do diffusion transformers (DiTs) represent image content and learn rules for reusing it to generalize? We develop an aggregator--predictor view of DiTs as input-adaptive local denoisers, in which context aggregation and patch prediction provide functional roles for interpreting attention and MLPs. We first establish that, for Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) priors, the global Bayes denoiser can be approximated using only a subset of context patches, with error decaying exponentially in context radius. We further show that patchwise linear denoisers, often invoked to explain diffusion generalization, recover the empirical local denoiser with sufficiently informative aggregation. Within this view, AdaLN-modulated attention naturally parameterizes an input- and noise-dependent aggregator, while the MLP admits a learned key--value representation for tokenwise patch prediction. Our experiments support this view. DiTs trained on real images exhibit noise-dependent denoising contexts resembling those in the analytic GMRF setting, while attention mass exhibits a qualitatively corresponding broadening pattern. In a controlled CelebA64 study, shared-memory patch predictors used in place of DiT MLPs achieve competitive denoising and generative performance. Finally, cross-dataset component transplantation reveals compatibility patterns consistent with the proposed roles of QK in spatial weighting, VO in feature transport, and MLPs in patch prediction. Together, these results provide a component-level account of DiT denoising and motivate architecture-specific fine-tuning and controlled intervention.
authors: Gyeonghun Kang, William Xingxu Chen, Xiang Cheng
bullets: Models DiTs as local denoisers that aggregate relevant context patches and predict clean patches.
Shows that, for GMRF priors, near-optimal denoising can use a limited context whose approximation error decreases exponentially with context radius.
Interprets AdaLN-modulated attention as a noise- and input-dependent aggregator, and MLPs as learned key–value patch predictors.
Experiments on real images, CelebA64, and component transplantation support these functional roles and identify QK with spatial weighting and VO with feature transport.
The findings motivate architecture-specific fine-tuning and controlled component interventions.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced.
authors: Samuel Foo Enze, Manthan Patel, Fan Yang, Linus Kramer, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
bullets: Addresses sample-inefficient RL learning from panoramic LiDAR under sparse rewards and the memory cost of existing 3D encoders.
Uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to process wide-angle LiDAR range images and handle azimuthal seams.
Pretrains on synthetic data with range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and BEV prediction, then freezes the encoder for policy learning.

Semantic and BEV supervision improve success rates by 32.03 percentage points in procedural training environments and 23.73 points in realistic out-of-distribution tests versus reconstruction-only pretraining.
Zero-shot real-world deployments demonstrate navigation in dense crowds, low light, and construction zones.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: System overview. (a) A mobile robot observes the environment with LiDAR, odometry, and proprioception. (b) The LiDAR scan is projected into a panoramic range image. (c) Our pretrained encoder compresses the range image into a spatial latent for the navigation policy. (d) During pretraining, task-aligned decoders supervise range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird’seye-view (BEV) prediction. (e) The frozen encoder transfers to realworld navigation in dynamic environments, construction sites, and low-light environments without real-world training.

Fig. 3: Pretraining and policy architecture. (a) The encoder compresses the range image into a spatial latent that three decoder heads read in parallel: range reconstruction, per-return semantic segmentation, and privileged BEV occupancy and ground height. A fully connected bottleneck precedes the BEV deconvolutions, mapping the polar latent onto the Cartesian grid. Insets detail the depthwise-separable encoder block and the transposed-convolution decoder block. All heads are discarded after pretraining. (b) The frozen encoder feeds attention over noisy proprioception and the relative goal into the recurrent SRU policy that predicts the action.

Fig. 4: Simulation environments. (a) Maze, (b) stairs, (c) pits, (d) side wall, (e) Gascola, (f) ModernCityDowntown (City), (g) AbandonedCable (Cable), and (h) dynamic obstacles, where the orange cylinders are moving pedestrians. For the results in Table I, the environments in the blue box (a)–(c) are examples of the environments used for RL training, whereas all environments are used for evaluation.

(a) Six dense depth views are fused in 3D and projected onto the target spherical LiDAR grid, then corrupted with noise and random masking to form the encoder input. (b) A similar approach generates the semantic target from segmented images. (c) The privileged BEV occupancy and ground-height target is rendered from the scene mesh.

Fig. 5: Representative LiDAR (blue) and depth (orange) policy trajectories. (a) The depth policy detours into a dead end before recovering, whereas the LiDAR policy recognizes it earlier and takes a direct route. (b) The depth policy repeatedly revisits the same local clutter, whereas the LiDAR policy escapes and reaches the goal.

papers.tldr: RangeNav is a compact LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained with navigation-aligned tasks to improve robot navigation in crowded and cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: Large language models are typically trained with next-token prediction (NTP), which rewards predicting specific tokens rather than explicitly accounting for the semantic similarities between different words or expressions. Prior work has addressed this limitation by augmenting training data with minimally varying sentences that replace a target word with conceptually related alternatives, e.g., "The tired coach ran home" $\rightarrow$ {"The tired trainer ran home", "The tired instructor ran home", ...}. Such concept augmentation improves performance, but it remains unclear whether its effectiveness depends on where in the sentence the concept is expressed. We reproduce and extend prior work $\textit{beyond nouns}$ to verbs and adjectives, asking whether the part of speech (POS) carrying the concept signal affects perplexity and downstream performance. We find different patterns across evaluation settings: concept augmentation improves perplexity most consistently on news, independent of the POS used, whereas verbs provide the most reliable downstream gains. Despite these behavioral differences, representational analyses using CKA and linear probing show that the conditions yielding the largest downstream gains are not necessarily those that most alter the model's internal representations. Together, these results suggest that the effectiveness of concept augmentation depends on where and how conceptual information is introduced during training.
bullets: Extends prior concept-augmentation work beyond nouns to verbs and adjectives to study part-of-speech effects.
Concept augmentation most consistently improves perplexity on news across POS conditions.
Verb-based augmentation provides the most reliable downstream performance gains.
CKA and linear-probing analyses show that representation changes do not necessarily predict downstream improvements.
Results suggest that both the location and form of conceptual information matter during post-training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the concept-augmentation and evaluation pipeline. Datapoints are drawn from arXiv, news, YouTube, or the combined corpus, and target words are selected by part of speech. For each POS condition, training data are either left unchanged (vanilla) or augmented with context-aware or dictionary-based synonym or hypernym substitutions. Each resulting corpus is used to further train Llama-3-8B with the standard next-token prediction objective, producing 96 post-trained models, which are subsequently evaluated through LoRA-based fine-tuning on seven downstream classification tasks.

Figure 8: Reproducibility check against the noun-only experiments of Iyer et al. (2026). Comparison of the original results with our noun-based conditions. Left: perplexity, colored by post-training corpus. Right: downstream accuracy, colored by task. The diagonal indicates identical performance. Our pipeline recovers the same broad trends, with small differences due to data reprocessing and the revised downstream fine-tuning procedure.

Figure 4: Change in language-model quality against change in downstream performance, each measured relative to the model’s own vanilla counterpart. Each point is one post-trained model; the x-axis is the reduction in perplexity averaged over the four evaluation corpora, and the y-axis is the gain in accuracy averaged over the seven downstream tasks. Points in the shaded upper-right quadrant improved on both measures. Marker shape and colour denote the substituted POS; filled markers are hypernym substitution and open markers denote synonym substitution. The correlation is r = +0.38 (p = 0.033) for context augmentation and r = +0.30 (p = 0.096) for dictionary augmentation.

Figure 3: The effect of concept augmentation on perplexity depends on both post-training corpus and POS. Perplexity improvement of concept-augmented models relative to their matched vanilla baselines, separated by post-training corpus. Positive values indicate lower perplexity after augmentation. Points show context-aware and dictionary-based augmentation for nouns (N), verbs (V), adjectives (Adj), and all three parts of speech (ALL); dotted horizontal lines show the mean improvement for each corpus. Augmentation improves perplexity most consistently when post-trained on news (+5.5%), while it decreases performance on arXiv (−8.2%). The relative effect of each POS also changes substantially across corpora.

Figure 9: Absolute perplexity across post-training and evaluation corpora. Each panel corresponds to one post-training corpus, and the x-axis denotes the evaluation corpus. Co lor denotes the augmented POS. Solid lines show concept-augmented models and dotted lines show their corresponding vanilla conditions. Values are averaged across synonym and hypernym settings.

Figure 1: Illustration of POS-specific concept augmentation. For the same input sentence, we generate synonym and hypernym substitutions using either context-aware or dictionary-based concept extraction. Rows show augmentation applied to nouns, verbs, adjectives, or all three POS categories together.

Figure 5: Downstream effects depend on both the augmented POS and evaluation task. (a) Mean accuracy change relative to the matched vanilla baseline for each semantic-relation×corpus×POS condition, averaged over the seven downstream tasks and the context-aware and dictionary-based variants. Positive values indicate improvement over vanilla; outlined cells mark the best POS within each row. Verbs achieve the strongest mean performance in six of the eight settings. (b) Range of accuracy changes across augmentation conditions for each downstream task. GLUE, SNLI, and Logical Fallacy are substantially more sensitive to the augmentation choice than Spam, Hate Speech, and Emotion.

Figure 6: POS affects when downstream fine-tuning stops. Mean standardized stopping point across downstream tasks, grouped by the POS augmented during post-training. Adjective-augmented models stop significantly earlier than all-POS models (p = 0.001), indicating that the breadth of the concept signal affects downstream convergence.

Figure 7: Post-training corpus affects early finetuning speed. Standardized accuracy gain between fine-tuning steps 250 and 500, grouped by post-training corpus. Models post-trained on the combined corpus improve significantly faster over the first interval than models post-trained on YouTube (p = 0.004).

Table 1: Downstream accuracy change by augmented POS. Mean accuracy change in percentage points relative to matched vanilla models, separated by semantic relation, post-training corpus, and augmented POS. Context-aware and dictionary-based variants are averaged. Bold denotes the strongest POS within each relation-corpus condition. Verb augmentation is strongest in six of the eight conditions.

Table 2: Downstream accuracy change by augmentation source. Mean accuracy change in percentage points relative to matched vanilla models, separated by semantic relation, post-training corpus, and concept source. Results are averaged across POS conditions and downstream tasks. Bold denotes the stronger source within each row.

Table 6: Mean POS-probe accuracy change relative to the untouched base model. Values are percentagepoint changes averaged over POS targets, corpora, and semantic relations. All three variants become more POSdecodable in later layers, including the matched vanilla models.

Table 4: Concept-specific change in POS-probe accuracy relative to matched vanilla models. Values are percentage-point differences between the concept-augmented and matched vanilla probe accuracies. All-POS augmentation shows the clearest positive concept-specific effect, particularly for dictionary-based augmentation. These entries are differences of point estimates; bootstrap confidence intervals in the probe analysis are defined relative to the untouched base model rather than for the concept-minus-vanilla contrast.

papers.abstract: General-purpose robots must handle tasks, objects and environments they were never trained on, yet zero-shot generalization remains one of the least solved problems in physical AI. In digital AI, zero-shot capability grew with the volume and, above all, the diversity of training data, much of it sourced from the crowd. Robotics instead relies on paid collection by a few well-funded teams, which yields volume without diversity. We formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, and show that more samples from the same collectors shrink the unseen region only slowly, while each new contributor can extend it. Building on this and on zero-shot learning, we propose a shared latent space for robot actions that combines multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label learning. As a scalable source of diverse data, we propose a community of developers building applications on one standard, approachable robot, Origami. We close with a testable hypothesis and an evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data.
bullets: Frames zero-shot physical-AI generalization as coverage of the deployment distribution.
Argues that repeated samples from the same collectors reduce the unseen region slowly, while new contributors can expand coverage.
Proposes a shared latent space for robot actions using multimodal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label learning.
Introduces a community-driven data strategy centered on applications built for the approachable Origami robot.
Provides a testable hypothesis and evaluation protocol linking real-robot zero-shot success to contributed-data diversity.

papers.abstract: Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives; coding agents keep the raw history and let the model search it with its own tools. We ask whether designed memory still helps once the model is strong enough to search for itself. On one LoCoMo conversation (419 turns, 152 questions), we run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code), each with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5, and record what every rollout costs. This is a short empirical study, with one conversation and one run per cell. Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model: Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than a whole full-context rollout. Agent memory also has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it: a stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out. With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the cost-accuracy frontier, scoring 99% for less than half the cost of full context; its one miss is a wrong answer key. Part of that lead comes from photo captions that only the agents could read: on the 88 questions whose evidence has no photo, Pi and full context differ by one answer.
bullets: Evaluates full context, BM25, Mem0, and Zep across three coding agents and three language models on one 419-turn conversation with 152 questions.
Mem0 improves over full context only for GPT-4o-mini, while constructing its memory costs more than a full-context rollout.
Memory quality is limited by the model that writes it; a stronger reader cannot recover information omitted by a weaker writer.
With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi achieves 99% accuracy for under half the cost of full context.
The study uses one conversation and one run per experimental cell; Pi’s advantage partly comes from reading photo captions unavailable to other methods.

papers.abstract: Compositional zero-shot learning (CZSL) aims to recognize novel combinations of previously observed objects and attributes. Prior work showed that large-scale vision-language models encode decomposable semantic structures that can be recomposed to enable generalization. The Geodesically Decomposable Embeddings (GDE) framework formalizes this by identifying directions in the tangent space at the Frechet mean of the embedding distribution, which encode primitive visual concepts. Unseen attribute-object compositions can be synthesized through vector addition of these primitives. We revisit the assumption that compositional generalization requires explicit attribute-object pair re-composition. By means of new compositional scoring functions and extensive evaluations, we show that directly using the decomposed primitives suffices for recognizing unseen compositions. In that, we gain insights on how the geometry of the embedding manifold (Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic) and dataset structure affect compositional reasoning. Across models (CLIP, DINOv2, MERU, HyCoCLIP), we show that compositional structure consistently emerges as primitive representations, enabling inference on CZSL benchmarks (MIT-States, VAW-CZSL, UT-Zappos50K, Clothing16K) and group robustness on Waterbirds and CelebA. Code: https://github.com/nis-research/Compositionality-with-Primitives.
authors: Puru Vaish, Meelad Dashti, Christoph Brune, Pascal Mettes, Tatiana Tommasi, Nicola Strisciuglio
bullets: Reexamines whether explicit recomposition of attribute-object pairs is necessary for compositional generalization.
Introduces new compositional scoring functions that directly use decomposed primitives.
Analyzes how Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic geometry and dataset structure influence compositional reasoning.
Finds consistent primitive-based compositional structure across CLIP, DINOv2, MERU, and HyCoCLIP.
Demonstrates inference on four CZSL benchmarks and group robustness on Waterbirds and CelebA.

papers.abstract: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce DeepEvolve, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley--Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth.
authors: Zhipeng Chen, Yunsen Liang, Yanxi Chen, Hongkang Zhao, Lingyun Feng, Ruiyang Ren, Guoxin Chen, Jia Deng, Feng Chang, Chuan Hao, Ran Tao, Jian Yang, Ji-Rong Wen, Bryan Dai, Wayne Xin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of AI systems with frozen parameters that rely on external updates.
Uses future-event prediction in a living environment that continuously generates verifiable tasks.
Feeds prediction reasoning back into capability through search–prediction decoupling, parameter-level evolution, and reusable skill distillation.
Ranked first on the external FutureX leaderboard for three consecutive weeks, with up to a 195% rating improvement.
Placed among the top three across four base LLMs on synthesized evaluation, exceeding the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley–Terry points.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of DEEPEVOLVE for recursive self-improvement in real-world event forecasting. a, The closed loop connects question generation, forecasting, and evolution, with resolved outcomes supplying verifiable rewards and updates feeding into subsequent rounds. b, PROMETHEUS generates questions through templates and agent-driven discovery, followed by temporal validation, deduplication, conflict detection, and diversity-aware selection. c, BRANCHUS separates evidence gathering, by a search team of a scheduler, searcher, and critic, from probabilistic prediction, by a predict team. The search team is time-sensitive, as its result depends on when it runs, while the predict team is time-invariant, reasoning only over the search team’s cached evidence and reasoning trajectories. Both teams retrieve relevant forecasting skills. d, ATHENA updates the predict team’s parameters using cached evidence and verifiable rewards, distills search trajectories into reusable forecasting skills, and converts observed weaknesses into task-synthesis skills for PROMETHEUS. Resolved outcomes inform parameter and environment updates but are withheld from the behavior-level judge.

papers.abstract: Understanding and modeling light transport in human-centric scenes is a longstanding challenge. While recent progress in diffusion models has boosted research in relighting, precise illumination control still lags, primarily due to the scarcity of diverse, high-quality, precisely labeled video relighting datasets. Existing end-to-end relighting approaches model light transport implicitly through neural networks, which substantially complicates controllability. In contrast, some works resort to path-traced irradiance cues as an explicit blueprint for light transport. However, such constructed irradiance cues are prone to artifacts and hinder generative quality when directly used as control signals. With the key observation that noise corruption removes high-frequency artifacts and preserves low-frequency light transport, we introduce an asynchronous joint-modeling paradigm that facilitates fine-grained illumination control. During two-stage training, we force the model to jointly denoise RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames with separate timesteps scheduling. A domain matching strategy is applied to the second stage to bridge the domain gap between irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps. At inference time, we introduce an asynchronous hijacked generation pipeline that facilitates flexible illumination control. For training data, we develop a multi-illumination high-quality synthetic video dataset with paired irradiance maps using a powerful game engine. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model exhibits robust generalization to real- world scenarios and outperforms prior approaches in both lighting fidelity and generative quality. The code and dataset will be publicly released.
authors: Henglei Lv, Bailin Deng, Xiaoqiang Liu, Yichen Wang, Haoxian Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Lin Gao
bullets: Addresses limited high-quality, precisely labeled video-relighting data and poor controllability in implicit light-transport models.

papers.abstract: Vision-language perception has achieved impressive progress in aligning natural language with visual observations, yet grounding high-level semantics into part-level physical interaction remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose UniRAP, a unified model for inferring part-level physical affordances and mapping language instructions to actionable geometric representations. UniRAP formulates this problem as a conditional multimodal generation task, integrating visual inputs, textual instructions, and optional prompts into a shared spatiotemporal representation space through a unified interface token mechanism. To predict executable contact geometry, we introduce a Unified Affordance Decoder (UAD), which jointly performs object detection, part-level affordance segmentation, and 4-DoF interaction pose estimation by leveraging intermediate segmentation features. In addition, we propose a curriculum-based transfer training strategy that progressively adapts the model from general visual parsing to interaction-aware perception, improving data efficiency under limited textual annotations. Experiments show that UniRAP achieves state-of-the-art performance on referring expression segmentation, affordance grounding, and interaction pose estimation, while maintaining strong spatiotemporal consistency in dynamic video scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of UniRAP as a unified perception framework for language-guided physical manipulation.
authors: Linfei Li, Ruining Hu, Lin Zhang, Zhong Wang, Fengyi Zhang, Ying Shen, Binqiang Wang, Xin Zhang

Applies curriculum-based transfer training to improve data efficiency with limited textual annotations.
Reports state-of-the-art results across referring-expression segmentation, affordance grounding, and interaction-pose estimation, with strong spatiotemporal consistency in dynamic videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of UniRAP Model. Given visual input xv, text prompt xt, and optional visual reference prompts xr, a multimodal model F produces <SEG>-conditioned outputs. Concurrently, visual features from xv are aggregated with memory bank representations via memory attention. The resulting features are aligned with <SEG>derived embeddings through an MLP projector and decoded by an affordance decoder D to generate segmentation masks, region detections, and 4-DoF interaction poses for unified vision–language spatiotemporal actionable perception.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is one of the few practical tools available for overseeing capable AI systems, but it is fragile: a model's reasoning is only useful to a monitor if it remains coupled to what the model actually does. This coupling can be degraded during training through, for example, CoT compression, optimization against a monitor, and out-of-context generalization from synthetic documents. In this work, we propose an unsupervised post-training objective based on maximizing mutual information between CoT and the output for improving CoT monitorability. Across three model organisms with degraded CoT, it recovers most or all of the lost monitorability. Applied to undegraded policies, it further improves judged monitorability, improves prediction of unsafe behavior by CoT monitors and activation probes, and increases the prevalence of consequential reasoning. These results suggest that monitorability should be treated as a trainable attribute of the policy. A dedicated monitorability post-training stage can extend current practices that protect CoT from direct optimization pressure.
authors: Usman Anwar, Tim Bakker, Christos Louizos, David Krueger
bullets: CoT monitoring is fragile when reasoning becomes decoupled from the model’s actual behavior.
The proposed objective maximizes mutual information between CoT and outputs.
Across three degraded model organisms, the method recovers most or all lost monitorability.
For undegraded policies, it improves judged monitorability and prediction of unsafe behavior by monitors and activation probes.
It also increases consequential reasoning, suggesting monitorability is a trainable policy attribute.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers are widely used in image-editing services. To preserve both efficiency and privacy, existing systems commonly rely on cloud-device collaboration. Keeping request-specific inference on the device avoids sending personal images and prompts to the cloud. These workloads often use common templates, such as in face swapping and virtual try-on, enabling KV state to be precomputed and reused across requests. However, this reusable state is large and scales with the number of templates, making it impractical to store all of them on mobile devices. Storing them in the cloud addresses this capacity issue, but cache transfer is placed onto the inference path and can even be slower than on-device computation, especially under fluctuating mobile networks. We introduce SAKURA, a cloud-edge architecture that delivers reusable attention state to mobile devices under a bandwidth budget. It first uses a fine-grained token-importance-aware compression method to preserve image quality under limited transfer budgets. At runtime, SAKURA adaptively selects the cache representation for each upcoming shard based on network bandwidth. To enable efficient execution, we develop a pipelined runtime that overlaps cache transfer and reconstruction with on-device execution. We evaluate SAKURA using three editing tasks and two diffusion models, using a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone. SAKURA reduces latency by 1.82x and 3.27x over CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively. It also reduces cache storage by 3.06x over uncompressed cache, while preserving image quality.
authors: Shuncheng Jie, Desen Sun, Ri Hong, Yuyang Tian, Hong Zhang, Sihang Liu
bullets: Targets cloud-device image editing where request-specific inference stays on the phone for privacy, but reusable KV caches are too large to store locally.

Reports 1.82× and 3.27× lower latency than CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively, with 3.06× lower cache storage than uncompressed caches while preserving image quality.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.
authors: Johannes Keller, Albrecht M. Blo{\ss}e, Adrian Lindenmeyer, Thomas Neumuth, Daniel Schneider
bullets: Targets costly failures by identifying situations where a VLA policy lacks training knowledge.

Vision-language backbone heads reduce uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately 50× versus ensemble scores and lower setup costs.

papers.abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.
authors: Ido Levy, Segev Shlomov, Leshem Choshen
bullets: Introduces LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled, compositional RAG evaluation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promising reasoning capabilities, but reliable physical interaction requires planning that accounts for when actions are executable and how they change the world. These preconditions and effects are environment-dependent and often not captured by MLLMs, making adaptation challenging. Yet existing approaches either require costly environment-specific training or rely on unstructured interaction experience that is difficult to reuse. Therefore, we introduce CausGround, a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework that distills interaction experience into reusable action-centered causal knowledge. CausGround identifies action preconditions and effects and organizes them in a factorized world-state representation capturing object attributes and inter-object relations. At planning time, task-relevant causal dependencies are grounded in current observations to support backward reasoning over preconditions and forward reasoning over effects for action selection and multi-step planning. We evaluate CausGround on simulated high-level planning, interaction reasoning, and real-world robot manipulation. On adapted VirtualHome and RoboCasa benchmarks, CausGround improves vision-based high-level planning across MLLM backbones, increasing average task success from 24.9% to 53.3% on VirtualHome and closed-loop planning success from 43.0% to 57.0% on RoboCasa. On SWITCH, average interaction reasoning accuracy increases from 25.8% to 31.9%, indicating improved action selection, recovery, and verification. Moreover, real-world experiments show that CausGround reasons backward from MLLM-interpreted goals to derive executable high-level action sequences for sequential manipulation. These results demonstrate that reusable action preconditions and effects support long-horizon embodied planning across diverse environments without parameter updates.
authors: Yijun Shen, Diqi He, Jinbang Guo, Wanyue Zhang, Jiaming Mi, Huan Yang, Zhongyuan Wang, Zhiwei Yu, Kai Zhang

papers.abstract: Large-scale aerial resources provide a foundation for learning navigation across diverse environments. However, existing resources remain limited in providing (1) densely sampled flight demonstrations for learning different policy formulations and (2) broad environment coverage for standardized closed-loop evaluation. To address these limitations, we introduce AirPlayground, a unified benchmark for training and evaluating aerial navigation policies across diverse environments. We first construct 94 photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) environments spanning indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation settings, with aligned collision geometry. Building on these environments, we develop a scene-adaptive pipeline for automated expert flight collection, yielding 94K demonstrations and 46.5M synchronized observation-state-action samples at 50 Hz. We further provide an extensible API that supports training different policy formulations on this shared corpus and evaluating them under unified protocols in the corresponding environments. We benchmark seven baselines spanning four policy paradigms across three navigation settings in seen and unseen environments, and further examine scaling behavior with ACT. Scaling ACT's training corpus from 5 to 70 scenes raises median success rates on seen and unseen environments from 30.6% and 16.8% to 41.2% and 29.4%, respectively. Through this shared training and evaluation framework, AirPlayground supports analysis of how offline prediction errors relate to closed-loop outcomes. Our analyses highlight the roles of prediction errors, execution protocols, and scene interactions in closed-loop performance.

papers.abstract: During steady pouring, images and robot pose may remain nearly unchanged while transferred mass accumulates, making the return decision ambiguous for a whole-task vision-language-action (VLA) policy. We present FlowVLA, which separates motor generation from physical-completion estimation. A shared $\pi_{0.5}$ action expert learns approach, pour, and return with boundary-aware supervision. A target-independent estimator fuses visual, joint, wrist-wrench, and recurrent force-belief histories to maintain an estimate of transferred mass. The controller initiates return when this estimate plus predicted residual outflow reaches the requested mass. In coffee-pot/water experiments, FlowVLA achieves 13.1 g goal-balanced mean absolute error (MacroMAE), lower than all tested VLA baselines. Across all attempts, 53.7% both complete the task and finish within +/-10% of the requested mass. The same model interpolates to held-out 150/250-g targets without retraining. Independently trained models further evaluate the formulation in three additional container-fluid settings.

papers.abstract: Generative image compression (GIC) delivers strong perceptual quality at low bitrates. However, GIC methods with strong perceptual quality often rely on pretrained diffusion models with high latency, while recent lightweight GIC methods reduce latency but deliver lower perceptual quality. We observe that, for lightweight GIC methods at low bitrates, coarse deterministic quantization can collapse nearby encoder latents corresponding to different fine details to the same point, making these details difficult to recover. Motivated by this, we propose GR-GIC, an efficient GIC that delivers competitive reconstruction performance with fast inference. For better performance, we introduce Guided Refinement (GR), which combines latent refinement guided by entropy context with adaptive perturbations for training regularization, jointly improving reconstruction at low bitrates. For fast inference, we introduce reorganized projected residual vector quantization (P-RVQ), which equivalently reorganizes residual updates into low-dimensional lookups to expose greater parallelism and reduce sequential computation. Experiments on Kodak show that for performance, compared with OneDC, GR-GIC achieves BD-rate savings of 23.19%, 37.71%, 22.30%, and 22.14% for LPIPS, DISTS, PSNR, and FID, respectively. For fast inference, the highly optimized implementation of GR-GIC encodes and decodes in 4.60 and 5.98 ms on an NVIDIA A100. Specifically, the reorganized P-RVQ implementation achieves a $3.14\times$ average speedup over the original implementation under the same FP32 setting. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, GR-GIC achieves latency comparable to lightweight GIC methods.
authors: Hao Cao, Yinhuan Huang, Wenqi Guo, Zhijin Qin, Jungong Han

(c) GR uses entropy context to define a Gaussian refinement distribution around the recovered latent and introduces adaptive perturbations during training. (d) GR-GIC combines competitive reconstruction performance with fast inference.

papers.abstract: Large pretrained models such as CLIP are widely used as frozen feature extractors. However, their embeddings inherit spurious correlations from training data, introducing bias into the features. A growing body of research has sought to address this issue through post hoc debiasing, leaving the backbone untouched. We discover that despite differing mechanisms, these methods require the bias feature to be identified and expressed in text. This dependency is not innocuous. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate that this requirement incurs an unforeseen penalty in certain scenarios. For example, on the UrbanCars benchmark, having two co-occurring bias attributes, the recent methods underperform a vanilla classifier on biased frozenbackbone features, and even providing ground-truth bias identities does not close the gap. We show that the pattern that such methods seek is readily observable in the frozen geometry. Specifically, cross-class training pairs placed closest together by the frozen encoder almost always share a spurious attribute, regardless of the bias type, without requiring access to the bias labels. Based on this, we propose a novel approach to identify such pairs and learn a single linear map that transforms the features to perform post-hoc debiasing. The proposed approach achieves competitive performance across all datasets without access to bias attribute annotations or any LLMs.
authors: Divyaansh Mertia, Chirag Bhutra, Himanshu Shekhar, Shubham Bagwari, Pratik Mazumder
bullets: Existing post-hoc methods depend on identifying and expressing bias features in text.
This dependency can hurt performance: on UrbanCars, recent methods underperform a vanilla classifier, even with ground-truth bias identities.
Cross-class pairs that are closest in frozen embedding space usually share a spurious attribute, across bias types.
The proposed method identifies these pairs and learns one linear feature transformation for debiasing.
It achieves competitive performance across datasets without bias annotations or LLMs.

papers.abstract: Pixel language models process text as rendered images instead of a finite vocabulary, which gives them strong cross-lingual transfer abilities. However, not much is known about how these abilities are influenced by larger-scale pretraining. In this paper, we train a family of MPIXEL models along three axes of variation: more languages, more scripts, and larger model capacity under fixed per-language compute. In evaluations on five tasks covering 83 languages, we find that scaling acts locally: each axis improves the added languages and scripts, while increased capacity mitigates the curse of multilinguality from pretraining on more languages. Transfer to unseen scripts improves with multilingual pretraining, but does not further improve with scaling. On typologically distant low-resource languages, our models outperform subword and character-level baselines across many writing systems. We also show that larger pixel models reserve more layers for visual processing, and that cross-lingual alignment weakens as more languages are added. Overall, our findings characterize how multilingual scaling improves pixel language models.
authors: Ilker Kesen, Jenny Kunz, Kasra Malihi, Desmond Elliott
bullets: Evaluates MPIXEL models across more languages, more scripts, and larger capacity under fixed per-language compute.
Across five tasks and 83 languages, each scaling axis primarily benefits the corresponding languages or scripts.
Larger models mitigate the curse of multilinguality, but transfer to unseen scripts does not improve further with scaling.
Pixel models outperform subword and character-level baselines on many typologically distant, low-resource languages.
Scaling increases visual-processing layers, while cross-lingual alignment weakens as more languages are added.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. Recent digital agents test this idea by rewriting their own code and checking each version with executable tests. Bringing these mechanisms into the physical world requires learning from partial observations through costly trials, while accounting for changing operating conditions and potentially irreversible consequences. We position RSI within robot learning and trace pathways from improving robot capabilities to improving the processes that generate them. We examine how physical experience can strengthen these improvement mechanisms and when the resulting gains can support further self-improvement of the mechanisms themselves. Gains carry forward only when feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement, benefits to later learning, and procedure improvement. Some systems also change the improver's knowledge or tools, but the physical studies reviewed here have yet to isolate gains attributable to recursion. We synthesize these findings into evaluation principles and research directions for machines that, trial by trial, safely improve the way they improve.
authors: Meng Luo, Zechen Bai, Shanqing Xu, Yanlin Li, Kaixin Li, Mengchen Qian, Weifeng Lu, Ran Zhang, Yingtian Zou, Ziyang Luo, Wei Chen, Hongzhan Lin
bullets: Physical RSI must handle partial observations, costly trials, changing conditions, and potentially irreversible failures.
The paper connects robot capability improvement with improvement of the learning or development procedures themselves.
Improvements transfer only when feedback targets remaining needs, the recipient can use the change, benefits generalize across tasks or hardware, and practice remains safe and affordable.
Existing manipulation studies show behavioral, future-learning, and procedural gains, but have not isolated benefits specifically caused by recursion.
The paper proposes evaluation principles and research directions for safe, trial-by-trial improvement of physical AI.

papers.abstract: Learning motion planning policies that remain reliable under closed-loop execution is a central challenge in Autonomous Driving (AD). Imitation Learning (IL) scales well to large AD datasets but suffers from distribution shift, causal confusion, and compounding errors under closed-loop execution. In contrast, Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically requires handcrafted rule-based rewards and massive simulation. We study a simple closed-loop IL framework that uses RL purely as an optimization tool, guided by a trajectory-distance reward derived from logged expert data. We refer to this training strategy as Expert-Guided RL (EGRL). Through a controlled empirical study we find evidence that the training procedure, rather than model size and complexity, accounts for a substantial part of the performance gains. We then introduce DriveMLP, a lightweight MLP policy trained with EGRL, as a simple instantiation of these findings. It achieves a score of 86.51 on the nuPlan Val14 Reactive benchmark, a +3.2 point improvement over the previous best IL planner (Flow Planner), with >15x faster inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/alessandro-canevaro/DriveMLP .
authors: Alessandro Canevaro, Julian Schmidt, Hang Yu, Ye Jin, Sajad Marvi, Georg Martius, Julian Jordan
bullets: Addresses imitation learning’s distribution shift, causal confusion, and compounding errors during closed-loop execution.
Uses Expert-Guided RL (EGRL): RL optimizes a trajectory-distance reward derived from logged expert demonstrations.
Introduces DriveMLP, a simple and lightweight MLP policy trained with EGRL.
Scores 86.51 on the nuPlan Val14 Reactive benchmark, improving over the prior best IL planner by 3.2 points.
Achieves over 15× faster inference, suggesting training strategy can matter more than model complexity in this setting.

papers.abstract: Long-term agent memory is shifting from predefined workflows toward learnable policies for memory construction and retrieval. Existing learning-based methods either optimize construction alone or combine retrieval-side online reinforcement learning (RL) with offline construction supervision, limiting co-adaptation between the two stages. In this paper, we explore end-to-end online RL for a unified memory manager (Uni-Mem) that learns both capabilities under a shared policy. However, joint optimization with existing RL algorithms such as GRPO faces confounded group comparisons and sparse feedback over long memory-management trajectories. To this end, we propose Stage-Decoupled GRPO, which alternates construction and retrieval optimization while controlling variation from the other stage within each rollout group, yielding stage-specific learning signals. We further introduce Event-Wise Credit Assignment (ECA), which localizes feedback to responsible events and propagates event-level advantages to their constituent operations. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show that Uni-Mem outperforms the strongest RL-based memory, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly learning memory construction and retrieval via Stage-Decoupled GRPO and ECA.
authors: Zhiqian Xia, Jielong Tang, Ling-An Zeng, Shixiong Kai, Rong Yao, Hao Kong, Xiao Dong, Wei Wang, Mingxuan Yuan, Siyu Xia, Haifeng Xia

Event-Wise Credit Assignment assigns feedback to responsible events and their constituent operations.
On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, Uni-Mem outperforms the strongest RL-based memory method reported.

papers.abstract: Financial crime detection requires identifying illicit activity within large transaction networks, where suspicious behaviour is rare and unfolds over time. Existing graph-based methods capture relationships among accounts but typically underuse the temporal behaviour encoded in account transaction histories. We introduce Temporal-Context Edge Enrichment (TCEE), a framework that addresses this gap by summarising each account's transaction history with a frozen time-series foundation model (TSFM), and enriching each transaction's representation with the relevant temporal context from these summaries. These enriched representations can be scored directly for edge classification, or fed into a graph neural network (GNN) as edge features to capture broader structural information. Across six AMLWorld datasets, TCEE improves PR-AUC over the strongest evaluated baseline on five by a relative 10.8% on average, while training 6.0x faster end-to-end. Feeding TCEE's representations into a GNN raises PR-AUC a further 4.8% on the four smaller datasets. On an Ethereum phishing dataset, we show that TSFM-generated account representations fed into a GNN are also effective for node classification, improving PR-AUC by 14.5% over the strongest baseline. As TSFMs continue to advance, our results suggest they can strengthen financial crime detection by capturing temporal signals that complement graph-based approaches.
authors: Danae Natalie Savvidi, H. \c{C}a\u{g}r{\i} Bilgi, Kubilay Atasu, Arie van Deursen
bullets: Addresses the underuse of temporal account behaviour in graph-based illicit-activity detection.
Summarises each account’s transaction history with a frozen TSFM and enriches transaction-edge representations with relevant temporal context.
Representations support direct edge classification or integration as edge features in a GNN; TSFM account representations also support node classification.
Across six AMLWorld datasets, TCEE improves PR-AUC on five and trains 6.0× faster end-to-end; GNN integration provides further gains on four smaller datasets.
On Ethereum phishing detection, TSFM-based account representations improve node-classification PR-AUC over the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale model capacity efficiently, yet their substantial memory footprint poses a major barrier to deployment. Expert pruning reduces this footprint, but most methods focus on which experts to remove and prune every layer equally. We propose SPARE (Sparsity Allocation via Routing Entropy), a training-free, selector-agnostic method that decides how many experts to remove from each layer using routing entropy, the entropy of tokens' normalized Top-K gate weights on calibration data. When a token's gate weight is spread evenly, removing one active expert discards little of it, so SPARE prunes layers with more diffuse routing more aggressively. A perturbation bound under random pruning formalizes this intuition, and controlled interventions with a fixed selector link concentrated routing to larger output changes. With the same selector and budget, SPARE improves average accuracy over uniform allocation on Mixtral, Qwen3, and DeepSeek models, especially at high pruning ratios. At 50% expert pruning, it raises the eight-task average of Qwen3-30B-A3B from 57.2% to 63.8%, and the math, code, and science average of DeepSeek-R1 from 80.1 to 82.8.
authors: Yifan Yang, Hanling Yi, Dongquan Yang, Feng Lin, Rong Xiao, Aijun Li, Xiaotian Yu
bullets: Targets the memory cost of MoE deployment by choosing how many experts to remove per layer.
Uses token gate-weight entropy on calibration data: layers with more diffuse routing are pruned more aggressively.
Training-free and selector-agnostic; supported by a perturbation bound and controlled interventions.
Outperforms uniform allocation on Mixtral, Qwen3, and DeepSeek models, particularly at high pruning ratios.
At 50% pruning, Qwen3-30B-A3B improves from 57.2% to 63.8%, while DeepSeek-R1 improves from 80.1 to 82.8% on the reported task averages.

papers.abstract: Accurate short-term forecasting of atmospheric seeing is of significant interest for astronomical observations and free-space optical communication systems, where rapid variations in optical turbulence can affect system performance and operational planning. In this work, we benchmark machine learning models for predicting atmospheric seeing up to two hours in advance, with a particular focus on probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty quantification. We compare two probabilistic approaches, Gaussian Processes (GPs) and a normalizing-flow- based model (FloTS), against deterministic recurrent neural network (RNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) baselines. All models are trained and evaluated on seeing measurements from the Maunakea summit. We assess the models using both deterministic metrics, including the root mean square error and the Pearson correlation coefficient, and probabilistic metrics that evaluate the quality and calibration of predictive uncertainty estimates. The results show that deep learning approaches outperform standard recurrent networks for short-term forecasting, with LSTM and FloTS achieving the best overall predictive accuracy. While Gaussian Processes provide a useful probabilistic baseline, their predictive distributions are limited by the Gaussian assumption. FloTS combines competitive forecasting accuracy with flexible uncertainty quantification and produces the most informative probabilistic forecasts.
authors: Mary-Joe Medlej, Rahul Srinivasan, Simon Prunet, Aziz Ziad, Christophe Giordano
bullets: Targets short-term atmospheric seeing prediction for astronomy and free-space optical communications.
Benchmarks Gaussian Processes and FloTS against deterministic RNN and LSTM baselines using Maunakea summit measurements.
Evaluates both forecast accuracy and the quality and calibration of predictive uncertainties.
LSTM and FloTS achieve the best overall predictive accuracy, while FloTS produces the most informative probabilistic forecasts.
Gaussian Processes offer a useful baseline but are constrained by their Gaussian predictive assumption.

Each cell reports RMSE (top) and correlation (bottom, in parentheses). The background colour represents a composite performance score computed as the equally weighted average of min–max normalised RMSE (inverted) and correlation, where a score of 1 indicates the best performance and 0 the worst across all models and time steps. Red borders highlight the two best overall models, LSTM and FloTS, which consistently achieve the highest composite scores across all forecast horizons.

Figure 2. Comparison of the FloTS seeing prediction before and after calibration for the August case study. The top panel shows the uncalibrated prediction, while the bottom panel shows the calibrated prediction. In each panel, the left side shows the input sequence used for forecasting, and the right side displays the two-hour forecast horizon. The black curve indicates the observed target sequence, while the red, purple, and green dashed curves show the GP, RNN, and LSTM predictions, respectively. The heatmap represents the probability density predicted by FloTS. For visualization, the density is normalized independently at each forecast timestep. Calibration redistributes probability mass within the predictive density, modifying both the dispersion and the local non-Gaussian structure of the forecast distribution.

papers.tldr: Probabilistic deep-learning models, especially FloTS, provide accurate and informative uncertainty-aware forecasts of atmospheric seeing up to two hours ahead.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) is a challenging task for surveillance systems due to the scarcity and diversity of anomalous events. While semi-supervised VAD approaches have advanced the field, many rely on computationally intensive optical flow networks to capture motion dynamics. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are also widely used for spatial encoding, but their effective receptive field is highly local. To address these limitations, we introduce MS2CAST, an end-to-end semi-supervised predictive VAD framework. For spatial encoding, we employ a multi-scale cross-attention encoder that fuses the hierarchical feature representations from a vision transformer (MViTv2-S) and a CNN (ConvNeXt-T) to exploit their distinct receptive fields. To model spatiotemporal dynamics without optical flow estimation, we integrate two interchangeable spatiotemporal modules in the latent space. One module (SwinLSTM) incorporates a Swin Transformer, while the other (VMRNN) integrates Vision Mamba blocks. Our objective function combines L1 loss, Gradient Difference Loss (GDL), and Multi-Scale Structural Similarity Index Measure (MS-SSIM) to ensure pixel-wise accuracy, sharpness, and structural integrity. Evaluations across the UCSD Ped2, CUHK Avenue, and ShanghaiTech datasets demonstrate frame-level Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Area Under the Curve (AUC) scores that are competitive with top-tier techniques while maintaining a peak GPU memory usage of under 1 GB.
bullets: Addresses scarce and diverse anomalies while reducing reliance on computationally intensive optical flow.
Fuses hierarchical features from MViTv2-S and ConvNeXt-T to capture complementary spatial receptive fields.
Uses either SwinLSTM or VMRNN to model latent spatiotemporal dynamics.
Combines L1, Gradient Difference, and MS-SSIM losses for accurate, sharp, and structurally consistent predictions.
Shows competitive frame-level ROC-AUC performance on UCSD Ped2, CUHK Avenue, and ShanghaiTech, with peak GPU memory below 1 GB.

papers.abstract: Many robotic construction applications, such as progress tracking, require registering a sensor trajectory to a prior 2D floor plan. Visual capture is attractive for its low cost and availability, but aligning a visual simultaneous localization and mapping (VSLAM) map to a floor plan is difficult; VSLAM recovers geometry only up to an unknown similarity transform, the sparse point cloud is cross-modal to the symbolic floor plan, sites are only partially built during capture, and construction sites are visually repetitive, degrading map quality while removing distinctive features. Existing methods address at most two of these challenges. We thus introduce Reading the Room(RR), a global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous, sparse, semantic VSLAM maps to partially built floor plans. Our key idea is to define a single robust, differentiable, class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function that governs all stages of the pipeline. We develop two global initialization schemes, leveraging a single inaccurate user-provided correspondence if provided, or estimating the initialization globally using a cross-modal matching network. Both schemes are designed to find initial candidates with respect to the energy function, which is then directly optimized for local refinement. We evaluate RR on 33 sequences across three active construction sites against classical and learning-based baselines, achieving a 4.5x improvement in mean absolute trajectory error over the strongest baseline in the general unconstrained setting, which increases to 7.6x when an anchor is provided.
authors: Bjorn Stragier, Emilia Szyma\'nska, J. Micah Prendergast, Lukas Rosenberger Schmid
bullets: Addresses unknown scale, cross-modal map alignment, incomplete construction, and repetitive visual environments.
Uses a robust, differentiable, class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function throughout the pipeline.
Initializes registration either from one inaccurate user correspondence or via a cross-modal matching network.
Globally finds candidate alignments, then directly optimizes the energy for local refinement.
Evaluated on 33 sequences across three construction sites, improving mean absolute trajectory error by 4.5× over the strongest baseline generally and 7.6× with an anchor.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of Reading the Room. To align a sparse VSLAM map to a symbolic floor plan, preprocessing first reduce the modalitygap by processing the 3D map into a BEV map (Sec. IV-A). A single energy function (Sec. IV-B) guides the remaining steps. If a known correspondence is provided it is leveraged to constrain global initialization, otherwise global initialization is performed using dense cross-modal feature matching (Sec. IV-C). Finally, the estimate is refined (Sec. IV-D) to minimize the energy function locally.

Fig. 3: Qualitative registration results for one representative sequence per site, increasing in difficulty from top to bottom. VSLAM BEV maps are rotated and scaled for visualization; this does not reflect their initial condition for registration. On Site A, all three methods recover visually similar trajectories, consistent with the small floor area, high coverage, and unique structural layout of the site. In Site B, the RoMa+MatchAnything collapses the entire map into several rooms. This yields a low cost as the outer walls align with the room walls, highlighting the challenge of scale-ambiguous registration. In Site C, both RoMa+MatchAnything and our approach fail due to the symmetry of the scene and align the sparse observations flipped. If a single noisy user-provided anchor is available, our method can leverage this to recover the right symmetry and achieve a good solution in spite of orientation and scale ambiguity.

Fig. 1: This work presents a method to align a noisy scaleambiguous VSLAM trajectory to a floor plan. Our solution is able to operate in early construction phases (a) where notable parts of the floor plan may not yet have been built (b). This leads to missing structures in the sparse VSLAM map in addition to the crossmodality gap to the symbolic floor plan (c). Our method overcomes these challenges, achieving good trajectory alignment (d).

papers.abstract: Indoor localization systems are critical for Industry-4.0 applications. Visible Light Communication (VLC)-based systems offer advantages such as immunity to electromagnetic interference, high accuracy, and energy efficiency, but their performance is hindered by environmental variability across deployment areas. This paper presents a transfer learning (TL) framework for VLC-based indoor localization that enhances cross-area robustness while reducing data requirements. Using real-world measurements from four distinct areas of a Bosch manufacturing facility, we show that fine-tuning a deep neural network (DNN) pre-trained on source area data with only 40% of target-area measurements recovers 97% of full-data performance, thereby reducing the amount of target data needed. We further introduce the Transfer Efficiency Score (TES), a composite metric that identifies the most effective source models for transfer without exhaustive evaluation. Guided by TES, the framework selects the best source model, yielding localization errors as low as 40.9 cm with success rates above 86%. Validation on an unseen area confirms its generalization capability, with a 3.28 cm mean error achieved using the TES-selected source model. Overall, the proposed framework provides a scalable and data-efficient pathway for industrial VLC localization, substantially reducing deployment costs and computational burden while maintaining high accuracy in diverse and dynamic environments.
authors: Masood Jan, Wafa Njima, Xun Zhang, Alexander Artemenko
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by environmental differences between deployment areas.
Fine-tunes a DNN trained on a source area using 40% of target measurements, recovering 97% of full-data performance.

papers.abstract: Multimodal inputs may be missing or degraded, raising distinct questions of evidence availability and trust. We introduce a reliability-aware Gaussian Product-of-Experts (PoE) in which an input-dependent reliability weight tempers each modality's latent precision, while missing experts are omitted. We characterize how reliability and availability affect posterior information and expert influence. Across two clinical multimodal tasks, the full framework remains competitive with complete inputs and achieves its clearest mean-AUROC advantage under modality absence, particularly on HAIM-MIMIC-MM. Ablations show a substantial gain from missing-aware training and an additional HAIM improvement from reliability weighting under matched PoE, missing-aware, and consistency training. Unseen test-time corruptions are used diagnostically and reveal modality-dependent reliability-weight and latent-uncertainty responses, including failure under severe degradation. Thus, reliability weighting provides an explicit evidence-control mechanism, while learning dependable quality signals remains an open challenge.
authors: Patitapaban Palo, Abhisek Tiwari, Mattia Carletti, Anshul Thakur, Xiao Gu, David A. Clifton

papers.abstract: Object detection models for autonomous driving commonly experience substantial performance drops when deployed under adverse weather due to the domain shift between training data and real-world operating conditions. This degradation is especially evident when models trained on clear-weather images encounter foggy environments with reduced visibility and contrast. To address this challenge, we introduce FogTTA, an online test-time adaptation framework designed to improve the robustness of Transformer-based object detectors in fog. Using RF-DETR as the underlying object detector, FogTTA enables real-time adaptation to the streaming target domain without requiring source data or retraining. The framework follows a teacher-student design, where the deployed model serves as the teacher and generates pseudo labels from weakly augmented target inputs. These predictions are subsequently refined through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering. The student model then learns from strongly augmented target sample using the Varifocal loss to mitigate pseudo-label noise. The teacher is updated via exponential moving averaging to ensure stable and continuous adaptation. Experiments show that FogTTA outperforms prior baselines, delivering improved detection accuracy and stability while maintaining real-time performance.
authors: Ali Abedi, Q. M. Jonathan Wu, Ning Zhang, Shiqi Tian
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by the domain shift from clear to foggy driving environments.
Uses a teacher–student test-time adaptation framework with pseudo-label refinement through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering.
Trains the student on strongly augmented target images with Varifocal loss to reduce pseudo-label noise.
Updates the teacher via exponential moving average for stable, continuous adaptation.
Experiments report improved accuracy and stability over prior baselines while maintaining real-time performance.

papers.abstract: Edge medical segmentation must reconcile small model size, high accuracy, and fast inference. TernScope addresses this tradeoff through model--hardware co-design, learning a compact segmentation network whose low-bit operators also simplify hardware execution. Split-channel large-kernel blocks preserve spatial context with limited computation, while branch fusion removes redundant inference paths. Ternary Progressive Quantization-aware Training (TPQ) then adapts the fused network from deep to shallow layers, through the decoder, and finally to the input and prediction layers. All 25 convolutions use ternary weights and 8-bit activations, enabling packed storage and multiplier-free computation. The resulting model uses 0.2483 M parameters and 0.0949 GMACs while retaining competitive segmentation accuracy on in-domain and external datasets. Under the same 45 nm technology, TernScope reduces compute-array area by 88.46% compared with the original Gemmini, a systolic-array accelerator with 8-bit $\times$ 8-bit multipliers. These results demonstrate a path from accurate lightweight medical segmentation to compact low-bit hardware.
authors: Zhuoyu Wu, Wenhui Ou, Qiawei Zheng, Xuhong Qiu, Wenqi Fang, Rapha\"{e}l C. -W. Phan
bullets: Targets the tradeoff among model size, segmentation accuracy, and inference speed in edge medical imaging.
Uses split-channel large-kernel blocks and branch fusion to preserve spatial context while reducing computation.
Applies Ternary Progressive Quantization-aware Training across the network, with ternary weights and 8-bit activations for packed, multiplier-free execution.
The model has 0.2483 M parameters and 0.0949 GMACs while maintaining competitive accuracy on in-domain and external datasets.
At 45 nm, its compute-array area is reduced by 88.46% versus the original Gemmini accelerator.

papers.abstract: Perceptive locomotion policies typically observe a dense robot-centric elevation map, although only the terrain beneath and around the next footsteps informs the control decision. Learned encoders compress the whole visual input, leaving the policy to work out which inputs matter while learning the baseline locomotion task. Learning both at once slows training and, without computationally expensive attention mechanisms, makes generalization to new terrain harder. We instead remove redundant inputs from the elevation map before the policy sees it. A lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts future footholds from proprioception and the velocity command alone, and we sample the elevation map only in small patches around these predicted footholds. We train the prediction model alongside the locomotion policy, periodically retraining it on new policy rollouts as the robot's gait matures. This allows the perception to anticipate where the policy will step, while the policy learns to leverage terrain information around those steps. With the proposed lightweight preprocessing, the policy reaches a given terrain difficulty in roughly a third of the training iterations required with the complete map. It outperforms policies that observe the complete map where footholds are sparse, including in narrow walled corridors, and on unseen terrain, and it matches an attention-based encoder trained at several times the cost. The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid traversing various obstacles, stairs, gaps, and step-downs beyond the training distribution in both indoor and outdoor environments.
authors: Matthias Heyrman, Chenhao Li, Ioannis Dadiotis, Marco Hutter
bullets: Dense elevation maps contain substantial information irrelevant to the robot’s next foot placements.
A foothold prediction model uses proprioception and velocity commands to predict future steps and sample only nearby terrain patches.
The predictor is trained alongside the locomotion policy and periodically updated from new policy rollouts.
The approach reaches a target terrain difficulty in roughly one-third as many training iterations as using the complete map.
It performs well on sparse-foothold and unseen terrain, including narrow corridors, and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 in indoor and outdoor environments.
