papers.abstract: Mid-training (MT) is a training phase in LLM training pipelines that continues pretraining (PT) on smaller datasets of higher value. Taking the PT and MT phases as a whole, training usually starts with only PT data and then transitions completely to MT data. In this work, we view this complete transition from PT to MT data as a special case of a broader class of data mixing schedules that specify how the proportions of PT and MT tokens in each batch change over training. Under fixed total training compute and MT token budgets, we ask: Is this complete transition to MT data optimal for minimizing final MT loss? We show that the answer depends on the learning rate (LR) schedule: one data schedule may outperform another under one LR schedule, but changing only the LR schedule can reverse the outcome. Specifically, when the LR decays throughout continued training, introducing MT data earlier and mixing it with PT data lowers the final MT loss compared with placing all MT data at the end of training, but this result is reversed if we use constant LR. We therefore study how to jointly choose when to introduce MT data and when to decay the LR through ablation studies, and find that it is better to decay the LR only after MT data enters training. Finally, we develop a theoretical model that explains why the optimal data schedule for a fixed MT token budget depends on the LR schedule.
authors: Haodong Wen, Kairong Luo, Tingkai Yan, Wenguang Chen, Kaifeng Lyu
bullets: The study asks whether switching completely from pretraining (PT) data to mid-training (MT) data is optimal under fixed compute and MT-token budgets.
With a decaying learning rate, introducing and mixing MT data earlier improves final MT loss versus placing all MT data at the end.
With a constant learning rate, this comparison reverses, showing that schedule choices are interdependent.
Ablations suggest delaying learning-rate decay until after MT data enters training is preferable.
A theoretical model explains why the optimal data schedule depends on the learning-rate schedule.

figures.caption: Figure 3: LR should decay well after MT enters training for TS and ZL data schedules. The bottom row shows how final MT loss changes with relative LR decay duration for TS and ZL across three MT budgets. ZL reaches its lowest MT loss at 20%, and TS at 40%, improving on both Const (0%) and MDR (100%). The top row illustrates TS (left) and ZL (right) at a 10% MT budget, paired with LR schedules of different relative LR decay durations, measured as percentages of the time from MT entry to training completion. See Section 2.3 and Appendix D for the setup and further discussion.

Figure 4: The optimal data schedule can have three stages under LR decay. The first two columns show an abrupt switch from pure PT to pure MT. With stronger LR decay in the last two columns, the teal curves instead include a mixing stage in which the MT ratio increases continuously. This change occurs at both MT budgets shown. See Theorem 3.1 for the theoretical result and Appendix M for the numerical setup.

Figure 32: Numerical validation of Theorem I.3. Solid curves show the schedules predicted by the closed form solution, while markers show the optima obtained by directly optimizing the expected validation loss using different numerical methods. The two solutions agree for both MT data budgets considered.

Figure 25: Changing MT data from mathematics to code preserves the best tested relative LR decay duration for both TS (left) and ZL (right). Both datasets use the same MoE model and 10B-token continuation with a 25% MT budget and final MT ratio 100%. The horizontal axis gives decay duration as a percentage of each schedule’s MT data window, with zero denoting Const and 100% denoting MDR. The vertical axis gives final MT loss minus the corresponding Const loss for that dataset and data schedule. Points show measured values, and rings mark the lowest tested losses at 20% for TS and 10% for ZL. Lines connect tested values.

Figure 5: LR-dependent data-schedule preferences also occur in MoE. Left to right: 4B continuation tokens with a 25% MT budget; 10B tokens with 25% MT; and 10B tokens with 47.75% MT. All three settings use the same 2.99B-parameter model. At a final MT ratio of 100%, Const can outperform MDR. See Section 2.2 and Appendix F for the setup and full results.

Figure 6: Gradual MT entry reduces router imbalance under data distribution shift. TS produces sharp spikes when the MT ratio jumps, while ZL avoids comparable spikes. Under Const (left), both schedules use the same LR trajectory, so this difference comes from the data schedule. MDR (right) shows a similar pattern, although LR decay starts at different times for TS and ZL. These MoE runs use 10B continuation tokens and a fixed 25% MT budget. Dotted lines mark MT entry. See Appendix G for setup and diagnostic details.

Figure 11: A short final LR decay improves on Const and MDR. The lowest tested MT losses are 1.5215 at a relative LR decay duration of 40% for TS (top) and 1.5203 at 20% for ZL (bottom). These dense model runs use a 10% MT budget. TS ends at 80% MT with a 1,250-step MT window; ZL ends at 100% MT with a 2,000-step window. Hollow TS markers show repeats at 20%; the 40% minimum was not repeated.

Figure 12: TS and ZL favor different relative LR decay durations. TS (top) reaches its lowest tested loss of 1.4275 at 40%, and ZL (bottom) reaches 1.4392 at 20%. Nearby short decay durations give similar losses. Both dense model runs use a 25% MT budget and end at 100% MT, with MT windows of 2,500 steps for TS and 5,000 for ZL. These configurations have no repeated runs.

Figure 13: The best tested relative LR decay duration remains 40% when TS ends at lower MT ratios. At a final MT ratio of 80% (top), this gives a loss of 1.3831, with repeats at 1.3834 and 1.3846. At 60% MT (bottom), it gives 1.4039, with similar losses at relative LR decay durations between 20% and 80%. These dense model runs use a 47.75% MT budget and MT windows of 5,969 and 7,958 steps, respectively. The scan ending at 100% MT appears in Figure 3.

Figure 14: TS favors a relative LR decay duration of 40%, while ZL favors 20%. Their lowest tested losses are 1.3690 for TS (top) and 1.3857 for ZL (bottom). For ZL, MDR and FDR differ by only 450 decay steps and yield similar losses of 1.4221 and 1.4249, respectively. Both dense model runs use a 47.75% MT budget and end at 100% MT, with MT windows of 4,775 steps for TS and 9,550 for ZL. This ZL configuration has no repeated runs.

Figure 24: Changing the PT checkpoint preserves the preferred data and LR schedules among the shared configurations. Const and FDR favor opposite TS endpoints (left). A relative LR decay duration of 20% gives the lowest tested loss, while MDR remains worse than Const (right). The right panel shows loss changes relative to each checkpoint’s own Const baseline at a final MT ratio of 100%. These MoE runs start from 20B, 30B, and 40B checkpoints of the same PT trajectory and use 4B continued training tokens with a 25% MT budget. The 40B checkpoint has additional sampled durations.

Figure 22: Const and FDR favor opposite TS endpoints even from earlier PT checkpoints. After either 20B PT tokens (left) or 30B (right), Const gives its lowest tested MT loss when TS ends at 100% MT, while FDR favors 25%. Both use 4B continued training tokens and a 25% MT budget. The checkpoints come from the same PT run.

Figure 31: Consistency of the SDE calculation, the exact discrete SGD second moment recursion, and Monte Carlo simulation for α = 0.25. Results are shown for a constant learning rate (left) and linear decay with c = 0.8 (right), across four representative data schedules. Error bars give two standard errors of the Monte Carlo mean.

Figure 33: Numerical illustration of the KKT mechanism. Left: At the two stage schedule with α = 0.25, the marginal value of MT data is increasing under a constant learning rate, whereas linear decay with c = 0.8 violates the switching condition around (1 − α)T . Right: At the numerical optimum under linear decay, the normalized marginal value equals the KKT multiplier throughout the interior mixing phase and satisfies the appropriate inequalities on the two boundary phases.

Figure 2: Across all three MT budgets, replaying PT data improves MT loss under FDR, but not under Const or MDR. The three panels show final MT loss as the final MT ratio in the second TS stage varies. Under the FDR regime, the lowest tested loss occurs when this stage mixes PT and MT data. Under the Const and MDR regimes, it occurs with pure MT data (100%). Large circles mark these minima, while other hollow markers show repeated runs. See Section 2.2 and Appendix C for the setup and full results.

Figure 27: TS produces a transient load balancing spike, while gradual MT entry avoids a comparable peak. The upper panels compare TS at several final MT ratios, including Const and MDR at 100% MT; the lower panels compare TS and ZL under MDR at final MT ratios of 100%, 75%, and 50%. These MoE runs use 4B continued training tokens. Training loss (left) and the logged load balancing statistic (right) are shown every 20 training steps.

Figure 28: Smaller TS data shifts produce smaller load balancing spikes, while ZL avoids a comparable peak. The upper panels compare TS switches at steps 1,788, 1,589, and 1,192 for final MT ratios of 100%, 75%, and 50%; the lower panels compare TS and ZL under MDR at the same endpoints. These MoE runs use 10B continued training tokens. Training step is horizontal, with training loss on the left and logged load balancing on the right. Final validation losses are reported separately in Tables 11 and 12.

Figure 15: The best tested TS and ZL decays span nearly the same number of training steps. TS (top) reaches 1.6080 at a relative LR decay duration of 20% (47 steps), while ZL (bottom) reaches 1.6000 at 10% (48 steps). These MoE runs use 4B continued training tokens, a 25% MT budget, and a final MT ratio of 100%. Their MT windows last 238 and 477 steps, respectively. Hollow TS markers repeat MDR; neither minimum was repeated.

Figure 16: The best tested TS and ZL decays both last 119 steps. TS (top) reaches 1.4853 at a relative LR decay duration of 20%, while ZL (bottom) reaches 1.4872 at 10%. These MoE runs use 10B continued training tokens, a 25% MT budget, and a final MT ratio of 100%. Their MT windows last 596 and 1,192 steps, respectively. Hollow TS markers repeat MDR; the best TS and ZL configurations have no matched data repetitions.

Figure 21: Increasing the MoE MT budget preserves the best tested relative LR decay durations. TS (top) favors 20%, and ZL (bottom) favors 10%; both correspond to 228 decay steps. These runs use 10B continued training tokens with a 47.75% MT budget and end at 100% MT. Their MT windows last 1,138 and 2,277 steps, respectively. These configurations have no data stream repeats.

Figure 23: Delaying LR decay improves on Const and MDR from both earlier PT checkpoints. The lowest tested MT losses are 1.6562 after 20B PT tokens (top) and 1.6260 after 30B (bottom), both at a relative LR decay duration of 20% (47 steps). Each MoE TS run uses 4B continued training tokens, a 25% MT budget, and a final MT ratio of 100%, giving a 238-step MT window. Only 20% and 40% are tested beyond Const, MDR, and FDR.

Figure 26: Gradual MT entry reduces load balancing spikes. Under Const (left), TS and ZL use the same LR at every step, allowing us to compare the data schedules without also changing the LR. TS produces a sharp spike when the MT ratio suddenly increases, while ZL avoids a comparable spike by introducing MT data gradually. MDR (right) shows a similar pattern, although LR decay begins at different times for TS and ZL. Rows show MoE experiments with 4B (top) and 10B (bottom) tokens of continued training. Curves compare final MT ratios of 100%, 75%, and 50%. Dotted lines mark when MT data first enters. The 10B results also appear in Figure 6.

Figure 29: The router initially assigns MT tokens unevenly across experts and becomes more balanced during MT training. Checkpoint routing diagnostics for the MoE TS+Const run with 10B continuation tokens and a final MT ratio of 100%. Top: imbalance by layer on DCLM and FineMath at steps 1,750, 2,250, and 2,384. Bottom: FineMath expert shares before the switch, at training end, and their difference, with expert and layer indices as coordinates. Shares are relative to uniform routing. These diagnostics describe one run, without replica averaging.

Figure 19: Longer MoE continued training narrows the MDR–Const loss gap. For TS, extending training from 4B to 10B tokens reduces the primary-run gap from 0.0310 to 0.0115 at a final MT ratio of 100%, while the best tested relative LR decay duration remains 20%. The upper panels show final MT loss and its change from each horizon’s Const baseline; the lower panels vary the final MT ratio. All runs use a 25% MT budget. In the difference panel, circles and local error bars at MDR show the three-run mean and ±s3, computed from unrounded losses relative to the primary Const loss; they do not estimate uncertainty at other durations or in the Const baseline.

Figure 8: FDR favors earlier MT mixing, while Const and MDR favor ending with MT data alone. For both TS and ZL, the lowest tested MT loss occurs at a final MT ratio of 20% under FDR and 100% under Const and MDR. These dense model runs use a 10% MT budget over 20.97B continued training tokens, including 2.10B FineMath tokens.

Figure 9: Changing the LR schedule changes the preferred final MT ratio. FDR gives the lowest tested MT loss at 40% MT for TS and 50% for ZL; Const and MDR favor 100% for both. These dense model runs use a 25% MT budget over 20.97B continued training tokens, including 5.24B FineMath tokens.

Figure 10: ZL losses under FDR change little across its tested final MT ratios. They vary by only 0.001, while Const and MDR favor a final MT ratio of 100%. TS covers eight final MT ratios; ZL covers five from 95.5% to 100%. These dense model runs use a 47.75% MT budget over 20.97B continued training tokens, including 10.01B FineMath tokens. Hollow overlays show selected data sampling repeats.

Figure 7: Illustration of different LR schedules and data schedules. Rows show TS and ZL, and columns show Const, FDR, and MDR. Solid lines and shading show the MT ratio on the left axes. Dash dotted lines show LR relative to its peak on the right axes. Both data schedules use a 25% MT budget and end at 100% MT, so ZL introduces MT earlier. MDR therefore begins LR decay earlier for ZL than for TS. Time starts at the shared PT checkpoint.

Figure 30: ZL+MDR preserves expert load rankings better than TS+Const, although both reach nearly balanced MT loads. (a) Both schedules bring FineMath (MT) loads close to uniform in most layers; one denotes equal assignment shares across experts. (b) Initially more heavily used experts lose share, while less used experts gain it. Each point represents one expert in one layer. The horizontal axis shows its share before MT entry time minus the uniform share, and the vertical axis shows its final minus initial share, both in units of 1/64. Points on the dotted line end at the uniform share. (c) Despite similar final balance, the ordering of experts changes more under TS+Const. The higher rank correlations under ZL+MDR mean that experts receiving relatively more FineMath assignments initially tend to remain more heavily used at the end. All checkpoint measurements use held-out data. These 10B-token MoE continuations use different LR schedules, so the comparison does not isolate the effect of the data schedule. See Table 14 for the setup.

Figure 17: Const gives the lowest tested MT loss among the three baseline LR schedules. MDR favors a final MT ratio of 50% for both TS and ZL. These MoE runs use 4B continued training tokens with a 25% MT budget. Hollow overlays repeat TS+MDR at a final MT ratio of 100%.

Figure 20: Const and FDR favor opposite TS endpoints at a larger MoE MT budget. Const favors a final MT ratio of 100%, while FDR favors 47.75%. At 100% MT, ZL improves on TS under FDR but has higher MT loss under Const and MDR. These runs use 10B continued training tokens with a 47.75% MT budget, starting from the 40B-token PT checkpoint. ZL is tested only at 100% MT. Each point is one run.

Figure 18: Longer MoE continued training narrows the TS loss gap between MDR and Const. At a final MT ratio of 100%, TS+MDR is closer to TS+Const than after 4B tokens, while ZL+MDR remains worse than ZL+Const. These runs use 10B continued training tokens with a 25% MT budget. Hollow overlays repeat TS+MDR at 100% MT.

Parentheses give the final MT ratio γend in percent. Both MDR minima after 4B continued training tokens occur at γend = 50%, so MDR does not select γend = 100% at both continued training token budgets.

Figure 6 provides the separate control with identical LR trajectories.

Table 13: Expert load imbalance on DCLM and FineMath for the MoE TS+Const run with 10B continuation tokens and a final MT ratio of 100%. Each value is the average of Iℓ across the 12 layers, as defined in Equation (3). The first checkpoint is 38 steps before the data switch. papers.selection_reason: Studies joint data and learning-rate schedules for LLM mid-training, relevant to LLM training and foundation-model development.
papers.title: Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together
papers.tldr: Data-mixing and learning-rate schedules interact strongly in mid-training, so they should be designed jointly rather than independently.

papers.abstract: A transformer MLP gives each hidden channel two roles: a reader that decides when the channel responds, and a writer that decides what it adds back to the residual stream. Read as a key--value memory, the layer can be measured one factor set at a time: the pairing of readers to writers is carried only by their shared index, invisible to any quantity computed from one factor set alone. Yet training couples the two factors through their joint update, so we ask what reading them together shows. The block supplies the joint instrument: the MLP writes back into the very stream it reads, so the exact Jacobian of its update is square, and its agreement with its own transpose resolves into reader--writer terms whose inner products give each channel, read as a couple, a signed pairing coordinate. Ranked by this coordinate, each block we measure has a small core of strongly coupled channels; where initialization gives either sign equally, the core is nearly all opposed: each writer points against the direction its reader responds to. This opposed core recurs from the smallest models trained from scratch to released checkpoints; its sign is in place within a few percent of training and holds while the coupling grows. Read as couples, most channels return their contribution against the reader that fired it, and the readers of later blocks take it up; few show in the logits. Training holds the couples in place: flipping the opposed writers moves the output toward common tokens, and a writer permuted onto another reader regrows to fit that reader while the reader stays.
authors: Giyeong Oh, Sunghee Ahn, Youngjae Yu
bullets: Treating readers and writers jointly reveals coupling that is invisible when either factor set is analyzed alone.
The MLP’s exact square Jacobian is compared with its transpose to derive a signed reader–writer pairing coordinate for each channel.
Across models and checkpoints, strongly coupled cores are usually opposed: writers point against the directions that activate their readers.
Most channels return contributions against the reader that triggered them, while later blocks can take up these contributions; few appear directly in the logits.
Perturbations support functional coupling: flipping opposed writers shifts outputs toward common tokens, and permuting a writer onto another reader causes it to regrow to fit that reader.

figures.caption: Figure 6: The effective core and the corpus. (a) Each block’s final top-16 by |mh|, negative minus positive members over sixteen, at every saved state of medium and at twenty-four public checkpoints of OLMo; tokens on both axes, OLMo’s on a log scale. (b) Tiny models, one marker and colour per depth (legend): the pairing coordinate summed over each block’s core at the end of training against relative depth; natural streams as a band with their median, streams with the unigram frequencies kept and the context destroyed as dashed lines.

Figure 2: The sign across the population, and four core channels read as couples. Left: every channel of three medium seeds at its reader–writer angle θh and, outward, its norm product; the 90◦ line separates opposed (above) from amplifying (below); colour the block, cores outlined, A–D marked; above the line lie 83.2% of channels, 98.5% of cores, half at initialization. Right: four core channels; each cell names its kind, logit or stream couple, each row whether the norm product’s top sixteen holds it, the logits moved, later readers, and the return on its reader. # marks a leading space.

Figure 5: Weight-level pairing along the stack. (a) Web text, eight blocks: the raw-row coordinate mw,h = ⟨kh, vh⟩ over all 1,024 channels of each block, three seeds pooled, split at zero into opposed (blue) and amplifying (red) halves; dots mark one seed’s sixteen core channels. (b) Share of channels with mw,h > 0 per block at {4,6,8,12} blocks on relative depth, seed means.

Figure 1: Paired channel geometry. (a) Read one factor at a time, an MLP’s readers ūh and writers vh are two factor sets that look patternless on their own. (b) Read as couples, most reader and writer couples roughly line up, pointing opposite ways. (c) What couples show is a signed axis, the pairing coordinate mh = ⟨ūh, vh⟩, whose sign the norm product lacks. (d) Measured, in the strongest couples the writers point against their readers through the stack, most strongly mid-stack; the models trained here release toward both ends, OLMo-1B only at the output (mean cosine of the sixteen strongest, small at context 256∗ and 1,024†).

Figure 3: Learned pairing and update geometry. (a) A re-pairing keeps both weights and changes only who pairs with whom. (b) Trained updates are symmetric far beyond any re-pairing. (c) Negative eigenvalues carry most of the symmetric part’s energy, where re-pairing gives one half; only OLMo-1B’s last block, whose couples flip, and the small model’s first expand (tiny, small and medium: blockwise medians over three seeds). (d) Most of the symmetry is mutual: channels reading each other’s writer contribute more than the couples on their own.

Figure 11: Weight-level pairing, gated against elementwise. OLMo-1B (a) and GPT-2 small (b) at their final public checkpoints. Left: the distribution of mw,h over every channel of each block, split at zero into opposed (blue) and amplifying (red) halves; dots are the block’s sixteen core channels of the effective coordinate at their weight-level value, and the axis covers every dot. Right: share of channels below zero per block, effective against weight-level. On the gated model the input blocks’ effective cores sit in the amplifying half of the weights; on the elementwise model the cores sit on the opposed side at every depth and the two shares run together.

Figure 26: From profiles to classes. Stored channel profiles (activation contexts, replayed forward) yield three registers per channel: the input that fires it, the contribution’s first-order response on later readers, and its direct push on the next-token logits, at the strongest firings and at typical activations. Grey stages are measured; orange stages are language-model annotation, with the engine of each stage under its column.

Figure 21: Every channel, with and without order. Left: the effective pairing coordinate mh of all 1,024 channels of each block over training (gray), one eight-block run of the corpus recipe on the web stream (top) and on the same stream with its token order removed (bottom); the sixteen channels that end as the block’s core are coloured, blue if opposed and orange if amplifying. Without order no channel leaves the bulk. Right: the stream cut into chunks of ℓ tokens with only the chunk order shuffled; the core sum (top) and the number of amplifying core channels (bottom) at the end, three seeds (band). Order within a few dozen tokens is enough to form the opposed cores. On these GELU models the weight-level coordinate agrees in sign but selects a different top sixteen (Appendix E.2).

Figure 7: The couple census. Three medium seeds. (a) Every channel by family, area by share, classes inside. (b) The same families block by block, each bar one block’s channels; (a) is the average of the bars.
Figure 4: Writers grow back, readers stay.

Figure 9: The minimum eigenvalue and its scale dependence. Smallest eigenvalue of S = sym(J̄) per block, three medium seeds against their 60 same-factor re-pairings each. (a) In raw units the trained operator’s most contracting direction is more negative than every re-pairing in every block. (b) Once each operator is divided by its own RMS eigenvalue ∥S∥F / √ d, the trained curve crosses the re-paired band, less extreme than its re-pairings through the middle of the stack and more extreme only in the first five and last two blocks: the raw separation is mostly the trained operator being larger.

Figure 12: The gate separates the two readings. (a) Share of channels whose weight-level and effective coordinates agree in sign, by relative depth; the band is the range of the elementwise families trained here. (b) The same agreement before (open markers) and after (filled) removing the reader contributions at negative-gate positions, with the small GELU control. (c) Opposed share as the negative gate is scaled toward zero, input block against middle band; crosses at zero are random deletions of matched size.

Figure 23: Angle, scale, and the reader-size dependence. Top: every channel of one medium seed at an early, a middle, and a late block, as in Figure 2: distance from the origin is the reader–writer norm product (square-root scale), the angle is the angle between the two, so opposed channels (mh < 0) lie above the line. Filled dots are the sixteen core channels by |mh|; open squares and diamonds are the sixteen largest readers and writers. The core sits at the large-reader, most-opposed corner and overlaps the largest readers (eight, six and four of sixteen), while the largest writers scatter across the angle: opposition is organized by the reader, not by the writer. Bottom: opposed share by reader-norm quartile on the large sign panel, one line per seed, averaged over each eight-block band. Amplifying channels sit mostly in the smallest-reader quartile.

Figure 16: The same final-block channels through training. Rows follow endpoint rank. Left: each channel’s pairing coordinate divided by its maximum absolute value over the saved states; outlined cells are in that state’s top-16. Middle: reader–writer cosine. Right: absolute-coordinate rank among all 8,192 channels. Color magnitudes in the left panel are comparable within a row only.
Figure 15: Backtracking every endpoint core. Each row is one block’s sixteen final core channels, held fixed across the ten saved OLMo checkpoints. Counts are not averaged across blocks.

Figure 22: Corpus composition readings. Rounded percentages in five surface categories, read from raw-lens lists under the corpus taxonomy. Each row contains 384 channels, except the eligible amplifying sets for permuted web (180). Freq. denotes common-token lists; Morph. denotes morphemes; Norm is the writer-norm-matched set. Colors share one scale across streams for these five qualitative categories.

Figure 18: Symmetry along Pythia training. Top: negative-energy share of the symmetric part minus one half; bottom: the fixed-denominator gap G of Equation (27), which the axis writes as C(J̄)− EπC with the trained denominator; one line per block, coloured by relative depth, against training tokens on a log axis with label 0 at the left edge. Ticks above each panel mark the labels of the sparse replay. The 2.8B column uses those labels only.

Figure 13: Formation and recovery controls. (a) Three tiny-seed gap trajectories; gray shows one step-zero null SD, maximized across seeds. (b) Mean block signed-sum z relative to its uninterrupted control. (c) Reader permutation: writer following (solid), reader returning (dashed). In (b,c), lines are seed means, bands their ranges, and colors identify break steps; resumed training ends at step 20k.

Figure 27: What the core writes. (a) Median promoted-token frequency rank across lens depths; more frequent is up. Removing leading unembedding directions narrows the medium core’s separation from its controls. (b) Common-token, morpheme, and semantic-field readings of the same four sets, with colors and markers shared across panels. Each set contains 1,152 medium channels; the full taxonomy and raw-rank comparisons are in Tables 16 and 18.

Figure 25: Flipping opposed writers favors common tokens. Selected writer vectors are negated in every medium block: most negative mh (opposed) or largest positive mh (amplifying). Both panels show selected minus activity- and size-matched flips. Thin curves show three seeds and thick curves their mean; shading marks 16 of 4,096 writers per block. Frequency error bars at 16 are 95% paired-window bootstrap intervals, conditional on the three endpoints.

Figure 17: The conditional comparison across released labels. (a) Blockwise-median ΓC per size at the released labels, equally spaced on the axis; the open marker is the 2.8B label 65k standing in for the duplicated 64k bytes. The gap departs its ensemble mean at labels 512–1k, grows through the middle of training, and plateaus. (b) Per-block ΓC at the final label against relative depth: one hump at every size, near the mean at the first block and closing toward the output.

Figure 8: Endpoint gap along the stack. ΓC by relative depth for the tiny depth ladder, the two small contexts, and the medium; lines are seed means, bands the seed range. Every cohort peaks inside the stack, the tiny ladder at blocks 1, 3, 5 and 6, the small at blocks 4–6, the medium at block 11; the small and medium start near zero at their input block.

Figure 20: Core channel signs across the full corpus grid. The effective coordinate mh of every endpoint core channel, sixteen per block, for six corpora, four depths (four, six, eight and twelve blocks) and three seeds (shape and offset) on the exact-reader panels of Section F.3. Every natural corpus forms opposed cores with a few amplifying members in its last blocks; at twelve blocks the input block adds small positive members; the two order-free controls stay at zero.

Figure 10: Symmetric and antisymmetric energy. (a) Squared norms of the symmetric S (Sym) and antisymmetric K (Antisym) parts of the panel-mean Jacobian, relative to their own re-pairing means, three medium seeds; gray the mean and full 60-draw range. (b) Mean eigenvalue of S divided by its RMS eigenvalue.

Figure 19: Core formation across GPT-2 seeds. Five GPT-2 small replications (Karamcheti et al., 2021). Top: for every block, the balance of the block’s sixteen-channel core, opposed members minus amplifying over sixteen, against training tokens, one line per seed; the dotted line marks twenty tokens per parameter. Bottom left: the tokens at which each block’s core turns majority opposed, one marker per seed, blocks in depth order. Bottom right: the opposed share of all channels by depth band. Step 0 sits at the left edge of each axis.

Table 1: Training hyperparameters. One column per cohort; the small column reads context 1,024 / 256 where its two cells differ. The context-256 SwiGLU family of Figure 3b differs from that cell only in its branch (gated, hidden width 2,046 for parameter matching, 123.5M parameters). papers.abstract: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) generates natural-language questions from structured graph evidence and a target answer. When the input graph is temporal, a valid question must also preserve the answer field, time condition, reference event, and temporal order that determine the answer set. Existing KGQG methods and prompting baselines can produce fluent questions that alter these conditions, causing temporal semantic drift. This paper studies temporal KGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question problem and proposes ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented and constraint-aware generation framework. ChronoSynth first constructs a Temporal Intent State to make the intended question semantics explicit. It then retrieves compatible typed question patterns from an indexed pattern memory, adapts them to the input graph, and validates the generated question. Validation feedback guides revisions when a supported inconsistency is detected. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ demonstrate state-of-the-art generation performance, with ablations supporting the contributions of its components.
authors: Feng Liang, Weixin Zeng, Runhao Zhao, Mingjun Zhou, Shaoshi Yang, Xiang Zhao
bullets: Targets temporal semantic drift in KG question generation, where questions may alter the answer field, time condition, reference event, or temporal order.
Builds a Temporal Intent State to explicitly represent the intended question semantics.
Retrieves compatible typed question patterns, adapts them to the graph, and validates the generated question.
Uses validation feedback to revise questions when supported inconsistencies are detected.
Achieves state-of-the-art generation performance on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ; ablations support its component contributions.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied across the scientific discovery pipeline, from synthesizing literature to generating hypotheses to informing experimental design. A unifying principle behind these tasks is the need to continuously update beliefs as evidence accumulates, for which Bayesian inference provides a natural framework. However, existing work assumes that LLMs cannot carry out principled Bayesian belief updating in context, instead relying on simplifications and heuristics. To challenge this assumption, we present a principled evaluation of Bayesian reasoning capabilities in LLMs, analyzing both the model's internal consistency as well as its ability to recover an externally determined posterior. Specifically, we build an evaluation framework spanning qualitative epistemological examples to probe probabilistic coherence, quantitative benchmarks of Bayesian inference capabilities, and analyses of the impact of non-Bayesian updates on downstream task performance. Across different scenarios, we find that LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating their beliefs in context. However, when equipped with modern reasoning abilities and code execution capabilities, their performance drastically improves, enabling even the close approximation of analytically intractable posteriors. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs with access to appropriate tools could already be used to make complex belief updates in scientific discovery, enabling rapid acceleration of the efficiency and scale of AI-powered scientific discovery.
authors: Linus Filbry, Luckeciano C. Melo, Yarin Gal
bullets: Evaluates whether LLMs can perform principled Bayesian belief updating in context.
Tests probabilistic coherence, quantitative inference, and effects of non-Bayesian updates on downstream tasks.
Finds that LLMs generally violate Bayes’ rule during belief updates.
Reasoning abilities and code execution markedly improve performance, including on analytically intractable posteriors.
Suggests tool-equipped LLMs may support complex belief updates in scientific discovery.

Middle: Posterior Fidelity, as KL divergence between LLM posterior and Bayesian oracle. Right: Downstream Task Performance, assessing how non-Bayesian updates affect success in Experimental Design.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember task-relevant information beyond its short observation window. Existing memory-augmented policies typically retrieve relevant information from history and reason over it at execution time, placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high-level model. To address this challenge, we propose PAL (\textbf{P}lan first, \textbf{A}ct \textbf{L}ater), a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable \texttt{subtask\_list}. A high-level vision-language model (VLM) converts streaming visual observations into the \texttt{subtask\_list}. At execution time, the VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the \texttt{subtask\_list} and passes it to a low-level vision-language-action (VLA) policy. To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two-stage data generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and then uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification to generate training data that better match the state distribution encountered during execution. We evaluate our approach on memory-dependent benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL achieves a \textbf{56.05\%} success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul, at 44.51\%. In real-world experiments across four manipulation tasks, \pal{} reaches \textbf{60.83\%} overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00\%) and FrameSamp-Modul (28.33\%). These results show that proactively writing future-relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves long-horizon visual reasoning and robot control. Code and videos can be found on our website: https://qinghangliu.github.io/pal-webpage/
authors: Qinghang Liu, Conglin Wang, Zongsheng Li, Boyong He, Han Gao, Pengcheng Wang, Tao Sun, Lige Liu, Chang Liu

papers.abstract: Unlike question answering, where a query specifies a perceptual target, open-ended detailed captioning must determine what evidence to acquire and how to integrate it into a coherent global description. We propose Observation-Adaptive Video Captioner (OACap), a caption-centered agent that turns unsupported or missing information into targeted observation requests, uses spatiotemporal tools to acquire evidence, and iteratively verifies and revises the caption. OACap captions consistently improve performance across general video-understanding benchmarks using a fixed text-only reader. To better diagnose the information they preserve, we introduce Factual-Semantic Captioning Bench (FSCap-Bench). Its Core-Support Factuality Score (CSFS) combines claim precision with importance-aware fact coverage and responds as expected to four controlled perturbation types on 93.0-98.3% of valid caption pairs. Its Cross-Modal Semantic Round-Trip Score (CSRS) measures semantic preservation through a video-caption-video-caption round trip by matching atomic facts from source and recovered captions. Together, they connect downstream textual-memory utility with factual and semantic preservation.
authors: Hao Shi, Hong Yan, Xiaoyang Zhang, Qing Cui, Chao Huang

papers.abstract: Recent electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models increasingly emphasize model scale, potentially limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices and in everyday environments. We argue that transferable EEG features can instead be learned with a compact architecture and introduce BrainCodes, a lightweight foundation model pretrained through self-supervised learning on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants. Our architecture combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder that supports arbitrary electrode configurations. The pretraining objective explicitly encourages representations that capture spatial connectivity through channel positional encoding, and sensitivity to narrowband neural oscillations through an auxiliary training objective. Our model matches or surpasses the state of the art across diverse neurophysiological monitoring tasks, including sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive load estimation. BrainCodes transfers effectively to low-resource wearable devices while using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures. Beyond predictive accuracy, our evaluation framework characterizes the geometry and invariances of learned EEG representations across measurable spatial, temporal, and spectral signal properties.
authors: Kleanthis Avramidis, Ivan Tashev, Dimitra Emmanouilidou
bullets: Targets the resource and deployment limitations of increasingly large EEG foundation models.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are now routinely tested on theory of mind: whether they can work out what another person sees, knows, and means. A common design asks the model to report that perspective and then to act for the person, and reads a correct report beside a wrong action as a failure to use the perspective. That reading rests on a quiet assumption: that asking for the report leaves the action unchanged. We show that it does not. In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director who asks for "the largest block". Asking first which blocks the director can see raises the share of replies that choose this hidden block by 12 to 88 percentage points on six GPT models and by 17 on Qwen3.8-27B, even though the models mostly report correctly which blocks the director sees. Reasoning traces and prompt rewordings suggest why: the question shifts how the request is read, from the director's view toward the model's own. When the prompt states what the director knows and refers to, fewer than 1% of replies pair a correct report with a hidden-block choice. Any evaluation that elicits a perspective report before the action it scores needs a baseline without the question, and we deliver one: paired prompts that differ only in that question, a design any perspective-taking benchmark can adopt.
authors: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Kejia Zhang, Jingxin Yang, Youran Sun, Haizhao Yang
bullets: In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director requesting “the largest block.”
Asking models to report the director’s visual perspective first increased hidden-block choices by 12–88 percentage points across six GPT models and by 17 points on Qwen3.8-27B.
Models generally reported the director’s visibility correctly, suggesting the question changed how they interpreted the request rather than simply revealing a lack of perspective-taking.
Explicitly stating what the director knows and refers to reduced correct-report/hidden-choice pairings to below 1%.
The authors recommend paired prompts with and without the perspective question as a baseline for perspective-taking benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.

papers.abstract: Dynamic local community detection tracks the evolving community of designated seed nodes across graph snapshots. However, it faces two critical challenges: temporal supervision uncertainty, where sparse and outdated labels fail to provide seed-specific guidance under topology changes, and unbounded error cascades, where sequential policy transfer accumulates exploration errors over long horizons. To address these challenges, we propose DISRL, a Dual-scale Incremental Semi-supervised Reinforcement Learning framework. DISRL introduces a supervision construction module that dynamically generates seed-specific guidance from sparse known communities, and a dual-scale community exploration module that stabilizes policy evolution by decoupling short-term adaptation within temporal windows from long-term parameter consolidation across windows. Furthermore, we construct a dynamic graph benchmark with diverse community evolution scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DISRL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under various dynamic settings.

papers.abstract: Multimodal ocean modeling remains challenging due to substantial heterogeneity in data structures, physical semantics, and spatiotemporal characteristics across satellite imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy observations. Existing approaches largely focus on task-specific ocean modeling, while learning transferable representations from heterogeneous observations remains an open problem. To address this challenge, we propose YingLan, a multimodal ocean foundation model that integrates physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding, Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC), and ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining. Specifically, the dynamic encoding mechanism generates adaptive input projections conditioned on physical semantics and observation characteristics, enabling flexible representation of heterogeneous ocean variables. STIC models multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies through cross-scale interactions of latent temporal increments. The pretraining strategy further combines masked observation reconstruction with temporal evolution objectives to facilitate the learning of coherent ocean-state representations across different prediction horizons. YingLan is implemented using MindSpore and trained on Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs, demonstrating its compatibility with domestic AI computing infrastructure. In a seven-day sea surface salinity (SSS) forecasting task conducted in the Shenzhen coastal waters, YingLan achieves an average RMSE of 0.687508 PSU, corresponding to relative error reductions of 0.58%, 5.31%, and 12.42% compared with LangYa, XiHe, and GloNet2, respectively. These results provide initial evidence of the model's effectiveness in regional ocean forecasting, while broader cross-task and cross-regional evaluations remain necessary to assess its generalization capabilities.
authors: Sen Jia, Siqi Wei, Junyu Wang, Zijun Lv, Pan Liu, Meng Xu, Xiyou Fu, Yuxi Sun, Qiang Liu, Shuyu Zhang, Lin Mu

papers.abstract: Dynamic scheduling requires dispatching online arrivals while anticipating future jobs, as poor decisions can compound downstream costs under nonlinear tardiness objectives. We show that a pretrained large language model (LLM) can serve as the exogenous component of a structured world model, forecasting uncertain future job arrivals. Specifically, we exploit an afterstate decomposition, which separates known deterministic shop transitions from uncertain exogenous job arrivals, enabling the LLM to forecast only the latter through a compact belief representation. Building on this, we develop Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP), which combines an evolved, belief-conditioned dispatching strategy with short scenario-based rollouts. A surprise-triggered refresh mechanism queries the LLM only when newly observed arrivals deviate sufficiently from previous forecast, and online residual self-calibration further conditions the LLM on its recent forecast errors to handle nonstationary arrivals. Across diverse arrival distributions, AWMP reduces weighted tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop and 22-46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks, relative to the best of eight classical priority-dispatching rules.
authors: Ni Zhang, Haofeng Yuan, Jianan Zhou, Shiji Song, Zhiguang Cao
bullets: Targets dynamic job-shop scheduling, where poor dispatch decisions can compound downstream tardiness.
Uses afterstate decomposition to let the LLM model only uncertain exogenous arrivals via a compact belief representation.
Combines belief-conditioned dispatching with short scenario-based rollouts in Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP).
Reduces LLM queries through surprise-triggered refreshes and adapts to nonstationary arrivals using online residual self-calibration.
Across diverse arrival distributions, weighted tardiness decreases by 6–21% on dynamic job-shop and 22–46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks versus the best of eight classical rules.

papers.abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.
authors: Yongqiang Chen, Chenxi Liu, Deyu Zou, Zhenhao Chen, Tongliang Liu, Bo Han, Kun Zhang

papers.abstract: Language models are being explored as the interface through which space robots interpret operator commands and select among verified skills. Running them onboard calls for low-bit compression, and flight use adds requirements that generic post-training quantization leaves implicit: a fixed memory budget and storage format, a static artifact under configuration control, and behavior close to the full-precision model validated on the ground. We treat compression as a ground-segment step and study QSelect, which composes one static low-bit model from compatible AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound checkpoints by assigning each linear module to one quantizer family and scoring every substitution at the final next-token distribution. The default fidelity mode needs no labels or tuned thresholds and accepts a substitution only when the forward KL divergence from the BF16 reference decreases; an optional target-adapted mode adds answer likelihood on a small labeled set. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.2-3B at 3 and 4 bits, composed models reach lower mean held-out perplexity than every single-family model in all six settings, and the fidelity mode lowers perplexity and KL further. In a matched scaffold, final-output scoring gives lower held-out KL than representation-similarity scoring in all 12 paired runs. With labels from training or development splits of the evaluated task families, the target-adapted mode raises 3-bit pooled accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points over the best single-family model. At 3 bits, unquantized embedding and output layers make up 43-46% of the packed artifact. All evaluations use general-domain benchmarks on a ground GPU; space-domain tasks and flight hardware are left to future work.

papers.abstract: Finding K most similar elements for a query in a large gallery of neural network (NN) embeddings is essential in various areas of computer science and industrial applications of artificial intelligence. This paper proposes search algorithms for structured latent spaces (LS) of NNs which allow to speed up top K item retrieval owing to O(1) complexity small candidate gallery subset search. ArcFace-pretrained IResNet50 models are finetuned using Latent Space Configuration (LSC) methodology to obtain new distribution of embeddings with desired geometric properties. Applying the proposed algorithms to embeddings obtained from finetuned models leads to several times speed-up over baseline exhaustive search. Specifically, we report up to 3 times speed-up on GPU and 40% speed-up on CPU compared to the baseline method GPU speed. These results are obtained for the original and reduced numbers of LS dimensions. The results show that LS dimensionality reduction allows to further accelerate the search and even improve rank-N metrics.
bullets: Targets efficient retrieval of the K most similar items from large embedding galleries.
Fine-tunes ArcFace-pretrained IResNet50 models to impose structured geometric properties on the latent space.
Uses structured latent-space search with an O(1)-complexity candidate subset instead of exhaustive comparison.
Reports up to 3× GPU speed-up and 40% CPU speed-up relative to the stated baseline.
Dimensionality reduction further accelerates retrieval and can improve rank-N metrics.

papers.abstract: Managed and wild bees sustain roughly a third of the global food products, yet colonies face mounting stress from climate-change including extreme weather patterns, altered parasite and disease patterns. Timely assessment of colony condition such as understanding colony strength, brood area, honey and pollen storage, comb usage, is essential to adaptive management. However, manual hive frame inspection is slow, costly, and quality depends on scarce expertise. We present an artificial targeted intelligent system framework focusing on edge deployable pipeline that turns hive frame photographs into interpretable and action-oriented inspection report. The pipeline includes an object detector to detect biologically-meaningful comb-cell classes; detections are distilled into structured fact schema; facts are converted into constrained factual text; the text triggers a grounded knowledge-base for interpretations and recommendations. Knowledge-base entries are required to be triggerable by evidence expressed in the fact schema. We built our system based on open source FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset and favour reproducible, edge-deployable models over large general purpose frontier models. We additionally release FAIRHiveText-1K dataset that turns FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset into interchangeable facts and text interpretation of the facts, making it easy for further LLM-based research into this area. We also propose a pathway to develop the grounded knowledge-base that will be helpful in providing interpretable and actionable reports from the facts.
authors: Asaduz Zaman, Mohaimenul Azam Khan Raiaan, Malika Nisal Ratnayake
bullets: Addresses the slow, costly, and expertise-dependent nature of manual hive-frame inspection.
Detects biologically meaningful comb-cell classes and distills detections into a structured fact schema.
Generates constrained factual text that triggers interpretable recommendations from a grounded knowledge base.
Prioritizes reproducible, edge-deployable models over large general-purpose language models.
Introduces FAIRHiveText-1K and outlines a pathway for developing evidence-triggered knowledge-base entries.

figures.caption: Figure 2: On-device inference pipeline. A YOLO-based detector processes a hive-frame image, and a fact builder combines its prediction with inspection metadata into structured frame facts, which an Edge-LLM renders as a frame description. The description retrieves the top-k supporting claims from the ApiExpert RAG-KB (Fig. 1), and the same model generates a personalised inspection report conditioned on the frame description, retrieved claims, and hive context and history. Completed reports are stored in the hive history, informing subsequent inspection.

Figure 1: Knowledge-base construction. Annotations from FAIRHiveFrames-1K yield structured facts, which an LLM expands into FAIRHiveText-1K with round-trip validation; external domain knowledge is scored for quality and fact-schema groundability, then expert-validated into the ApiExpert RAG-KB.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have shown strong potential for robot manipulation by jointly learning visual dynamics and executable actions. However, their video and action objectives do not explicitly constrain the 3D geometry that is crucial for precise manipulation. Recently, geometry-aware WAMs introduce depth or 4D prediction branches, whereas representation alignment methods supervise intermediate WAM features with pretrained 3D foundation models. Yet we find that such pointwise alignment benefits the video features but degrades action learning, since dense geometric feature targets overly restrict compact action features. To address this limitation, we propose Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF), which transfers geometric priors from a frozen 3D foundation model by aligning pairwise feature relations instead of pointwise features. Specifically, RGF applies three complementary relational objectives, where intra-frame and cross-view relations transfer scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to the video features, while action-temporal relations couple action dynamics to geometric scene evolution. Applied only during training, RGF requires no explicit geometry branch or extra inference module. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate the effectiveness of Relational Geometry Forcing, showing consistent gains across diverse manipulation scenarios and WAM paradigms.
authors: Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Jiabing Yang, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: WAMs lack explicit constraints on the 3D geometry needed for precise manipulation.
Pointwise alignment with 3D foundation-model features can help video representations but hurt compact action representations.
RGF aligns intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal feature relations to transfer geometry, correspondences, and scene-action dynamics.
The method is training-only and adds no explicit geometry branch or inference module.
Experiments in simulation and the real world show consistent gains across diverse manipulation settings and WAM paradigms.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF). The WAM predicts future multi-view frames and an action chunk through its video and action experts, while a frozen 3D foundation model encodes the same frames into per-timestep 3D features. RGF aligns pairwise relations among intermediate video and action features with those induced by the 3D foundation model through intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal objectives. All auxiliary components are removed during inference.

Figure 1: Geometry transfer paradigms for WAMs. (a) Explicit geometric modeling adds a geometry branch that predicts depth or 4D outputs. (b) Pointwise geometric alignment regresses intermediate features toward dense geometric targets, which benefits the video expert but degrades action learning. (c) RGF aligns pairwise feature relations instead, benefiting both the video and action experts.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), particularly through group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), has emerged as a central paradigm for the post-training of large language models (LLMs). While RLVR is highly effective at enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, it commonly induces \textit{distribution sharpening}, whereby the policy distribution becomes excessively peaked and rare-yet-correct trajectories are progressively suppressed, thus diminishing sample diversity. To this end, we promote flat-reward optima in RLVR to smooth the policy distribution. We theoretically link flat reward RLVR to reduced distribution sharpening, and empirically show improved sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy. Our method, called \texttt{Flat}-RLVR, searches for flat reward regions via sharpness-aware minimization during LLM post-training, combining this with GRPO variants to achieve better trade-offs between sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.
authors: Yeonbum Kim, Hyun Kyu Lee, Sung Whan Yoon
bullets: RLVR can sharpen LLM policy distributions, suppressing rare but correct reasoning trajectories.
Flat-RLVR promotes flatter reward optima to mitigate this distribution sharpening.
The method combines sharpness-aware minimization with GRPO variants during post-training.
Theory connects flatter reward solutions with reduced distribution sharpening.
Experiments report higher sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy, balancing sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.

papers.abstract: Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.
authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Bozhou Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited coverage of offline demonstrations for contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical deployment states.
Uses provenance-conditioned supervised learning to update policies online from human- and policy-generated data.
Evaluated on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, improving task progress and full-task completion over warm-start policies and matched offline demonstrations.
Performs comparably to a fixed-policy data-collection baseline while providing updated checkpoints during deployment.
Each task-specific post-training session completes in under one hour, with learning and checkpoint handling running asynchronously.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The pipeline of TIDE. The robot executes policy actions with human takeover when needed. The system records executed actions and labels their human or policy source. The learner combines this online data with offline demonstrations to update the video model and action expert using provenance conditioning. Updated policies return to the robot at episode boundaries, while data collection and learning proceed asynchronously within the same deployment session.
Fig. 3. Real-world evaluation tasks. Initial and successful final states for four bimanual manipulation tasks.

Fig. 6. Autonomous evaluation over 20 no-takeover rollouts per method–task pair. (a) Mean milestone-normalized task progress. (b) Binary full-task completion. Labels report completed rollouts out of 20.
Fig. 4. Real-robot setup. The bimanual UR5e platform uses Robotiq 2F85 grippers, one third-person RealSense D455 camera, and two wrist-mounted RealSense D405 cameras.

Fig. 5. Action representation study. Offline-only comparison of eight action spaces using the same data, initialization, and training budget. Jointrelative actions perform best and are used in subsequent experiments.

(b) TIDE achieves higher normalized task progress than variants without provenance conditioning or using only human-executed online data, highlighting the value of source conditioning and learning from policyexecuted experience.

For each task, the top and bottom rows show no-takeover rollouts from the warm-start policy and final TIDE checkpoint, respectively, with time progressing from left to right. The warm-start policy fails to complete the tasks in these examples, whereas TIDE completes the full manipulation sequences, illustrating improved autonomous execution after online post-training.

papers.selection_reason: Human-in-the-loop online post-training for robot manipulation directly fits embodied manipulation and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: TIDE enables robots to improve manipulation policies during deployment by learning directly from human interventions and policy rollouts without critics, rewards, or action scorers.

papers.abstract: As-built BIM reconstruction from point clouds demands semantic, volumetric, parametric, and editable building components, beyond 2D layouts or planar abstractions. Yet existing scan-to-BIM pipelines often rely on handcrafted rules, heuristic optimization, or manual correction, while learning-based methods fall short of recovering wall thickness, opening geometry, and component-level BIM structure. We introduce CRAB, a BIM-ready cuboid reconstruction framework that encodes walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns as compact architectural cuboids with IFC-compatible semantics and parameters. CRAB bridges point clouds and editable BIM by combining ProposalNet, which predicts coarse component cuboids, with AssemblyNet, a relation-aware Flow Matching model that refines geometry, predicts structural relationships, and enables automatic structural correction and human-guided editing. To address limited cuboid-level supervision, we extend Structured3D with component-wise cuboid annotations and construct cuboid-based procedural scenes. Experiments show CRAB surpasses floor plan and plane-based alternatives in component completeness, geometric accuracy, and generalization. For interior wall thickness estimation, CRAB achieves a mean error of 2.80 cm, with 79.50% of matched walls within 3 cm. The project page is available at https://vcc.tech/research/2026/CRAB.
authors: Haoran Xiong, Jing Wang, Shanshan Pan, Zihao Yan, Minglun Gong, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets scan-to-BIM limitations in recovering wall thickness, openings, and structured building components.
Represents walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns as compact architectural cuboids with semantic and parametric information.
Combines ProposalNet for coarse cuboid prediction with AssemblyNet for relation-aware refinement, structural correction, and human-guided editing.
Extends Structured3D with cuboid annotations and creates procedural cuboid-based scenes to support training.
Reports a 2.80 cm mean error for interior wall thickness, with 79.50% of matched walls estimated within 3 cm.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of CRAB. Given a raw indoor point cloud, ProposalNet encodes the scan and autoregressively predicts an initial set of semantic cuboids for walls, doors, and windows. AssemblyNet represents each proposal with centerline-based cuboid tokens augmented by semantic, relation, and edit-control flags, and refines them through intra-cuboid, inter-cuboid, and cuboid–point attention. A velocity head performs relation-aware flow-matching refinement of cuboid geometry, while a relation head infers structural dependencies such as wall adjacency and door/window affiliation. The refined cuboids and relations are finally instantiated as editable BIM-ready components, converting unstructured scans into component-level architectural models.

Fig. 7. Qualitative comparison on Structured3D. Each column shows one scene, with rows showing the input point cloud, floor plan baselines, plane baselines, our cuboid reconstruction, and the ground truth. Compared with RoomFormer, CAGE, SceneScript, and SpatialLM, CRAB recovers more coherent wall structures and more accurate door and window geometry in ambiguous, non-Manhattan, and incomplete regions.

Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison on real-world scanned scenes. Each row shows one scene: input point cloud (left), SpatialLM (middle), and ours (right). CRAB better preserves wall continuity and opening geometry under practical noise and clutter.

Fig. 4. Qualitative comparison with a plane-based representation. Zoomed views compare the same local structures in GT, CRAB, and SpatialLM. CRAB’s volumetric cuboids better preserve wall thickness, component extent, and opening-wall consistency than the plane-based representation.

Fig. 6. BIM conversion from cuboids and relations. The same cuboid-relation graph supports different junction assignments: Corner-Joint BIM uses explicit corner joints, Cross-Joint BIM uses explicit cross joints, and WallIntegrated BIM merges junction regions into connected wall elements.

Fig. 2. Representative samples from CrabSet, combining S3D-derived residential and procedurally synthesized scenes for cuboid-level supervision. The synthesized subsets vary boundaries, scales, and corridor-centered layouts, covering non-uniform wall thicknesses, non-Manhattan contours, service shafts, and diverse circulation patterns.

Table 1. Structural supervision in indoor building datasets. We compare whether each dataset provides 2D floor plan, structured 3D plane, and volumetric component-level annotations for BIM-oriented reconstruction.

Table 2. Quantitative comparison of representation choices on Structured3D. CRAB improves both component recovery and BIM-critical volumetric attributes, especially wall thickness and opening height, over floor plan and plane-based alternatives. Best and second-best results are highlighted in green and blue.

Table 4. Comparison of full-scene refinement with plane-based and cuboidbased AssemblyNet, using planes from SpatialLM and cuboids from ProposalNet, respectively. Cuboid-based AssemblyNet improves the initial reconstruction results, whereas plane-based AssemblyNet degrades them.

Table 5. Ablation of cuboid parameterization. Oriented boxes perform well on compact components such as doors and windows, but are less suitable for long and thin walls, where longitudinal extent and thickness play strongly asymmetric geometric roles. Our centerline-based parameterization explicitly separates these two factors, improving wall geometry and thickness reconstruction andmaking it more suitable for BIM-oriented reconstruction.

papers.title: CRAB: Cuboid-based Representation for As-built BIM from Point Clouds
papers.tldr: CRAB reconstructs editable, IFC-compatible BIM components from point clouds using cuboid proposals and relation-aware geometric refinement.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) understand music, yet struggle to locate a described moment in time. We ask whether this reflects missing temporal information or a bottleneck in how the time span is extracted. Using a paired-query probe built from Slakh2100 stem activations, we attach a state query (e.g., ``only piano and bass are playing'') and a change query (e.g., ``the guitar drops out, leaving piano and bass'') to the same span and vary how much preceding audio the model is shown. Across frozen LALMs, three ways of extracting the span ask different questions: full-track prompting asking whether the model can say when; windowed yes/no scoring asking whether it verifies the moment when handed the segment, and whether it needs what came before; attention asking whether it can find the moment on its own. State queries score above baseline without context, while change queries improve with preceding context in most short-segment models; 30s padded encoders show no comparable recovery. Prompting and attention expose almost none of this. Prompting failures thus understate what LALMs can verify, though not what they can locate, by an amount set by query type and encoder.
bullets: LALMs struggle to identify when a described musical moment occurs, raising questions about missing temporal information versus extraction bottlenecks.
A paired-query probe compares state descriptions (what is playing) with change descriptions (what just stopped) over the same audio span and varying preceding context.
State queries perform above baseline without context, while change queries usually benefit from preceding audio in short-segment models.
Full-track prompting and attention reveal little of this contextual ability; windowed yes/no scoring exposes more verification capacity.
Thirty-second padded encoders do not show comparable recovery, indicating that effects depend on query type and encoder design.

A sparse texture (only piano and bass) that begins right after a stem departure (guitar) becomes one target span with two queries sharing the same audio, so chance is identical. (b) In Exp. 2 the model sees a window that ends with the judged 2 s segment and begins C seconds earlier; at C=0 the departure lies outside the window and cannot be verified.

Fig. 2. Exp. 2, oracle-duration R@1@0.5 versus preceding context C for state (blue) and change (red) queries on the 570 evaluation pairs. Change queries recover with context in three of the four short-segment models (left); the three 30 s padded models (right) degrade as C grows regardless of training.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of temporal information extraction in frozen audio-language models; meaningful for multimodal model understanding.
papers.title: Heard But Not Said: Prompting Understates Temporal Information of Musical Moments in Frozen Large Audio-Language Models
papers.tldr: Frozen large audio-language models can often verify musical states, but prompting and attention substantially understate their ability to use temporal context and locate musical changes.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models have emerged as an alternative to autoregressive models, enabling parallel token generation. However, standard masked diffusion language models use a shared noise schedule across positions without explicitly encoding which positions should be resolved first. Many tasks exhibit a natural priority among positions: document titles and section headings can guide the generation of body text, while Sudoku cells determined directly from the initial clues can help resolve more difficult cells. To incorporate this notion of priority (or hierarchy) among token positions, we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model (HMDLM), which augments each token position with a hierarchy level available as part of the training data, and requires zero or minimal additional annotations. It factors generation into two passes: the first predicts a hierarchy distribution over masked positions, the second predicts token distributions conditioned on it. Giving each hierarchy level its own noise schedule induces a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier while keeping decoding fully parallel. Our formulation is mathematically grounded, and we re-derive the forward and reverse processes and the NELBO for this factorization. Our evaluation shows that for the task of language generation on LM1B, HMDLM reduces perplexity by more than 1.5 points over Anchored Diffusion Language Model (ADLM), a recently proposed strong diffusion baseline; on WikiHow, we see a drop in perplexity of up to 4.4 pts on ADLM and up to 7 pts against MDLM. An LLM judge on WikiHow prefers HMDLM generations (the two variants combined) more than $2\times$ as often as the baseline. On the task of solving Sudoku puzzles requiring multi-step reasoning, it improves solution accuracy by up to $8.6\%$ absolute points over existing diffusion baselines.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
authors: Hong Ting Tsang, Boyi Zhang, Haoyu Huang, Jiaxin Bai, Yufei Li, Yisen Gao, Zhongwei Xie, Hongyu Luo, Jeff Z. Pan, Yangqiu Song
bullets: Evaluates 923 questions across persona-grounded histories spanning 11–24 sessions and four modalities.
Targets meaningful spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media.
Uses matched controls to isolate failures in representation, retrieval, delivery, and reading.
Finds modality-dependent representation loss, substantial residual reading errors even with gold evidence, and weak abstention.
Moves evaluation beyond a single leaderboard score toward component-level diagnosis.
