papers.abstract: Predictive representations for robot manipulation should connect scene geometry with the state changes induced by actions. Our intuition is that understanding what an action will change starts with understanding where things are: complementary RGB and depth observations ground a common scene representation from which to infer those changes. Guided by this intuition, we introduce \textbf{DepState-JEPA}, a dual-stream RGB--Depth joint-embedding predictive architecture that connects spatial understanding with action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, \textbf{DepState}. Built on V-JEPA~2.1, the framework uses depth both as a complementary observation stream and to ground both modalities in metric 3D space, aggregating shared information into DepState while retaining modality-private features for decoding. Ray-conditioned readouts predict local features without target depth; after an action-conditioned transition, the same decoders predict future RGB and depth features using the predicted state and fixed initial private features. Robot-state readouts provide recursive proprioceptive inputs; object-trajectory supervision and calibrated forward kinematics shape state learning through motion targets and joint--TCP consistency. Comparisons show stronger RGB-encoder transfer after RGB-D adaptation, feature completion, conditioned visual forecasting, and manipulation success. Within-model ablations identify contributions from depth content, metric coordinates, and future-state matching, with additional control gains from FK regularization.
authors: Xiujian Liang, Liuyuan Na, Zehao Du, Jiacheng Xu, Weixi Song, Mingyang Sun, Xingjun Ma, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun

Uses a dual-stream RGB–Depth JEPA architecture with shared DepState features and modality-private information.

Adds robot-state readouts, object-trajectory supervision, and forward-kinematics consistency to shape state learning.
Reports gains in RGB-encoder transfer, feature completion, visual forecasting, and manipulation success; ablations support depth, metric coordinates, future-state matching, and FK regularization.

papers.abstract: Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras. As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings. However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets. Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated. Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.
bullets: Thermal sensing supports activity understanding in darkness while exposing less personal appearance information than RGB.
The evaluation covers fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and withholding unsupported answers on two person-centric thermal datasets.
Models recognize broad activities but often miss coughing, sneezing, and yawning, and generate inaccurate timelines.
Models frequently hallucinate actions involving objects; preprocessing and extra reasoning provide only limited, model-dependent improvements.
Variable abstention behavior limits reliability for practical robotic use, despite evaluation across locally deployable and robotics-focused VLMs.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate why vision-language models (VLMs) produce errors by decomposing them into two sources: visual-representation failures, in which the visual evidence required for the correct answer is not encoded, and visual-utilization failures, in which this evidence is encoded but not successfully used. We propose to estimate the visual-utilization failure rate using lightweight probes and derive theoretical bounds on the true rate that account for probe imperfections. We introduce VELens (Visual Evidence Lens), a rank-based probe that traces visual evidence for both a target object and its ground-truth attribute, such as color, material, or shape, across VLM layers. We evaluate VELens on over 6,000 images using LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Our method achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.95 and 0.91, respectively, and outperforms alternative probes in both low-resource and unseen-attribute settings. Using it to diagnose errors, we estimate that visual-utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%, respectively. Overall, our study identifies visual utilization as the dominant bottleneck in VLMs and suggests that a central opportunity for improvement lies in developing better mechanisms to locate, route, and use the visual information they already encode.
authors: Anat Veikherman, Mor Ventura, Nitay Calderon, Lihi Zelnik-Manor, Roi Reichart
bullets: Decomposes VLM errors into visual-representation failures and visual-utilization failures.
Introduces VELens, a rank-based probe that traces object and attribute evidence across model layers.
Uses lightweight probes with theoretical bounds to estimate utilization-failure rates despite probe imperfections.
Evaluated on over 6,000 images with LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B; VELens achieves ROC-AUCs of 0.95 and 0.91 and outperforms alternative probes.
Estimated utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%.

papers.title: Encoded but Unused: Bounding the Sources of VLM Errors
papers.tldr: The paper finds that most VLM errors arise from failing to use visual evidence that is already encoded, rather than failing to encode it.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning offers a powerful framework not only for imitation learning but also for understanding the neural computations supporting social interactions and decision-making. Inferring rewards from interacting agents is challenging because observed choices reflect both personal preferences and expectations about others. Existing methods often require additional environment interaction, repeated policy optimization as an inner loop, or restrictive assumptions about environment dynamics and action spaces, limiting their applicability to fixed behavioral datasets. We introduce Multi-Agent Unilateral Inverse Temporal Difference Learning (MA-UITD), an offline method for inferring explicit agent-specific rewards from joint demonstrations in continuous-state environments with either discrete or bounded continuous actions. Its core idea is to represent the long-term consequences of each agent's own actions through belief-conditioned successor features that average over other agents' behavior. Shared reward features and agent-specific preference vectors connect these unilateral values to the target reward function, while inverse temporal-difference consistency and noise-contrastive behavioral learning enable inference without known dynamics or an inner policy-optimization loop. Across simulated cooperative, competitive, and general-sum tasks, MA-UITD outperforms baselines in discrete-action settings and infers behaviorally compatible reward profiles in continuous-action settings. When applied to experimentally collected social-foraging trajectories, MA-UITD inferred distinct spatial and interaction-dependent reward structures for leaders and followers, providing a quantitative characterization of latent behavioral objectives that may be relevant for understanding the neural computations underlying social behavior.
authors: Zeyuan Zhang, Yiyun Yang, Yuan Cheng, Herbert Zheng Wu, Yusi Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of disentangling individual preferences from expectations about interacting agents in fixed behavioral datasets.
Uses belief-conditioned unilateral successor features to model each agent’s long-term action consequences while averaging over others’ behavior.
Combines shared reward features, agent-specific preferences, inverse temporal-difference consistency, and noise-contrastive behavioral learning.
Supports continuous-state environments with discrete or bounded continuous actions and avoids known dynamics or an inner optimization loop.
Outperforms baselines in simulated discrete-action tasks and identifies distinct leader–follower reward structures in social-foraging trajectories.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at 2D recognition but often fail to maintain consistent 3D relations across sparse viewpoints, leading to spatial hallucinations under occlusion and perspective changes. Existing methods commonly fuse all frames with dense geometry, incurring substantial computation and context overhead while encouraging blind reliance on imperfect estimators. We present Think-Capture, a query-conditioned framework that first identifies task-critical objects and then acquires their geometry on demand. A 3D toolkit lifts zero-shot masks into a common coordinate frame, and a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction compresses object and camera states into structured text. Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains the VLM on cases in which geometry either helps or misleads, teaching it when to use tool evidence and when to fall back on visual cues. Think-Capture-4B reaches 54.4% on MindCube-Tiny (+21.5 points over its backbone), 39.1% on the MMSI-Bench positional subset (+7.9), and 42.8% on ViewSpatial (+5.2). It also remains robust under coordinate and mask perturbations. The full stack fits one 24 GB GPU and serves as an asynchronous high-level reasoner on an Agibot G1. Our code is available at https://github.com/819346675/Think-Capture.
authors: Junjie Wang, Zhihao Yuan, Yunhan Tang, Sheng Xu, Jiaqi Mao, Xiaoyu Ye, Yueru Luo, Xu Yan, Chun-Mei Feng, Zhen Li
bullets: Targets spatial hallucinations caused by occlusion, perspective changes, and sparse viewpoints.
Identifies task-critical objects, lifts their zero-shot masks into a shared 3D frame, and compresses geometry into structured text.
Uses hierarchical GRPO to teach the VLM when to trust geometric tools and when to rely on visual evidence.
Think-Capture-4B improves over its backbone by 21.5, 7.9, and 5.2 points on MindCube-Tiny, MMSI-Bench positional, and ViewSpatial, respectively.
The system remains robust to coordinate and mask perturbations, fits on one 24 GB GPU, and runs as an asynchronous reasoner on an Agibot G1.

papers.selection_reason: Query-conditioned active 3D geometry acquisition for VLM spatial reasoning; strongly fits spatial intelligence and 3D-aware multimodal modeling.
papers.title: Think-Capture: Active 3D Geometry Acquisition for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Think-Capture improves VLM spatial reasoning by selectively acquiring and symbolically representing 3D geometry when it is useful, rather than densely processing every view.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering from low-altitude UAV imagery must deliver timely and accurate judgments to support disaster response under limited edge computing resources. Routine questions may be answered through direct decisions, whereas more challenging questions may benefit from step-by-step reasoning. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving models' visual understanding and generative reasoning capabilities, with limited exploration of efficient direct decision-making and its adaptive coordination with generative reasoning. We develop Disaster-S1 based on a vision-language model adapted to the disaster domain. Trained for option discrimination, it outputs a probability distribution over answer options in a single multimodal forward pass for fast decision-making. We further propose DisasterRoute, a dual-system routing framework that combines prediction confidence with disaster evidence to decide whether to accept the initial answer or invoke the disaster reasoning model DisasterVL for review. By allocating inference computation on demand, the framework retains the efficiency of direct decision-making and improves overall question-answering accuracy through selective review. Experiments on DisasterBench show that Disaster-S1 achieves superior accuracy with low latency, while DisasterRoute further improves accuracy through selective review at substantially lower latency than full reasoning.
authors: Tan Zhang, Xing Deng, Lu Zhang, Xiaofeng Zhu, Ping Hu
bullets: Targets timely UAV-based disaster QA under limited edge-computing resources.
Disaster-S1 performs fast option discrimination in a single multimodal forward pass.
Routes answers using both prediction confidence and disaster evidence.
Invokes DisasterVL selectively for review instead of applying full reasoning to every question.
On DisasterBench, selective review improves accuracy while maintaining substantially lower latency than full reasoning.

papers.selection_reason: Dual-system routing between fast direct VQA decisions and generative reasoning; relevant to multimodal LLM deployment and selective computation allocation.
papers.title: DisasterRoute: Evidence-Guided Dual-System Routing for Visual Disaster Question Answering
papers.tldr: DisasterRoute efficiently improves visual disaster question answering by routing only uncertain or insufficiently supported answers to a slower reasoning model.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires video-LLMs to process incoming video continuously while answering user queries with low latency. Recent methods reduce query-time cost by prefilling frames into KV caches during idle time and reusing the cached KVs at query time. To bound per-frame computation over unbounded video streams, these methods restrict the context available during prefill. This creates a fundamental context mismatch: the restricted context may omit information needed to properly contextualize video tokens, yet, still contain information irrelevant to the eventual query, which is unknown during prefill. We propose FrameBlend, a simple yet effective plug-and-play method to address this mismatch through selective KV recomputation, without requiring any additional training. At query time, FrameBlend re-prefills selected video tokens using query-relevant context and replaces their cached KVs with recomputed ones. Crucially, this recomputation enables shorter attention windows during idle-time prefill, substantially reducing prefill cost while improving accuracy. Experiments across three SVU frameworks and five streaming and offline benchmarks demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 3.9 pp. On RVS-Ego, FrameBlend reduces per-frame prefill FLOPs by over 20% and total processing time by 14-59% for retrieval-based frameworks, including the cost of query-time recomputation. These results demonstrate that a simple change in how contextualization is distributed between idle time and query time can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for SVU.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Sangyoon Lee, Jaeho Lee
bullets: Problem: Idle-time KV prefill must use restricted context, causing a mismatch because relevant query information is unavailable and irrelevant context may be included.
Method: At query time, re-prefill selected video tokens with query-relevant context and replace their cached KVs; no additional training is required.
Contribution: Enables shorter idle-time attention windows, lowering prefill computation while preserving or improving contextualization.
Results: Across three SVU frameworks and five benchmarks, accuracy improves by up to 3.9 percentage points.
Efficiency: On RVS-Ego, per-frame prefill FLOPs decrease by over 20%, while total processing time drops by 14–59% for retrieval-based frameworks.

papers.selection_reason: Selective KV recomputation for streaming video LLMs; directly combines video understanding with cache-efficiency and memory reduction.
papers.title: Cache Locally, Recompute Selectively for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FrameBlend improves streaming video understanding by selectively recomputing cached video-token representations with query-relevant context, reducing preprocessing cost while increasing accuracy.

papers.abstract: Personalized reward models require user-specific preference comparisons, but collecting such feedback is costly and provides only limited supervision for each user. At the same time, large pools of responses can be generated without user identities or preference labels, yet existing personalized reward models leave this data unused. Directly learning from these responses is difficult because pairwise objectives constrain relative scores within a prompt, whereas pseudo-labeling individual responses requires scores that are comparable across prompts for the same user. We propose \textbf{PerSPL} (Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning), a backbone-agnostic framework that uses pair-mean score centering to stabilize this cross-prompt score coordinate and iteratively turns unlabeled responses into user-specific training signals. Against seven representative baselines across four benchmarks---PersonalLLM, HelpSteer2, Reddit TLDR, and Chatbot Arena---PerSPL achieves the highest reported mean accuracy among the evaluated methods for both seen and unseen users. The two latter benchmarks provide real-user preference comparisons in summarization and open-domain chatbot interaction, respectively. These results indicate that unlabeled responses can provide additional supervision for personalized reward modeling when per-user preference labels are scarce.
authors: Xiaoan Xu, Tingzhou Wei, Juncheng Dong, Korel Gundem, Ethan X. Fang, Zhengling Qi
bullets: Addresses the high cost and limited coverage of collecting user-specific preference comparisons.
Uses pair-mean score centering to make scores comparable across prompts for each user.
Iteratively pseudo-labels unlabeled responses to augment personalized preference training.
Is backbone-agnostic and evaluated against seven baselines across four benchmarks.
Reports the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods for both seen and unseen users.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of PERSPL. A small set of labeled comparisons identifies each user’s preferences, while pair-mean score centering makes reward scores more comparable across prompts. A calibrator fitted separately for each user assigns pseudo-labels to confident responses from a shared unpaired pool and discards ambiguous ones. The reward model is then trained iteratively on both labeled and pseudo-labeled data.

papers.abstract: Autonomous industrial inspection requires strictly deterministic real-time inference under tight memory and computational constraints. However, existing Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) models suffer from prohibitive scaling: dense temporal memory grows with spatial resolution and sequence length, while fixed-capacity decoders fail to exploit the inherent sparsity of industrial scenes, creating a practical memory wall on resource-constrained edge platforms. We present DetM-Tracker, a streamlined VIS framework for autonomous industrial inspection, where target objects often exhibit highly similar appearance under constrained "micro" fields of view. DetM-Tracker eliminates architectural redundancy through three synergistic components: (1) Compact Scalar Memory, which condenses high-dimensional instance features into four-scalar descriptors, reducing temporal memory complexity from $O(T \cdot N \cdot R)$ to $O(T \cdot \hat{N})$. This mechanism effectively compresses frame-level representations into a bank of active instances, where $R$ denotes resolution, $N$ and $\hat{N}$ represent global and window-specific instance counts, respectively and $T$ the temporal window size; and (2) Dynamic Instance Channels, which adaptively allocate query capacity according to the actual number of visible objects; and (3) Entropy-Gated Skip Connection, which concentrates computational budget on high-uncertainty spatial regions to refine object boundaries in a single forward pass without auxiliary refinement heads. Our approach effectively bridges the gap between modern VIS models and the practical demands of industrial edge deployment, reducing inference latency by approximately 20$\times$ and VRAM consumption by 6$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art dense-feature baselines.
authors: You-Rui Lin, Jen-Chieh Wu, Tzu-Ti Wei, Jen-Jee Chen, Yu-Chee Tseng
bullets: Targets the memory and compute limits of edge platforms running autonomous industrial inspection.
Uses Compact Scalar Memory to reduce temporal memory complexity from O(T·N·R) to O(T·N̂) with four-scalar instance descriptors.
Dynamically allocates instance channels based on the number of visible objects.
Uses entropy-gated skip connections to refine uncertain object boundaries in a single forward pass.
Reports approximately 20× lower inference latency and 6× lower VRAM use than dense-feature baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the DetM-Tracker Architecture. The framework decouples VIS into persistent identity and dynamic temporal reasoning. Past states are distilled into Compact Scalar Memory s, which is processed by a memory encoder to produce resolution-invariant temporal tokens XM . These tokens provide context for Memory Attention to refine current-frame image features. The Mask Decoder then facilitates mutual refinement between image-conditioned features and Global Object Queries Pobj to generate initial masks. Finally, Entropy-Gated Skip Connection H(H(·)) selectively integrates high-resolution cues to resolve boundary ambiguities in a single forward pass.

Figure 6: Qualitative Comparison Across Environmental Complexities. While foundation models (SAM 2/3) exhibit mask bleeding and fragmentation in dense industrial arrays, DetM-Tracker maintains high topological fidelity. Especially in "Hard" scenarios with severe occlusions, our framework precisely resolves individual instance boundaries where baselines collapse into monolithic or incomplete masks.

Figure 7: Evaluation of Long-term Temporal Stability. Per-frame precision measured over a 300-frame industrial sequence. While foundation models like SAM 2.1 and LiVOS exhibit rapid precision decay and drift after initial frames, DetM-Tracker maintains near-optimal, consistent performance. Note the high-frequency fluctuations in SAM 3/3.1, indicating a lack of stable temporal memory for thin structures, whereas our framework effectively mitigates cumulative error.

Figure 5: Dataset Statistics. Our million-frame pipeline supports a three-stage curriculum: (a) Synthesis for geometric anchoring (972.9k frames), (b) Real-Unplugged for environment alignment, and (c) Real-Plugged for modeling complex occlusions and cable routing. The table (right) details the datasets statistics.

Figure 3: Compact Scalar Memory. Instance attributes [xc, yc, a, τ ] are extracted from T frames and stacked into a resolution-invariant bank S ∈ R(N̂×4). This scalar abstraction ensures O(T · N̂) memory complexity, decoupling VRAM overhead from spatial resolution.

Figure 4: Bidirectional Mask Decoder. Bidirectional Mask Decoder. Memory tokens Tmem and object queries Pobj undergo mutual refinement through symmetric decoder layers to yield imageconditioned features zmask and instance embeddings zobj . A final scaled dot-product generates the predicted masks zmask ∈ RN×N ′ . This design decouples tracking capacity from network dimensions, enabling high-cardinality segmentation in a single pass.

Figure 2: Reference Encoding. Initial identity anchoring is performed by processing geometric configuration (Conf.) and a reference image (Iref ) through parallel encoding streams to produce structural embeddings Fobj and visual features Fref . These modalities are integrated by an Object Decoder using a query-key/value mechanism to generate Global Object Queries Pobj . This initialization is executed only once per sequence, providing persistent prototypes that maintain identity across the temporal horizon while minimizing per-frame computational overhead.

Table 2: Detection Performance and Instance Robustness. Comparison against various foundation models, fine-tuned variants, and VOS baselines. DetM-Tracker achieves the highest stability and accuracy across all metrics.

Table 1: Quantitative Evaluation of Segmentation Capability. We compare our DetM-Tracker against foundation models (SAM 2/3), fine-tuned variants, and VOS baselines. Our model achieves superior segmentation fidelity while maintaining significantly lower inference latency and memory footprint.
Table 6: Multi-stage Training Configurations and Hyperparameters.

Table 4: Tracking Robustness Across Different Cabinet Layouts. Performance under increasing occlusion difficulty and instance density. Env1 and Env2 feature different server/switch arrangements under realistic camera noise.
Table 5: Hardware Infrastructure.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient deterministic video instance segmentation for edge deployment; fits temporal visual understanding and inference efficiency.
papers.title: DetM-Tracker: Deterministic and Memory-Efficient VIS for Autonomous Industrial Inspection
papers.tldr: DetM-Tracker enables deterministic, memory-efficient real-time video instance segmentation for industrial inspection by exploiting sparse scenes and compressing temporal instance memory.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding uses a target model to verify a tree of draft tokens in parallel. We study whether the resulting next-token distributions can help select the next tree. For unrestricted target models, we show that guaranteed exact reuse requires a distribution computed at the next round's complete context. We characterize when retaining this distribution requires sacrificing accepted tokens and establish conditions under which this loss persists across decoding rounds. Across six targets, we find that reranking first-token branches with a separately computed distribution at the current context improves expected acceptance over draft ranking, especially with small tree budgets. Drawing the first token from this distribution before allocating the tree further improves expected acceptance over pruning a preselected tree, even at equal mean tree size. In our experiments, both selection rules also decode faster than draft ranking when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting. Our findings show that making target probabilities available before tree allocation can improve the efficiency of speculative decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRows.
authors: Jungseob Lee, Giyoon Jang, Chailin Nam, Jiwoo Kum, Sihyeon Lee, Kyojun Choo, Jihun Song, Eunseo Song, Chanjun Park
bullets: Exact reuse of target distributions generally requires computing them on the next round’s full context.
Retaining reusable distributions may require sacrificing accepted tokens, with this loss sometimes persisting across rounds.
Reranking first-token branches using a separately computed current-context target distribution outperforms draft-based ranking in expected acceptance across six targets.
Sampling the first token before tree allocation improves acceptance over pruning a preselected tree, even at equal mean tree size.
Both target-informed selection methods can decode faster when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions. Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal. However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history. We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed. We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches. Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history. We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution. Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.
authors: Josh Qixuan Sun, Xiaoying Xing, Yurun Chen, Huaiyuan Weng, Wentao Zhu, Mark Crowley
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic for instruction-action binding at route forks.
Builds 3,252 matched contexts by pairing instructions that share the traveled route but specify different branches.
Keeps the agent state and navigation history fixed while comparing actions, action likelihoods, and visual attribution.
Finds that higher navigation success does not necessarily indicate more faithful instruction following.

papers.abstract: The scarcity of high-quality annotated visual data remains a critical bottleneck for autonomous-driving perception. Simulators provide training data at scale, but the limited realism of synthetic videos compromises perception performance in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose NeuralSRender, a sim-to-real video translation framework that enhances the photorealism of synthetic videos while maintaining geometric consistency with the source scenes. Built on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT), NeuralSRender uses a lightweight projector to inject geometric and material priors from G-buffers, and LoRA enables parameter-efficient adaptation. The model is trained in two stages: it first learns G-buffer conditioning from synthetic videos with accurate G-buffers, then adapts to real-world appearance using real videos with estimated G-buffers. During the second stage, an additional LoRA module is trained while the projector and first-stage LoRA remain frozen to reduce interference from estimation noise. NeuralSRender introduces only 1.45\% parameter overhead and can be trained on consumer-grade GPUs with 24 GB of memory. To support training and evaluation, we introduce GenReal, a large-scale driving video dataset comprising synthetic and real-world videos with corresponding G-buffers. Experiments demonstrate improved photorealism with competitive geometric consistency. Training perception models on our translated videos instead of raw simulator renders improves detection $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ on nuImages from 35.1 to 40.6 and segmentation mIoU on Cityscapes from 32.4 to 40.8. Our code, data, and model weights are available at: https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/NeuralSRender.
authors: Yipeng Lu, Youqi Liao, Zhenyu Wang, Yuning Peng, Zhen Dong
bullets: Targets the realism gap between simulator-generated videos and real-world autonomous-driving imagery.
Injects geometric and material priors through a lightweight G-buffer projector and adapts a pretrained video DiT with LoRA.
Uses two-stage training: synthetic G-buffer conditioning followed by real-world appearance adaptation with an additional LoRA module.
Introduces GenReal, a driving-video dataset containing synthetic and real videos with corresponding G-buffers.
Translated videos improve nuImages detection AP50 from 35.1 to 40.6 and Cityscapes segmentation mIoU from 32.4 to 40.8; geometric consistency remains competitive.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities. As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety-critical real-world systems. However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation. To compare the two families directly, we evaluate every selected representative model on one outcome: whether an adversarial patch worn on a person evades detection of the model. We report this by introducing a unified metric, conditional attack success rate (cASR), counted only on images the model still localizes under a matched gray occluder, and partition every failure into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch), and displacement (a box on neither). We benchmark the physical adversarial vulnerability of compact grounding VLMs against a range of object detectors, and find that the VLMs can be as vulnerable as the detectors. We disclose that failure mode is largely associated with the output format of a model rather than its architecture family. Of the three, only omission is visible to a downstream system; displacement and substitution return confident, well-formed boxes, making them potentially more dangerous failures. Further, we find that, under distribution shift, VLMs that primarily failed by omission instead shift to failing more by displacement/substitution. Thus, a grounding VLM can inherit the detector's vulnerability while showing the possibility to adopt more dangerous failure modes. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ericliang1/physical-adversarial-robustness.
authors: Eric Liang, Alan Luo, Kaiwen Yuan
bullets: Evaluates whether an adversarial patch worn by a person evades detection across representative VLMs and object detectors.
Introduces conditional attack success rate (cASR), measured only when the model localizes the person under a matched gray occluder.
Categorizes failures as omission, substitution, or displacement to account for differences in model outputs.
Finds failure modes are more closely linked to output format than architecture family; substitution and displacement can remain invisible to downstream systems.
Under distribution shift, VLMs that mainly omit detections may shift toward substitution or displacement failures.

papers.abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has established itself as a widely used method for training deep neural networks. Despite its popularity, existing convergence guarantees for SAM-type methods require smoothness, a restrictive assumption. Generalized smoothness conditions have recently been proposed in the analysis of gradient methods but remain underexplored for SAM. To analyze the effect of SAM's perturbation under generalized smoothness, we use relative gradient distortion to quantify how the sharpness-aware direction departs from the original gradient. Under $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness, we show that this distortion can become unbounded near stationarity for SAM and at large gradients for its unnormalized variant (USAM), with examples where SAM cycles and USAM diverges. We then establish a necessary condition for uniform distortion control among perturbations along the gradient whose nonnegative multipliers depend only on its norm. Motivated by this condition, we propose Curvature-Scaled SAM (CS-SAM), which scales both the perturbation and the descent step by suitable curvature upper bounds, and prove that it uniformly bounds the distortion. Under both $(L_0,L_1)$- and $(H_0,H_1)$-smoothness, we establish deterministic $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the best squared gradient norm on nonconvex objectives, last-iterate $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the function gap on convex objectives with a minimizer, and linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. With zero perturbation, our guarantees recover the rates for gradient descent with $(L_0,L_1)$- or $(H_0,H_1)$-based step-sizes. Minibatch experiments on computer vision tasks demonstrate competitive performance for both variants, with the $(H_0,H_1)$ variant achieving the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine annealing schedules.
bullets: Existing SAM and USAM updates can have unbounded gradient-direction distortion under generalized smoothness, causing cycling or divergence in examples.
The paper derives a necessary condition for uniformly controlling distortion among gradient-aligned perturbations.
CS-SAM scales both perturbations and descent steps using curvature upper bounds.
It proves deterministic convergence rates under $(L_0,L_1)$- and $(H_0,H_1)$-smoothness, including nonconvex, convex, and Polyak–Lojasiewicz settings.
Minibatch computer-vision experiments show competitive performance; the $(H_0,H_1)$ variant achieves the highest mean best-test accuracy across four reported settings.

papers.title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness
papers.tldr: CS-SAM adapts SAM’s perturbation and step size to local curvature, enabling convergence guarantees beyond standard smoothness.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive emergent reasoning capabilities, yet they remain constrained by fixed model parameters and finite context windows. Even when augmented with static retrieval, they can produce statements that are unsupported by, or even contradictory to, retrieved evidence. This leads to hallucinations, difficulty incorporating up-to-date information, and failures to correctly interpret or reconcile sources. Recent work addresses these limitations by tightly coupling step-by-step reasoning with interactive search, treating retrieval as an action within an iterative agentic loop rather than a one-shot preprocessing step. This study reviews frameworks that implement such reasoning-search loops by interleaving planning, querying, retrieval, integration, verification, and stopping. We analyze these systems through four architectural axes: retrieval coupling, controller design, knowledge source, and grounding strictness. We separately treat the learning signal as a cross-cutting dimension because prompting, supervision, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning can instantiate the same architecture while producing materially different search, stopping, and grounding behavior. We further distinguish benchmark difficulty from RSA-loop demand and synthesize controlled within-study ablations and quality-cost deltas, avoiding invalid pooling across heterogeneous model backbones, retrievers, corpora, and evaluation protocols. Our goal is to clarify the landscape of reasoning-search-augmented LLMs and outline a unified perspective on the design choices shaping future research.
authors: Biswas Poudel, Nilson Chapagain, Amit Kumar, Xianshun Jiang
bullets: Reasoning-search loops address hallucinations, stale knowledge, and failures to reconcile retrieved evidence in static-retrieval systems.
The taxonomy organizes systems by retrieval coupling, controller design, knowledge source, and grounding strictness.
Learning signals are treated separately because prompting, supervision, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning can alter search and stopping behavior.
The analysis distinguishes benchmark difficulty from the demands of the reasoning-search loop.
Controlled within-study ablations and quality–cost changes are synthesized without pooling incompatible experimental settings.

papers.abstract: Executing vision-language models (VLMs) aboard low-Earth orbit satellites enables flexible processing of observation data without first downlinking it to the ground. On commercial off-the-shelf payloads, however, a request may span multiple execution windows: power and thermal constraints, fault-triggered reboots, and competing payload demands can interrupt inference before it completes. Each shutdown discards volatile activations and KV caches, forcing an unprotected request to repeat work after restart. We present OrbitWeaver, a framework that preserves VLM inference progress across onboard interruptions through coordinated checkpointing and recovery. Its phase-aware checkpointing selects recovery boundaries according to the state lifetimes and computational characteristics of vision encoding, language-model prefill, and decoding, balancing storage traffic against recomputation. Its dependency-aware dynamic recovery schedules restoration from partially completed states across the layer and token-chunk dimensions. By overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recomputation, it reduces restart latency; the recovery planner computes an optimal execution order under its scheduling model within 100 ms. Experiments on satellite payload hardware using on-orbit telemetry traces show up to a 4.07-fold end-to-end speedup and a 3.56-fold reduction in SSD write volume over the evaluated baselines. A 72-hour deployment on two low-Earth orbit satellites demonstrates that OrbitWeaver retains inference progress and resumes execution across repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.
authors: Xiaolong Huang, Yinyuan Zhang, Daliang Xu, Yun Ma, Qing Li, Mengwei Xu, Shangguang Wang, Gang Huang, Xuanzhe Liu
bullets: Addresses interruptions caused by power, thermal, faults, and competing payload demands that otherwise discard activations and KV caches.
Uses phase-aware checkpointing across vision encoding, language-model prefill, and decoding to balance storage overhead with recomputation.
Employs dependency-aware recovery across layers and token chunks, overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recomputation.
The recovery planner finds an execution order within 100 ms under its scheduling model.
On satellite hardware and telemetry traces, it achieved up to 4.07× end-to-end speedup and 3.56× lower SSD write volume; a 72-hour deployment resumed inference across repeated shutdowns.

papers.abstract: In video action detection, modeling the temporal dependencies in continuous video streams is crucial. Previous methods based on deep neural networks can perform frame-level video recognition tasks. However, these methods struggle to model dynamic temporal patterns, facing challenges such as redundant frame information, difficulty balancing global and local features, and insufficient fusion of visual and textual features. To address these issues, we propose a video temporal attention module based on the Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention, which aggregates continuous temporal sequences into feature representations across diverse temporal scales while efficiently reducing redundancy. We also introduce a Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion module that leverages cross-attention at both latent and standard feature levels, achieving fine-grained fusion between video and textual features to enhance semantic alignment and feature interaction. Experimental results across multiple video recognition benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed methods achieve superior performance compared to existing methods, validating the effectiveness and generalization capability.
bullets: Addresses redundant frames, weak global-local temporal modeling, and limited video-text fusion in continuous video recognition.
Uses Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention to aggregate sequences across temporal scales while reducing redundancy.
Introduces Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion at latent and standard feature levels for fine-grained semantic interaction.
Experiments on multiple video recognition benchmarks report superior performance and generalization versus existing methods.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress in general visual understanding, yet they still struggle with fine-grained instance-level consistency verification, where the goal is to determine whether two images depict the exact same physical object under varying viewpoints, illumination, and backgrounds. This task requires both global semantic perception and precise examination of subtle local evidence, since semantically similar objects may differ only in small suspicious regions. To address this challenge, we propose LocalAgent, a collaborative agentic framework that integrates the complementary strengths of a generalist MLLM and lightweight specialist verifiers. The MLLM first reasons globally to identify suspicious local regions, which are then delegated to a Local Evidence Verifier (LEV) toolkit for fine-grained appearance and geometric matching. LEV comprises Local Appearance Consistency (LAC), which estimates appearance similarity under illumination and color changes, and Local Geometric Correspondence (LGC), which estimates spatial correspondence under viewpoint changes. LEV returns structured scalar evidence that the MLLM integrates for the final decision. We further introduce an auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) strategy, in which answer correctness dominates auxiliary tool-use and format signals, enabling the policy to learn when verification is necessary. Experiments show that LocalAgent improves mean accuracy by 4.9% over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline while invoking a verifier on only 12.13% of samples and preserving the general multimodal capabilities of the underlying MLLM. The open-source repository is available at https://github.com/Firefly-zoo/LocalAgent-main.
authors: Jiachen Guo, Xinshan Zhu, Boyun Wang, Yanyan Liang, Jun Wan, Feng Lin, Ajian Liu
bullets: Targets instance-level consistency under viewpoint, illumination, and background changes, where differences may appear only in small regions.
The MLLM identifies suspicious areas and delegates them to lightweight Local Evidence Verifiers for detailed analysis.
LAC evaluates local appearance consistency, while LGC measures local geometric correspondence; their structured evidence guides the final decision.
An auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning strategy teaches the model when verification is necessary while prioritizing answer correctness.
Reports a 4.9% mean-accuracy gain over the strongest CoT-RFT baseline, with verifier use on only 12.13% of samples.

papers.abstract: We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error. To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training. TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling. Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7x speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0x across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.
authors: Yupeng Chen, Kunxiang Zhao, Xingjian Wang, Yue Zhao, Yijing Wu, Ye Liu, Kai Li, Congliang Chen, Ruoyu Sun
bullets: Targets fragmented NPU computation and overhead caused by partially applied framework-level optimizations such as operator fusion.
Extracts task-specific optimization intents from mature GPU execution and transfers them to NPU program rewrites.
Iteratively refines rewrites using profiling to reduce costly trial-and-error tuning.
Reports an average 1.7× speedup across four workloads and nearly 2.0× across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records.
Evaluated workloads span LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training.

papers.abstract: Retargeting human motion to humanoids requires preserving motion semantics while accounting for the robot's physical constraints. Kinematic pipelines prescribe a robot trajectory through geometric matching, without establishing whether it can be executed under the robot's dynamics. Prior physics-supervised neural methods train bidirectional full-sequence models on physics-refined kinematic trajectories, remaining tied to prescribed kinematic solutions and requiring noncausal context. We propose SMR, a streaming neural motion retargeter learned from semantic-conditioned physics experts. We convert human motion into robot-aware task-space targets for body landmark positions, orientations, and velocities. Physics experts track these targets directly in simulation under contact, dynamics, and actuator constraints. We train a single strictly causal Transformer on their executed state trajectories that complete the motion and pass semantic and physical validity checks. At each incoming frame, the student uses only current and past human observations to generate a robot motion reference for a downstream whole-body controller. Experiments demonstrate that semantic-conditioned physics experts generate motion with higher semantic fidelity and physical validity than direct optimization-based retargeting, while the resulting streaming retargeter achieves improved closed-loop performance over kinematic and physics-refined baselines under a common whole-body controller.
authors: Chun Gu, Juntong Zhang, Jingyu Li, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometrically matched human-to-humanoid motion and motions that satisfy dynamics, contact, and actuator constraints.

Experiments report higher semantic fidelity and physical validity for the experts, plus improved closed-loop performance under a common whole-body controller.
Scope: the retargeter generates references for a downstream whole-body controller rather than directly controlling the humanoid.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones. We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it. Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy. We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold. Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models. In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy. Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.
authors: Junha Chun, Youngjoon Jeong, Taesup Kim
bullets: WAM generalization varies substantially with the choice of generative backbone.
The study introduces nuisance orthogonality to measure whether representations separate out-of-distribution visual variation from the in-distribution manifold.
Across image and video backbones, greater prior orthogonality predicts stronger robustness after policy training.
Robust WAMs exhibit nuisance suppression and more stable action generation under visual variations.
The work offers a geometric perspective on how backbone representations shape policy generalization.

papers.abstract: Human-in-the-loop (HIL) post-training improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies through expert corrections, but costly human supervision and repeated real-robot evaluation limit algorithm exploration and development. We introduce SimPT (Simulation-based Post-Training), a simulation framework that automates intervention-based VLA post-training by integrating policy rollouts, corrective data collection, policy training, and standalone evaluation. To automatically determine intervention timing and recovery strategies, we develop an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph that tracks task progress using privileged simulator state and retains stable snapshots during policy execution. After a rollout fails, a CuRobo-based expert attempts recovery from these snapshots, starting at more advanced task stages and falling back to earlier ones as needed to generate corrective trajectories. We implement and compare four post-training methods, RECAP, HG-DAgger, DPO+SFT, and FlowPRO, across seven RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Relative to a fixed-interval snapshot baseline, the Progress Graph reduces recovery attempts by 75.0% and increases recovery success from 93.4% to 98.9%. Using SimPT, we develop RECAP-CF-LPF, a refinement of RECAP that combines cross-fitting and low-pass filtering of value predictions. This refinement increases the overall success rate from 76.50% to 79.36% in held-out simulation trials. In real-robot HIL post-training, it increases the success rate from 72% to 96% across 25 scenarios of an Ethernet cable-insertion task. These results demonstrate the utility of SimPT for exploring and developing VLA post-training algorithms.
authors: Caicheng Wang, Zipeng Ye, Zhexuan Zhou, Zilong Huang, Xi Zhang, Yuchen Xie
bullets: Addresses the cost of human supervision and repeated real-robot testing during VLA post-training.
Integrates policy rollouts, corrective trajectory collection, policy training, and standalone evaluation.
Uses an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph with privileged simulator state and stable snapshots to choose recovery points.
A CuRobo-based expert recovers failed rollouts, while SimPT compares RECAP, HG-DAgger, DPO+SFT, and FlowPRO across seven RoboTwin tasks.
The Progress Graph reduces recovery attempts and improves recovery success; the proposed RECAP-CF-LPF refinement also improves simulated and real-robot success rates.

papers.abstract: Traditional robotic navigation systems separate mapping, planning, and low-level control through cascaded modules, introducing computational overhead and accumulated latency. End-to-end reinforcement learning offers a compact unified policy that maps onboard observations directly to control actions. However, on inherently unstable platforms such as two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robots, navigation progress and obstacle avoidance can conflict with attitude stabilization in a strongly state-dependent manner. We propose a lightweight state-dependent objective coordination method for integrated navigation and control. A pitch-conditioned scalarization coefficient $\beta(s)\in[0,1]$ adjusts the relative contributions of balance stabilization and navigation objectives during training, without extra control hierarchies or auxiliary attitude-stabilization controllers, such as proportional-integral-derivative (PID) or linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) controllers. To support zero-shot deployment, simulation training models execution delay, action hold, asynchronous and noisy observations, and dynamics uncertainty. Gradient analysis reveals persistent directional interference and state-dependent variation in the objectives' relative scales. Comparisons with alternative reward-weighting, constraint, training, and control-structure strategies show that PPO+$\beta(s)$, where PPO denotes proximal policy optimization, achieves 98% and 95% success rates with small attitude excursions on the fixed obstacle map and the randomly generated high-obstacle-density map, respectively. Zero-shot hardware experiments further demonstrate bounded attitude behavior and consistent obstacle avoidance using only onboard observations. Training and evaluation code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Xuhao Huang, Xitao Xu, Yuxin Zheng, Yunfan Ren, Zheng Gong
bullets: Addresses conflicts between navigation, obstacle avoidance, and balance stabilization in unstable mobile robots.
Uses a state-dependent coefficient β(s), conditioned on pitch, to adjust balance and navigation objectives during training without extra control hierarchies or PID/LQR controllers.
Trains with execution delays, action holding, asynchronous/noisy observations, and dynamics uncertainty to support zero-shot deployment.
PPO+β(s) achieves 98% success on a fixed obstacle map and 95% on a randomly generated high-obstacle-density map, with small attitude excursions.
Hardware experiments show bounded attitude and consistent obstacle avoidance using only onboard observations.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing high-fidelity 7T MRI from routinely acquired 3T scans offers a practical pathway to enhanced neuroimaging without the prohibitive cost of ultra-high-field scanners. While existing deep learning approaches have achieved promising results, state-of-the-art methods typically rely on either large-scale architectures exceeding 45 million parameters or computationally intensive ensemble strategies, limiting their practicality in resource-constrained clinical environments. In this work, we propose a compact multi-domain attention framework, termed DGCM-SSFA, that achieves competitive synthesis quality with only 11M parameters. The proposed architecture integrates two complementary modules into a U-Net Transformer backbone. First, a Dual-Granularity Cross-Modulated Feature Modulator (DGCM) is embedded at multiple hierarchical levels to enhance local edge and texture details through Sobel-guided spatial attention and depthwise frequency-aware channel attention with cross-branch gating. Second, a Sparse Strip Frequency Attention (SSFA) module at the bottleneck captures global spatial context via strip-pooled attention with near-linear complexity, while simultaneously performing FFT-based spectral modulation in the frequency domain. These two modules operate synergistically with the backbone's native channel attention, forming a triple-granularity feature refinement pipeline. Extensive experiments on the UNC and BNU 3T-to-7T MRI datasets across T1w and T2w modalities demonstrate that DGCM-SSFA achieves strong structural fidelity, attaining an SSIM of 0.8431 on BNU T2w---approaching the best benchmark value of 0.8624---and 0.8100 on BNU T1w, while using substantially fewer parameters than Transformer-based alternatives such as ResViT (123.4M) and FS-RWKV (45.4M).
authors: Zhichun Fan, Zhiqiang Chen, Lanling Liu, Lingjun Liu, Zhonghua Xie
bullets: Addresses the high cost of 7T MRI and the impractical computational demands of existing synthesis models.
Combines dual-granularity cross-modulated feature refinement with sparse strip spatial and frequency-domain attention in a U-Net Transformer.
Uses Sobel-guided spatial attention, frequency-aware channel gating, strip-pooled global context, and FFT-based spectral modulation.
Evaluated on UNC and BNU datasets for T1w and T2w MRI; it achieves SSIM values of 0.8431 on BNU T2w and 0.8100 on BNU T1w.

papers.abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.
authors: Jiongxiao Wang, Han Ding, Youzhi Luo, Yawei Wang, Yun Zhou, Linbo Liu, Panpan Xu
bullets: Addresses the limited environment-specific knowledge of black-box LLM agents in long-horizon tasks.
Argues that predicting every next observation is costly and often provides little task-relevant guidance.
Uses selective intervention to anticipate potential pitfalls within a bounded future and predict impending failures.
Trains in two stages: pitfall-labeled synthetic-data SFT, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM in the target environment.
Improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming reported baselines.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models generate a whole sequence in parallel, never drawing a single word at any intermediate step; only the final step turns embeddings into text. Models such as ELF now report autoregressive-level quality at a fraction of the sampling steps of discrete-token diffusion models, and this design principle -- no step-wise discretization -- is what their own ablations credit for the gain. We show that this same principle carries a hidden cost: a collapse of the lexical long tail. Measured against held-out human text, ELF's output matches the human rate on common words almost exactly, yet its rarest words appear at only 0.30x the human rate, a gap that does not close from 105M to 652M parameters and that no sampler setting these models expose can reach. A same-size GPT-2, in contrast, spans zero to above the human rate by its decoding rule alone. We trace the difference to what continuous diffusion models lack: with no step that ever draws a discrete word, every step is instead driven by an average over the candidates still in play, and averaging a rare candidate together with the common word competing for its slot lands on the common word. An autoregressive model avoids this because its decoding rule samples one candidate rather than averaging over all of them. We propose GRAFT, a training-free method that grafts this missing choice back onto a frozen model: while the model is still undecided, GRAFT commits the rare words the average would otherwise discard, then regenerates the sequence from scratch with those commitments held in place. Across three ELF scales and on LangFlow, an independent continuous dLLM, GRAFT restores the rare-word share of generated text from 0.42-0.77x the human rate to 0.82-1.10x, a relative gain of 34-109%, and moves the entire word-frequency profile closer to human on every model tested, by 2.7x on ELF-B and 12x on LangFlow.
bullets: Continuous diffusion models match human rates for common words but underproduce rare words, with the gap persisting across model sizes.
The issue arises because intermediate denoising averages competing word candidates instead of sampling one discrete candidate.
GRAFT identifies rare words likely to be lost, commits them while the model remains uncertain, and regenerates the sequence with those commitments fixed.
Across three ELF scales and LangFlow, GRAFT raises rare-word frequency from 0.42–0.77× to 0.82–1.10× the human rate.
The method moves word-frequency profiles closer to human text on every tested model, without additional training.

papers.title: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models

papers.abstract: Full fine-tuning has achieved remarkable success on reasoning-intensive tasks, but it often requires substantial GPU resource consumption. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) provides a promising alternative for reducing this cost, yet we observe a substantial performance gap on reasoning-intensive tasks. In this paper, we present three key observations showing that this gap is closely associated with norm-related under-adaptation, where PEFT produces markedly smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning. Based on these observations, we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), a simple yet effective strategy that adaptively strengthens insufficiently updated layers according to their weight-update norms. Extensive experiments show that NormTune consistently enhances multiple PEFT methods across challenging reasoning benchmarks. Specifically, when trained on S1K-1.1, integrating NormTune into rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA yields substantial average accuracy improvements of 24.24\%, 11.33\%, and 16.21\% , respectively, across AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025. Moreover, NormTune-enhanced rank-256 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA achieve performance comparable to S1 full fine-tuning, with respective average gains of 2.17\%, 0.93\%, and 3.00\% over this baseline.

papers.abstract: Reward hacking is a major problem in current production machine learning systems, resulting in costly and dangerous failures. Here we study how to monitor for and mitigate reward hacking in realistic settings, including tool calls and long contexts. We apply a dynamic intervention to steering directions obtained by three different methods: difference-in-means vectors from labeled rollouts, gradient optimization-based vectors, and vectors extracted when models reference an anti-reward-hacking model spec. This dynamic intervention perturbs model representations less than uniform steering vector addition to the residual stream, allowing for more precise edits. We find that we are able to cheaply and significantly reduce reward hacking without correspondingly significant costs to model coherence or capability, and that steering vectors originally extracted from coding environments also generalize to reducing reward hacking in other domains. Our results pave the way towards latent space monitoring and control over realistic production systems.
authors: Austin Meek, Kyle Cox, Matthew Nguyen, Austin J. Brockmeier, Steven Basart
bullets: Studies reward-hacking monitoring and mitigation in production-like scenarios, including tool calls and long contexts.
Dynamically intervenes on steering directions derived from labeled rollouts, gradient optimization, or anti-reward-hacking model-spec references.
The intervention perturbs representations less than uniformly adding steering vectors to the residual stream, enabling more targeted edits.
Finds steering vectors from coding environments can generalize to reward-hacking reduction in other domains.
Reports cheap, significant mitigation with no correspondingly significant losses in coherence or capability.

papers.abstract: Vision-based insertion requires correcting alignment errors while retaining useful behavior learned from demonstrations. We present ACT--Flow, an online learning framework that couples an adaptive Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) with a conditional residual flow policy. Following anchor-guided warmup, ACT absorbs successful executed actions through behavioral cloning, while residual targets are recomputed relative to the updated prior. A chunk-level critic learns from successful and failed interactions and evaluates final composed actions. Its estimates weight generated residual candidates for flow matching, complemented by supervision from successful real executions. Candidate scoring is confined to training; deployment uses RGB observations and samples one residual per action chunk. We evaluate the framework on power-plug, USB, and key insertion, together with cable routing and needle threading. Results show a five-task mean success rate of 66% at 20,000 post-initialization interaction steps, exceeding the strongest baseline by 18 percentage points at this checkpoint. Evaluations at matched checkpoints with the residual disabled show ACT's mean success increasing from 16% to 76%. Component ablations further support the complementary roles of behavior absorption, value weighting, and successful-action supervision.
authors: Yiqing Yuan, Zhi Li, Jinrong Yang, Mingshan Sun, Mei Yu Zhi, Yong Zhao, Liangliang Ren, Hui Cheng
bullets: Targets alignment correction in insertion and related manipulation tasks while preserving useful demonstration behavior.
Combines an adaptive Action Chunking Transformer with a conditional residual flow policy after anchor-guided warmup.
A chunk-level critic weights residual candidates during training, with additional supervision from successful real executions; deployment uses only RGB observations.
Achieves a 66% mean success rate across five tasks after 20,000 post-initialization interaction steps, 18 percentage points above the strongest baseline.
With residuals disabled, ACT's mean success rises from 16% to 76%; ablations support behavior absorption, value weighting, and successful-action supervision.

papers.abstract: Blind all-in-one image restoration must adapt a shared model to heterogeneous and sometimes mixed degradations without a task label at test time. We introduce WaFIR, a decoder module that decomposes features into Haar subbands, summarizes each subband with a compact Fourier descriptor, and routes it to prompt-conditioned spectral modulation experts. Unlike image-level frequency conditioning, WaFIR makes routing decisions at the subband level, enabling frequency-specific processing while retaining the task context learned by the backbone. Under a unified training and evaluation protocol for denoising, deraining, and dehazing, WaFIR improves average PSNR over the three tasks by 0.48 dB over the PromptIR baseline and by 0.38 dB over the recent Up-Restorer. Matched-capacity and routing controls show that the gain is not explained by additional parameters alone. On unseen noise intensities, descriptor-based routing is more robust than a discrete label-conditioned alternative and remains on par under compound degradations, while routing analyses show stable subband-dependent expert use across degradation types. These results support subband frequency structure as an interpretable complement to prompt-based conditioning for blind image restoration. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/WaFIR/README.md
authors: Trong Nhan Nguyen, Vu Hoang Minh Doan, Thanh Dat Le, Truong Tien Vo, Thi Thu Ha Vu, Tan Hung Vo, Jaeyeop Choi, Junghwan Oh, Truong-Son Hy
bullets: Targets denoising, deraining, and dehazing without degradation labels at test time.
Decomposes features into Haar subbands and makes frequency-specific, subband-level routing decisions.
Combines subband Fourier descriptors with prompt-conditioned spectral modulation experts.
Improves average PSNR by 0.48 dB over PromptIR and 0.38 dB over Up-Restorer under a unified protocol.
Routing remains robust to unseen noise intensities and compound degradations, with stable subband-dependent expert usage.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall architecture of WaFIR. A PromptIR-style U-Net is augmented at each decoder level by three modules. (1) SPMoE decomposes the feature via Haar DWT into directional subbands (LL/LH/HL/HH) for multi-resolution spatial–scale localization, describes each with a 6-D Fourier descriptor (SD), routes it to top-𝑘 Fourier Experts (SR) that modulate magnitude and phase in the global frequency domain, and reconstructs via cross-subband interaction (CSI) and Haar IDWT. Wavelet and FFT are complementary: the wavelet gives spatial locality a global FFT lacks; the FFT gives frequency (magnitude+phase) selectivity a wavelet subband lacks. (2) PGM generates a degradation-adaptive prompt 𝑃; (3) DIM fuses 𝑃 with the spectral output 𝑆 and the skip connection for the next decoder.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison and frequency-domain error analysis. Rows 1–2: derain and denoise (𝜎=50) examples; columns are degraded input, PromptIR, AdaIR, WaFIR (ours), and reference, with PSNR / SSIM below each patch. On derain (row 1) WaFIR improves +1.61 dB over AdaIR (ICLR’25) and +4.62 dB over PromptIR (NeurIPS’23); on denoise (row 2), beyond the higher scores, the zoom crops show WaFIR better preserves fine texture that the baselines over-smooth. Row 3: 1D intensity profile (𝑦=160); WaFIR (red) tracks the reference (black dashed) most closely at edges. Rows 4–5: residual maps |𝑥 − 𝑥gt | and their Fourier spectra. Rain leaves a directional high-frequency band in the residual; WaFIR suppresses it most, with the steepest spectral energy decay, confirming removal of degradation-specific frequency structure.

Center: D1 amplitude-invariant descriptor—four subbands form tighter, cleaner clusters, ruling out the amplitudeartifact hypothesis. Right: Actual routing weight vectors of the trained router—four arcs consistent with D1 structure, confirming genuine frequency-band specialization.

Figure 3: Line-structure recovery on Urban100. WaFIR restores thin, repeated lines coherently, without the ringing or block artifacts of spatial baselines, a direct benefit of subbandwise global Fourier modulation.

papers.abstract: Recovering dynamic 3D scene geometry, appearance, and the physical motion states that govern scene evolution from multi-view videos is important yet challenging. A key difficulty is that appearance can be deceptive. Under rendering supervision alone, a model may fit the observed images by changing color or opacity to compensate for inaccurate deformation, rather than recovering the true evolving geometry and motion. This issue is especially severe in scenes with fast or locally complex motion, where inaccurate trajectories can still produce plausible images over the observed frames, but lead to unreliable reconstruction and discontinuous future prediction. In this paper, we propose PhyMo, a framework for learning evolving dynamics from multi-view videos. We introduce a Motion-Aware Trajectory Representation that drives the model to recover accurate motion from deformation, rather than relying on appearance shortcuts to explain observed motion. On top of this, we propose a Continuous Motion Evolution module with bidirectional kinematic continuity constraint to promote temporally consistent evolution of displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Together, these designs yield geometrically faithful interpolation and continuous motion extrapolation. Experiments on four dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Shangjia Liu, Jinxi Li, Siyuan Zhou, Bo Yang, Bing Wang
bullets: Addresses inaccurate geometry and motion recovery when rendering supervision lets appearance compensate for deformation errors.
Uses a Motion-Aware Trajectory Representation to learn motion directly from deformation.
Adds Continuous Motion Evolution with bidirectional continuity constraints on displacement, velocity, and acceleration.
Produces geometrically faithful interpolation and continuous motion extrapolation.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across four dynamic-scene benchmarks.

The right module, Continuous Motion Evolution, bi-directionally sampling from the trajectory, Motion Network Mθ predicts velocity and acceleration and performs RK2 evolution , where bidirectional kinematic continuity loss and render loss are applied.

papers.abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) synthesize photorealistic novel views from dense image collections, but degrade sharply when few views are available. We attribute a specific, measurable defect to the objective itself: the rendering loss is a sum over independent rays and contains no term comparing densities that different rays assign to the same region of space, so nearby 3D points can settle on contradictory densities while every training pixel is reproduced correctly. We make this quantity explicit by measuring cross-ray density disagreement directly during training, and show that it stays high in vanilla NeRF, falls only incidentally under frequency-based regularization, and moves together with held-out quality in the sparse regime. We then close the gap with DriftNeRF, a drop-in regularizer that instantiates the drifting-field template on density samples: a masked exponential kernel aggregates densities from nearby points on other rays into a stop-gradient consensus target, and the resulting drifting field penalizes unsupported disagreement while leaving agreed-upon boundaries intact. The regularizer reads only sampled positions, ray identifiers, and predicted densities, so it requires no pretrained model, external geometry, or additional images, and transfers across field parameterizations. On NeRF-Synthetic it reduces residual disagreement by an order of magnitude, and across NeRF-Synthetic, DTU, and LLFF it improves 3-view PSNR over the strongest MLP-NeRF baseline by 0.42-0.65 dB and remains competitive with sparse-view Gaussian pipelines under a matched protocol without their depth, flow, or covisibility preprocessing.
authors: Juntang Wang, Yihan Wang, Sheng'en Li, Hao Wu, Dongmian Zou, Shixin Xu
bullets: Identifies cross-ray density disagreement as a key sparse-view NeRF failure mode: independent ray losses can fit pixels while producing contradictory 3D densities.
Measures this disagreement during training and finds it remains high in vanilla NeRF and correlates with held-out quality.
Uses a drop-in masked-kernel regularizer that builds a stop-gradient consensus from nearby samples on other rays.
Requires only sampled positions, ray IDs, and predicted densities, with no extra images, pretrained models, or external geometry.
Reports order-of-magnitude lower residual disagreement and 0.42–0.65 dB higher 3-view PSNR than the strongest MLP-NeRF baseline across several benchmarks.

Density field (bottom-left): the anchor density 𝜎𝑎,𝑖 is compared with cross-ray neighbors sg(𝜎𝑏,𝑗 ), whose stop-gradiented values are pooled into a consensus target 𝜎cross. Pipeline (right): the MLP 𝑓𝜽 produces color and density; the 𝜎 portal feeds two paths. Volume rendering yields pixel colors 𝐶 (𝒓) compared against ground truth 𝐶∗ (𝒓) via Lrender.
