papers.abstract: Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) communicate through short click sequences called codas, whose structure includes the rhythmic pattern of inter-click intervals (ICI) and the spectral composition of the clicks. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoder (DCCE), which explicitly encodes rhythm and spectral information with separate encoders before fusing them. We evaluate DCCE on three coda-understanding tasks: social unit, coda type, and individual identification. We compare DCCE against strong baselines from literature under a common linear-probe protocol and analyze the role of each channel and training objective through ablations. On 1,383 codas, shared partitions and validation-only layer selection support three random splits and three recording-date-disjoint folds. DCCE with unit pairing and type supervision achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901/0.865/0.597 for unit/type/identity. Raw ICI remains strongest for type (0.987), and ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference (0.724). An auxiliary identity objective improves spectral-branch identity prediction but does not improve the mean fused-identity score in this configuration. Date-grouped evaluation and four year holdouts expose generalization limits. The results support task-dependent combinations of timing and spectral information, without establishing independent biological channels or general architectural superiority. Code, notebooks, and complete results are available at https://dcce-research-site.vercel.app.
authors: Jo\~ao Victor Quintanilha, Emma Virnelli, Shuo Zhang
bullets: Evaluates social-unit, coda-type, and individual-identification tasks on 1,383 codas using linear probes across random splits and date-disjoint folds.

Achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901 for unit, 0.865 for type, and 0.597 for identity under the reported configuration.
Raw ICI is strongest for coda type, while ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference.
Date-grouped evaluation and year holdouts expose generalization limits; results do not establish independent biological channels or universal architectural superiority.

papers.tldr: DCCE separately encodes sperm whale coda rhythm and click spectra, improving some understanding tasks while revealing strong task and recording-date generalization limits.

papers.abstract: One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self-supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross-modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross-modality embedding learning using paired multi-modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) one-shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross-modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.
authors: Derong Yu, Qingsong Zhao, Yanbing Yue, Yikai Li, Zhi Zhang, Guoyan Zheng
bullets: Targets cross-modality one-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying or arbitrary FOVs.
Uses an end-to-end framework combining randomized synthesis of pseudo-data with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning.
Randomizes organ layouts, appearance, FOV, and pose to reduce domain-specific biases and improve robustness to contrast, resolution, and spatial-context changes.
Evaluated on adrenal-gland localization across three challenging datasets, where it consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, especially across modalities.
Scope demonstrated on paired, small, irregular adrenal glands; source code is publicly available.

papers.title: UNIVERS: Learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization

papers.abstract: We introduce MixAgent, an agentic pipeline for music post-production that follows the workflow of audio engineers to build interpretable and editable mixing plans guided by a reference song. A grouping agent first routes related input tracks, such as drum recordings, into subgroups. A planning agent then uses retrieved examples to choose and order audio effects, such as volume control and reverb, for tracks, subgroups, and the full mix. To refine the mix, a detector identifies what needs correction, and a critic proposes numerical parameter adjustments from tracks to the full mix. In our experiments, prompting recent multimodal models to listen and revise often worsens the mix, making reliable correction a central challenge. We therefore build MixCritic, a dataset of 45,657 repair critiques derived from parameters fitted to professional mixes, and train the critic with supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization on rendered audio outcomes. On MedleyDB, learned refinement reduces error by 19% relative to the initial mix, with preference optimization reducing it by 8.4% over supervised training alone. Retrieved examples further improve effects selection, and a human listening test shows that MixAgent gets higher quality ratings than mixes produced by Qwen3-Omni, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GPT-4o-audio.
authors: Jaywon Koo, Junghyun Koo, Marco A. Martinez-Ramirez, Wei-Hsiang Liao, Seungheon Doh, Qiyu Wu, Vicente Ordonez, Yuki Mitsufuji
bullets: Groups related tracks, plans and orders effects using retrieved examples, and supports edits from individual tracks to the full mix.
Uses a detector to identify mixing problems and MixCritic to propose numerical parameter corrections.
MixCritic is trained on 45,657 critiques derived from professional mixes, with supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization.
On MedleyDB, refinement reduces error by 19% from the initial mix; preference optimization adds an 8.4% improvement over supervised training alone.
Human listeners rate MixAgent mixes higher than mixes from several multimodal models; reliable automated correction remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Abdominal organ segmentation is essential in modern medical applications. While existing deep learning approaches demonstrate promising performance, their heavy reliance on large-scale image data raises concerns over generalization capability and privacy risks. This motivates the development of generalizable segmentation training paradigms based on domain-randomized image synthesis, facilitating generalization across unseen real image domains. However, existing paradigms either suffer from limited segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs, or require dataset-specific finetuning. To address these limitations, we propose ReSeg, a novel two-stage retraining-free framework for domain-agnostic zero-shot abdominal organ segmentation. At the first stage, our organ-agnostic synthetic data-driven pretraining approach exploits semantically and visually diverse synthetic images generated by a dedicated data engine to optimize a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). The network is thereby capable of learning semantic features robust against variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, resolution and spatial context, which provide universal representation capabilities that serve as a foundation for segmentation learning. Subsequently, in the second stage, we continue to train an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), whose encoder is initialized with the pretrained weights. This training process is facilitated by another dedicated data engine, which generates diversified visual images while strictly retaining the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs. Comprehensive evaluation on seven abdominal organ segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET demonstrates that ReSeg consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods while eliminating the need for real training images.
bullets: Addresses limited cross-domain generalization, privacy concerns, and the need for dataset-specific fine-tuning in abdominal organ segmentation.
Uses a two-stage framework: organ-agnostic synthetic pretraining of GSRNet, followed by organ-specific OESNet training initialized from the learned encoder.
Employs dedicated data engines to generate visually diverse synthetic images while preserving organ layouts and semantic structure.
Learns representations robust to anatomical, contrast, resolution, and spatial-context variations.
Evaluation across seven datasets and three imaging modalities shows consistent improvement over existing state-of-the-art methods without real training images.

figures.caption: Figure 2: A schematic overview of ReSeg. We leverage segmentation masks from the TotalSegmentator CT dataset (Wasserthal et al., 2023), excluding real images entirely. Two data engines, referred to as GenRep and GenSeg, are introduced to construct a Randomized Paired Image (RPI) database and an Anatomical Multi-view Image (AMI) database, respectively. ReSeg is a two-stage learning framework that is trained on these two databases. In particular, in stage I, the RPI database is used to train a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet), which learns organ-agnostic, generalizable semantic features with an Appearance-aware Semantic (AS) decoder and a Context-aware Semantic (CS) decoder. In stage II, an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet) is initialized with the pretrained encoder weights and then trained on the AMI database. OESNet is guided by semantic priors calculated by the well-trained GSRNet to enhance domain-invariant anatomical feature extraction within a Semanticsguided Segmentation (SS) decoder. We reduce the dimension of the embeddings to 3 using PCA and visualize them as RGB images. Embed.: embedding.

Figure 1: Illustration of the proposed two-stage retraining-free framework and the zeroshot segmentation performance. (a) We utilize organ shape templates to randomly sample images from a wide range of distributions and train the model on the synthetic images through two learning stages. Stage I learns organ-agnostic, generalizable semantic features that are robust to imaging variations, while stage II leverages these semantic priors to learn abdominal-organ-specific semantic features for image segmentation. In the inference stage, our model can segment real images from multiple domains without retraining or finetuning. (b) ReSeg achieves superior performance compared with existing state-ofthe-art (SOTA) methods on seven abdominal segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET. In particular, SynthSeg (Billot et al., 2023) is trained only on synthetic data while ZeroShotSAM (Shaharabany and Wolf, 2024) leverages Segment Anything Model (SAM) (Kirillov et al., 2023) to perform minimally-guided zero-shot segmentation using foreground prompt points as the input. The solid line in the radar plot depicts the average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) on each dataset.

Figure 5: Framework for the organ-agnostic semantic representation learning stage. During training, a synthetic image pair is randomly sampled from the RPI database to train a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). This network consists of a shared CNN encoder with two distinct decoders: an Appearance-aware Semantic (AS) decoder optimized via a Dual-view Prototypical Contrastive (DPC) loss, and a Contextaware Semantic (CS) decoder trained by a Multi-patch Context-aware Contrastive (MCC) loss. During inference, an input image is fed into GSRNet to generate the AS embedding and the CS embedding from the AS decoder and the CS encoder, respectively. These embeddings are then concatenated to produce the generalizable semantic embedding. We reduce the dimension of the embeddings to 3 using PCA and visualize them as RGB images. Embed.: embedding.

Figure 6: Framework for the abdominal-organ-specific segmentation learning stage. During training, a synthetic image with its GT segmentation label is randomly sampled from the AMI database and then randomly cropped to get an image patch with its GT segmentation label patch. The synthetic image patch is fed into an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), which employs the pretrained weights to initialize the encoder, followed by a Semantics-guided Segmentation (SS) decoder. In the inference stage, OESNet can segment on real images from multiple domains without finetuning. We reduce the dimension of the embeddings to 3 using PCA and visualize them as RGB images. Embed.: embedding. CE: cross entropy.

Figure 7: Architecture of the SS decoder in OESNet. The SS decoder is integrated with hierarchical SFE modules. Each SFE module takes the segmentation feature of the current layer f in d and the generalizable semantic embedding fs from the frozen GSRNet as inputs. Within the SFE module, fs is first aligned with f in d and then generates attention map to enhance the segmentation feature. After that, the feature undergoes multi-kernel processing and finally the output feature fout

Figure 3: Illustration of the Generalizable Appearance (GA) model. Given a label map L with L labels, GMMs are used to randomly sample intensities. For all label l ∈ {1, 2, · · · , L}, a lower bound aµ for the mean parameters are first drawn from a uniform distribution U(aLµ , a H µ ), where aLµ and aHµ are two fixed hyperparameters controlling respectively the lowest and the highest value for this dynamic lower bound. Then, for each label l in L, the intensity Il is sampled from a Gaussian distribution N (µl, σ 2 l ), where µl ∼ U(aµ, bµ), σl ∼ U(aσ, bσ), and bµ, aσ, and bσ are fixed hyperparameters. After GMMs, Perlin noise (Perlin, 1985) is applied, followed by random offline and online augmentations.

Left to right: input images, GT segmentation labels, and segmentation results of different methods including SynthSeg (Billot et al., 2023), ZeroShotSAM (Shaharabany and Wolf, 2024), DSPNet (Tang et al., 2025), UniverSeg (Butoi et al., 2023), VoCo (Wu et al., 2024), Anatomix (Dey et al., 2025), and the proposed ReSeg. Colors correspond to the organs as follows: red - the liver, green - the spleen, blue - the right kidney, yellow - the left kidney.

Left to right: input images, GT segmentation labels, and segmentation results of different methods including SynthSeg (Billot et al., 2023), ZeroShotSAM (Shaharabany and Wolf, 2024), DSPNet (Tang et al., 2025), UniverSeg (Butoi et al., 2023), VoCo (Wu et al., 2024), Anatomix (Dey et al., 2025), and the proposed ReSeg. Figure 4: Illustration of the two data engines for ReSeg. Both data engines use segmentation masks sampled from the TotalSegmentator CT dataset (Wasserthal et al., 2023). The GenRep data engine randomly samples organ shape templates from all patients to create randomized label maps with paired synthetic images, forming a Randomized Paired Image (RPI) database. In contrast, the GenSeg data engine extracts segmentations of all organs from one randomly drawn patient to synthesize pseudo-images while preserving the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs, constituting an Anatomical Multi-view Image (AMI) database.

Colors correspond to the organs as follows: red - the liver, green - the spleen, blue - the right kidney, yellow - the left kidney.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a generalizable pretraining framework (ReSeg) for 3D medical image segmentation using domain-randomized synthesis and semantic representation learning.
papers.title: ReSeg: Retraining-free segmentation of abdominal organs via generalizable semantic representation learning
papers.tldr: ReSeg enables retraining-free, zero-shot abdominal organ segmentation across unseen CT, MRI, and PET domains using synthetic-data-driven semantic representation learning.

papers.abstract: World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694). For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects. Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R2 over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task-seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p = 0.002). In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R2 of 0.755 - 0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors. These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.
bullets: A frozen dependency mask from paired interventions reduces synthetic OOD RMSE from 1.769 to 0.697, nearly matching the oracle mask at 0.694.
For robot link-mass extrapolation, finger-local models explicitly incorporate masses into inertia and dynamics-bias terms, with learned residuals for contact effects.
Using the known PD controller for action effects raises median 150-step joint R² from 0.609 to 0.727 across out-of-range mass tests.
A learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world-model configuration in 100-step forecasts.
Out-of-range physical inputs can help or harm prediction depending on how the model embeds them in the dynamics mechanism.

A separate object MLP predicts object-state changes. Joint integration and object updates produce future states, which are fed back for rollout prediction. Training uses simulator trajectories; evaluation uses link masses outside the training range.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses world models for embodied systems (CausalWorld) and handles physical parameter shifts using causal modeling, a key challenge in robotics.
papers.title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts
papers.tldr: Causal structure and physically explicit parameterization substantially improve world-model prediction under out-of-distribution physical changes.

papers.abstract: Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube $\{-1,1\}^{d}$, the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term.
bullets: Addresses reward-guided sampling from exponential tilts using only a diffusion model trained on base-distribution samples.
Exploits an exact identity: for discrete hypercube data, the denoiser of a linearly tilted density equals the base denoiser at a shifted and rescaled input.
Trains the denoiser with random diagonal data rescalings so it supports the required out-of-distribution evaluation points.
A single network handles binary reward tilts, class-conditional sampling, and infilling without fine-tuning or external guidance terms.

papers.abstract: We aim to address the problem of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Mode Averaging, a critical problem that emerges when distilling Flow Matching (FM) based behavior policies in offline Reinforcement Learning (RL): When learning over multi-modal datasets, standard distillation inadvertently forces the policy to interpolate across different behavioral modes, causing the generated actions to collapse into invalid, OOD regions. To resolve this, we propose Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD), a novel framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided generative trajectory alignment problem. By employing a dynamic coupling mechanism, VRD actively rectifies flow dynamics to explicitly decouple distinct behavioral modes, cleanly isolating high-value actions. Specifically, we instantiate VRD through two complementary algorithms: VRD-Q, which utilizes value-quantile behavior distillation to statistically filter out low-value behaviors, and VRD-R, which reorganizes the latent space to geometrically isolate high-value generative trajectories from the FM-based behavior policy. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that VRD improves existing generative baselines across diverse continuous control and planning tasks on the D4RL, OGBench, and Minari benchmarks, especially over those multi-modal, non-expert datasets.
authors: Ke Jiang, Wen Jiang, Yoshinobu Kawahara, Xiaoyang Tan
bullets: Addresses OOD mode averaging during distillation of Flow Matching behavior policies on multi-modal offline RL data.
Recasts policy distillation as value-guided alignment of generative trajectories with dynamic coupling to separate behavioral modes.
Introduces VRD-Q for value-quantile filtering of low-value behaviors and VRD-R for geometrically isolating high-value latent trajectories.
Empirical evaluations on D4RL, OGBench, and Minari show improvements over existing generative baselines, especially on multi-modal, non-expert datasets.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (RE-ZS-CoT), a prompting framework that systematically integrates domain-specific expert roles to enhance reasoning in large language models (LLMs) without task-specific examples. We assess two versions of our approach. In the first version, static role selection, we evaluate eight predefined expert roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading comprehension benchmarks to determine their impact on reasoning performance. In the second version, dynamic role selection, each model autonomously selects the single most suitable role for each benchmark, enabling adaptive task-role alignment without manual specification. Across 20 LLMs and seven benchmarks, RE-ZS-CoT frequently surpasses zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, achieving performance improvements of up to 44 percentage points. The results reveal a strong correspondence between static and dynamic versions; the benchmarks where static roles yielded improvements were almost always those where dynamic roles also outperformed baselines, though static selection achieved peak performance. Ablation studies further show that unconventional roles degrade performance, underscoring the necessity of task-role alignment. The framework's scalability is validated across model sizes (2b-14b parameters), with smaller models like Granite3.3-8b achieving remarkable proficiency in arithmetic reasoning. RE-ZS-CoT advances zero-shot prompting by unifying role specialization with chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a practical, resource-efficient solution for improving LLM capabilities across diverse domains.
authors: Ibrahim Khan, Thai Van Nguyen, Yi Xia, Pratch Suntichaikul, Mustafa Can Gursesli, Daniel Fernandez Galeote, Juho Hamari, Ruck Thawonmas
bullets: Evaluates static predefined roles and dynamically model-selected roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading-comprehension tasks.

Static and dynamic role selection show closely aligned benefits, although static selection achieves the best peak performance.
Ablations indicate that poorly matched or unconventional roles can hurt reasoning, highlighting the importance of task-role alignment.
The approach scales across 2B–14B-parameter models and is presented as a resource-efficient zero-shot prompting framework.

papers.abstract: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.
bullets: Amodal video segmentation must infer object regions hidden behind occluders in every frame.
Visible-mask tokens are retained while uncovered space-time tokens are masked and predicted by a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor.
A lightweight decoder converts observed and predicted features into complete object masks.
OccJEPA is deterministic, 33.5× faster than diffusion-based methods, and more accurate across SAIL-VOS, TAO-Amodal, and Kubric.
Controlled experiments attribute improvements to pretrained predictor weights rather than model capacity across 87M–1.85B-parameter world models.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overall framework of OccJEPA. The clip is cropped around the object’s visible mask. papers.title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation
papers.tldr: OccJEPA reframes object occlusion as masked-token prediction, using V-JEPA 2.1 to produce fast, deterministic amodal video masks.

papers.abstract: A learner's present predictions do not fully determine how it will learn next. We study the dynamics of hidden learning structure through two related operations. Fiber Regulation Theory (FRT) describes protected repair of existing function and the learning responses left available after repair. Fiber Acquisition Theory (FAT) describes the formation and renewal of trainable structure, distinguishing neutral installation, access to a learning signal, and additional functional directions. The two operations also constrain one another. A repair obligation can force a change in a learning channel, while acquired features can make new protected repairs feasible or reduce the minimum coefficient cost of existing ones. We characterize joint admissibility and response reachability, and give a finite supervised-learning construction in which the two operations together produce a favorable response absent from either operation alone. We implement protected head repair and fixed-capacity LoRA renewal in Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, under replay and output distillation. Across two training trajectories differing in seed and within-task example order, the coordinated policy achieves higher teacher-forced Exact than either separate policy in all four comparisons. It also has the lowest macro NLL under both learning rules on the second trajectory. The implementations realize structure-conditioned self-regulation within specified information and action constraints: accessible state readouts and arrived evidence guide repairs and structural renewals, and ordinary learning continues from the modified state.
bullets: Present predictions do not fully determine future learning behavior, motivating analysis of hidden learning structure.
Fiber Regulation Theory models protected repair and the learning responses remaining afterward.
Fiber Acquisition Theory models formation and renewal of trainable structure, including access to learning signals and new functional directions.
The theories jointly characterize admissibility and response reachability, with a finite supervised-learning construction demonstrating a synergistic response.

In Qwen2.5-32B experiments with replay and output distillation, coordinated head repair plus fixed-capacity LoRA renewal achieved higher teacher-forced Exact across four comparisons and the lowest macro NLL under both learning rules on one trajectory.

papers.abstract: A typed decision maps evidence, a question and a fixed set of options to a probability for every option, computed in one forward pass, by reading a language model's logits or a small head over its hidden states, instead of generating and parsing text. The commercial system Jev popularised this System~1 interface, and open reproductions have followed. We report two uses of the pattern. \emph{Part I} describes an in-house System~1 judge that triages about 148K agentic coding session records for a training corpus. It replaces a frontier LLM judge that cost on the order of \$1,000 per pass and whose stored labels matched a fresh two-judge consensus on only 26.9\% of the sessions where the two judges agreed; a self-hosted frozen backbone with a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a pointer head answers three typed questions in one forward pass, judges 1,000 sessions in about three minutes of one GPU, about \$0.06 at a reference rate and roughly 1\% of the frontier judge's cost, and keeps every session inside the organisation. \emph{Part II} asks whether a readout that adds no parameters can be competitive and whether training one helps. Applying the public Eikos recipe and corpus of about 25K decisions to three further backbones (1B, 2B and 35B), we read the frozen output layer of a LoRA-adapted decoder. On the 111 public hard items of JevBench our single-seed 35B, developed with those items in view, scores 79.3\%, not significantly different from the commercial reference (73.0\%, unadjusted $p=0.12$) and ahead of five open systems after Holm--Bonferroni correction; our 2B is ahead of all four kev checkpoints on the leaderboard. A single-seed ablation finds no detectable benefit from training the 26 letter rows of the output layer, and a retrain on a later corpus release moves the 2B's hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points, which shows how little small evaluations resolve.
authors: Yuchuan Weng, Chi Liu, Xin Chen, Srinivasan Manoharan
bullets: An in-house judge triages about 148K coding-session records using a frozen backbone, rank-16 LoRA adapter, and pointer head for three typed questions.
It evaluates 1,000 sessions in about three minutes on one GPU at roughly $0.06—about 1% of the frontier judge’s cost—while keeping data in-house.
A parameter-free output-layer readout reaches 79.3% on JevBench’s 111 hard items with a 35B model, not significantly different from the commercial reference.
Training the output-layer rows showed no detectable benefit, and a later corpus release shifted 2B hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points.
Results are limited by single-seed evaluation and development with public benchmark items in view.

papers.abstract: Currently, dexterous humanoid robot hands are widely considered the final hardware bottleneck that hampers generalist robots from physically assisting people at home and work. As conventional tendon-driven designs suffer from high cost, demanding maintenance, poor reliability, and short durability, alternative linkage-driven designs have increasingly gained attention. Despite their potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon-driven hands, integrating multiple degrees of actuation (DOA) in a single digit with linkage drivetrains is a challenge for design and fabrication. Only a few studies have managed to present functional humanoid hands that are completely linkage-driven and have at least three DOAs per digit without compromising actuator placement and other design preferences. Our work introduces a new linkage-driven hand featuring a unique flexure hinge. Together with elastic drive rods made of spring steel, the linkage drivetrains are significantly simplified. Unlike other linkage-driven designs of similar dexterity, our design does not require many miniature moving parts. As a result, the hand can be fabricated easily with a budget 3D printer. This not only significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using and developing dexterous humanoid robot hand functions, but also allows the hands to be sized much closer to regular human hands. The design offers desirable kinematic advantages as well. A prototype is evaluated for grasping and object manipulation. In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.
authors: Neel Adwani, Muhaiminul Islam Akash, Saffia Ouali, Ethan Liu, Cong Wang
bullets: Addresses the cost, maintenance, reliability, and durability limitations of tendon-driven dexterous hands.
Uses a novel flexure hinge and spring-steel elastic drive rods to simplify linkage mechanisms.
Avoids many miniature moving parts and can be fabricated with a budget 3D printer.
Prototype evaluations cover grasping, object manipulation, kinematics, and control.
Scope: the abstract does not report quantitative performance results.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for stochastic systems typically optimizes expected cumulative rewards, while reliable and repeatable behavior also depends on how the state distribution evolves over time. Optimizing expected return alone does not guarantee that this distribution converges to a desired target or remains stable. This paper develops a theoretical framework for learning policies that stabilize state distributions. We formulate the problem as a Dissimilarity-based Markov Decision Process (DMDP), in which the policy acts on the current state distribution and the objective measures its dissimilarity to a target distribution. We establish sufficient conditions under which the optimal policy makes the target distribution asymptotically stable. To support policy learning, we introduce a finite-dimensional representation of distributions and show how stability guarantees for its parameter dynamics extend to the underlying state distributions. We further develop certificates for the learned policies, including their deployment using estimated distribution parameters. These results quantify how learning and estimation errors affect the guarantees and identify conditions under which learned policies retain asymptotic stability. For practical implementation, we combine distribution estimates and target-dependent rewards with PPO and SAC. A computable example on a linear system illustrates the proposed theoretical certificates. Furthermore, experiments on a HalfCheetah task demonstrate the benefits of distribution feedback and explicit target matching for regulating the velocity distribution.
authors: Xun Shen, Yuepeng Wang, Daniyal Sajedi-Hosseini, Akifumi Wachi, Ken Kawano, Yoshihiko Fujisawa, Mehrshad Sadria, S\'ebastien Gros, Katsuki Fujisawa
bullets: Recasts reinforcement learning as a dissimilarity-based MDP where policies act on the current state distribution and minimize its mismatch with a target distribution.
Provides sufficient conditions ensuring the target distribution is asymptotically stable under the optimal policy.
Introduces finite-dimensional distribution representations and certificates covering learned policies, parameter estimation, and learning errors.
Combines distribution estimates and target-dependent rewards with PPO and SAC for practical policy learning.
A linear-system example validates the certificates, while HalfCheetah experiments show benefits for regulating velocity distributions.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language models by verifying drafted tokens in parallel. New draft-training objectives are usually credited with the acceptance they add over cross-entropy on externally written responses, yet many pipelines let the target rewrite them. We ask how much of that gain survives. With a vision-language target and a block drafter, we train three objectives on four versions of one corpus: cross-entropy on corpus tokens, token-level distillation from the target, and distillation gated to positions that would survive verification. Distillation and the gate add large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration, distillation adds a smaller gain and the gate little or none. The shrinkage persists across data orders, position weights, verifiers, decoding temperatures and, for distillation, initializations and learning rates. Most of it remains at matched supervised length and at each objective's best measured training length. A second vision corpus shows the shrinkage, as does a text-only replication, for distillation also with an autoregressive drafter. Objective gains should therefore be measured against a target-regenerated baseline and across training lengths. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRegeneration.
authors: Jungseob Lee, Hogun Seong, Euijun Choi, Sugyeong Eo
bullets: The study compares cross-entropy, target distillation, and verification-gated distillation across externally written and target-regenerated corpora.
Distillation and gating provide large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration, distillation’s gain shrinks and gating provides little or none.
This shrinkage persists across data ordering, position weighting, verifiers, temperatures, training lengths, and several initialization or learning-rate settings.
The finding replicates on a second vision corpus and in text-only experiments; distillation also shows it with an autoregressive drafter.
The authors recommend evaluating objective gains against target-regenerated baselines and across training lengths.

papers.abstract: We study a jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow of the squared maximum mean discrepancy generated by the energy kernels $K(z)=-|z|^q$, $0<q<2$, in every dimension $d\ge2$ as well as the one-dimensional range $1\le q<2$. Under subcritical density and finite-moment assumptions, we prove global well-posedness. The added jumps transfer mass toward smaller values of the first variation and dissipate the same MMD energy as the transport term. Under our hypotheses on the target and jump rates, every Borel probability measure with finite MMD energy and zero jump dissipation is equal to the target. Combining this rigidity with compactness and a second-moment identity yields convergence to the target from finite-second-moment data, without additional uniform-in-time density or moment assumptions. We also construct a global collision-free particle process whose energy is nonincreasing along each path. A quantitative mean-field estimate applies to general initial empirical approximations, including deterministic configurations; propagation of chaos for exchangeable data and long-time target approximation follow as consequences.
authors: Ansh Desai, Jason Liu, Srujan Roplekar, Matthew Rosenzweig
bullets: Addresses convergence of MMD gradient flows with energy kernels in dimensions d≥2 and for 1≤q<2 in one dimension.
Adds jumps that move mass toward lower first variation while dissipating the same MMD energy as transport.
Proves global well-posedness under subcritical-density and finite-moment assumptions.
Establishes convergence to the target using rigidity, compactness, and a second-moment identity, without uniform-in-time density or moment bounds.
Constructs a collision-free particle process and proves mean-field estimates for general empirical initializations; propagation of chaos and long-time approximation follow.
papers.selection_reason: Studies a jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow for Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) with energy kernels. This theoretical work on generative processes and particle dynamics is relevant to world models and generative modeling.
papers.title: A Jump-Modified Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Maximum Mean Discrepancy with Energy Kernels
papers.tldr: A jump-augmented Wasserstein flow for energy-kernel MMD is shown to be globally well posed, converge to the target, and admit a collision-free particle approximation with quantitative mean-field guarantees.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning (RL) requires both efficient rollout generation and training on long sequences. However, the memory requirements and model-specific operators of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next make this difficult with existing open-source implementations. To resolve these limitations, we introduce FlashNext-RL, a model-specific RL training optimization framework based on prime-rl, with vLLM for software engineering (SWE) rollout generation. Our main focus is BF16 training of the full 48-layer model on a single 8xB200 node, with the first two layers, the n-gram table, the sparse-attention indexer and the multi-token prediction head frozen. We optimize host offload, gradient accumulation and the kernels for mixture-of-experts, sparse attention and the gated residual stream. In the full-model development study, non-padding training throughput increases from approximately 395 tokens/s/GPU in the initial 32K-token configuration to 4,438 tokens/s/GPU in the optimized 131K-token configuration, with hardware matmul throughput (aka without considering the cost of attention components) increasing from approximately 20 to 213 TFLOPs/GPU. A controlled cumulative study on an 8-layer model further quantifies the contributions of individual optimizations. Together with three inference nodes, the system supports a live SWE RL run with a target batch of 1,024 trainable rollouts and a 131,072-token context limit. Over steps 5-15, an iteration takes 22.4 minutes on average, with bounded entropy and trainer-sampler mismatch KL. These results highlight the importance of tailoring RL training to the model's architecture, memory layout and kernel requirements, rather than relying only on general-purpose RL infrastructure.
bullets: Targets the memory and custom-operator challenges of full-model, long-sequence agentic RL.
Builds on prime-rl and vLLM, using host offload, gradient accumulation, and optimized MoE, sparse-attention, and gated-residual kernels.
In a full-model study, training throughput rose from about 395 to 4,438 non-padding tokens/s/GPU across the reported configurations.
Supports a live SWE RL run with 1,024 trainable rollouts and a 131,072-token context limit; iterations averaged 22.4 minutes over steps 5–15.
The study emphasizes architecture-specific optimization over reliance on general-purpose RL infrastructure.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for robotic and sequential decision-making systems. However, their action likelihoods are generally intractable, limiting the direct use of widely adopted policy optimization methods such as PPO and GRPO. We propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO), a framework that leverages Doob's $h$-transform for likelihood-free reinforcement learning fine-tuning of generative policies. DoobPO separates policy improvement from generative policy learning. It first learns a lightweight ratio model that represents the desired policy update, and then distills the resulting ratio-tilted target policy into the generative policy via conditional drift matching. This formulation applies uniformly to both diffusion and flow policies and supports a broad family of policy improvement rules, including PPO and GRPO. We prove that the practical conditional drift matching objective is gradient-equivalent to the ideal Doob drift matching objective. We further show that the induced diffusion process solves an endpoint-constrained stochastic optimal control problem. This establishes that it achieves the minimum-energy modification required to realize the desired policy tilt. Across MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, DoobPO achieves strong performance against competitive diffusion- and flow-policy baselines, showing a principled and practical route to RL fine-tuning for generative policies.
authors: Maojiang Su, Qijie Zhu, Yu Xiao, Shuyang Yu, Minshuo Chen, Zhaoran Wang, Han Liu
bullets: Addresses intractable action likelihoods that hinder standard policy optimization for generative policies.
Learns a lightweight ratio model, then distills the ratio-tilted target policy via conditional drift matching.
Works with both diffusion and flow policies and supports policy-improvement rules including PPO and GRPO.
The practical drift-matching objective is proved gradient-equivalent to the ideal Doob objective.
Experiments on MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks show strong performance against diffusion- and flow-policy baselines.

papers.abstract: Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $\tau^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.
authors: Tanqiu Jiang, Min Bai, Sadat Shahriar, Wanyu Du, Sandesh Swamy

papers.abstract: True whole-body medical imaging captures a patient from head to toe and provides comprehensive anatomical and/or functional information. This coverage enables reconstruction of the external body surface, yielding patient body models. However, scanner geometry (e.g., bore diameter), patient characteristics, and positioning can leave body regions missing (e.g., lateral arms/torso, hands, forearms, elbows), producing incomplete patient body models. Such incompleteness limits downstream medical analyses, including derivation of body-habitus metrics (BHMs), such as body volume and surface area, for injected radiotracer activity regimens, cardiometabolic risk assessment, and computational anatomical modeling for medical imaging simulation and radiation dosimetry. We present the Medical Body model Optimization-based Estimator (MedBOE), an automated, training-free framework for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions. Our innovation is to leverage the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) template, a parametric body mesh representing a broad range of body shapes and poses, in medical imaging. MedBOE aligns the SMPL template to the incomplete patient body models via attribute-guided optimization and estimates missing body regions through geometrically and volumetrically constrained deformation. We evaluated MedBOE using two public datasets: AutoPET (91 whole-body PET-CT images) and Human Implicit Tissues (HIT; 40 whole-body segmentations from MRI images). MedBOE achieved the best overall volumetric and geometric performance among evaluated methods. BHMs derived from MedBOE were within 2% error, suggesting low percentage errors for downstream analyses. MedBOE offers an automated, training-free method for estimating complete patient body models from whole-body images with missing body regions.

papers.abstract: Many problems in signal processing, machine learning, and neuroimaging provide several jointly observed measurements of one process, each mixing a component common to all of them with a component private to itself, and require the common component to be recovered without supervision. This problem has been studied in several communities, largely independently. Statisticians proposed canonical correlation analysis (CCA), introduced by Hotelling in 1936. Information theorists proposed two notions of common information, due to G\'acs and K\"orner and to Wyner. Engineers developed subspace methods for sensor arrays and multiuser communications to design multiview receivers. This tutorial presents the main results and tools each community developed for this problem in a single exposition, and explains the connections that emerge where they meet, distinguishing exact equivalences from special cases and analogies. We develop the information-theoretic foundation from first principles. We then introduce CCA and its extension to several views, followed by the engineering thread from blind multiuser detection to CCA as a blind receiver. Next, we turn to nonlinear CCA, covering kernel, deep, and probabilistic formulations, the conditions under which the common factor is identifiable, and connections to self-supervised learning. We conclude with a discussion of further extensions and open directions. The exposition is self-contained, so that readers from each of these communities can follow the parts developed by the others.
bullets: Addresses unsupervised recovery of components shared across multiple measurements while separating view-specific components.
Connects Gács–Körner and Wyner common information, classical and multiview CCA, and engineering subspace methods.
Develops the information-theoretic foundations and explains exact equivalences, special cases, and analogies across communities.
Covers kernel, deep, and probabilistic nonlinear CCA, including common-factor identifiability and links to self-supervised learning.
Concludes with extensions and open research directions; it is a tutorial rather than a report of new experiments.

The block in blue corresponds to W∗ = 1, the block in orange to W∗ = 2, and darker shades indicate larger probabilities. Each block equals PW∗ (w) times the outer product of the conditional PMFs PX|W∗=w and PY|W∗=w, as the arrows indicate, which reflects the conditional independence of X and Y given W∗. The two blocks occupy disjoint rows and disjoint columns, so each of X and Y determines the common part W∗ from its own value. Hence, X always reveals the block in which Y lies, but nothing more about Y, and vice versa.

Each color marks one atom, that is, the set of all outcomes at which the random variable generating the partition takes one particular value. The join is the coarsest partition that refines both σ(X) and σ(Y). The meet is the finest partition coarser than both, and the five atoms of the meet index the values of the common part W∗.

Hence, the two feasible sets are the circles where the sphere intersects those subspaces, and θ is the angle between a feasible pair. Minimizing ∥X1q1 − X2q2∥2 2 closes that angle as far as the subspaces allow. papers.abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.

papers.abstract: Accurate 6-DoF object pose tracking is essential for robotic interaction, yet conventional monocular pipelines frequently suffer from catastrophic divergence under rapid object motion. We present RoPT, a robust tracking framework engineered to overcome this limitation by unifying visual perception, temporal kinematics, and global re-localization into a tightly coupled closed loop. Unlike existing open-loop trackers, RoPT delivers three critical capabilities that fundamentally alter system resilience. First, the visual perception component tracks object masks to robustly handle partial and severe occlusions. Second, a kinematic factor graph regularizes frame-to-frame updates, forecasts forward pose predictions, and drives a parallel multi-hypothesis verification scheme to bypass local minima. Finally, an active re-localization module transforms the pipeline into a closed-loop system, making it failure-aware and capable of deterministic self-recovery. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework across challenging benchmarks alongside real-world robotic demonstrations, achieving significantly higher tracking survivability under rapid motion.

papers.abstract: Transformers are deployed as a special model class. Neural processing units (NPU) add dedicated operators for attention and normalization, and quantization relies on Transformer-specific algorithms. We show the computation does not force this. Every Transformer block, with attention, LayerNorm and a GELU MLP, compiles exactly into a generic deep neural network built from fixed affine maps, routing and the square, sigmoid and inverse square root, plus GELU or its sigmoid approximation. Without activation-activation products, every transform-wise compilation adds at least $N^2$ scalar nonlinear evaluations per head for dense scores. Keeping that one operation type removes this cost; its elementwise form, present on every surveyed NPU, suffices with the sigmoid and inverse square root. For top-$k$ attention with exchangeable tail scores, we prove that exact or conditional-mean tail mass gives an unbiased, minimum-mean-square-error estimate of the attention distribution, while tail drop is conditionally biased. When queries or agents cluster, centroids choose the keys first, reducing the number of computed scores from $N^2$ to $Nk$ per head. On DeiT-Tiny, MambaIRv2-Light and Pythia-70M the compiled models match their references with all keys, standard post-training quantization applies, and the exact tail-mass estimate beats tail dropping with half as many keys on DeiT-Tiny and, for $k\le8$, on Pythia-70M.
authors: Sergey Salishev, Zeev Volkovich, Oleg Granichin
bullets: Every Transformer block—including attention, LayerNorm, and GELU MLPs—can be represented using fixed affine maps, routing, square, sigmoid, inverse square root, and GELU-related operations.
Removing activation-activation products incurs at least N² additional scalar nonlinear evaluations per head for dense attention scores; retaining elementwise products avoids this cost.
For top-k attention with exchangeable tail scores, exact or conditional-mean tail-mass estimates are unbiased and minimum-MSE, unlike conditionally biased tail dropping.
Clustering queries or agents selects keys through centroids, reducing per-head score computation from N² to Nk.
Compiled models match reference models with all keys, support standard post-training quantization, and show improved approximation from tail-mass estimation on the reported models.

papers.title: Transformers as Generic Deep Neural Networks: Exact Compilation, the Cost of Removing Activation-Activation Products, and Multi-Agent Attention Clustering

papers.abstract: Scanning every passage in a long document seems thorough, but does it preserve more useful evidence or produce better answers? We compare 11 retrieval configurations spanning lexical and dense search, hybrid reranking, and full-document scanning with Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and Cloudflare Clef. Our evaluation uses 396 QASPER questions and 80 questions from eight complete textbooks, with common passages, a five-passage limit, and a fixed answer generator. On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), compared with 88.7% for Jev full scan and 81.3\% for OpenAI dense retrieval. Full scans examine every passage initially, yet later reduction steps can discard relevant evidence. Higher evidence coverage also does not consistently produce better answers: Hybrid + Decisions achieves the highest observed book Answer Accuracy among retrieval methods (0.892), despite recovering less reference evidence. Full scanning incurs substantially higher latency on books under the tested deployments, while reusable dense retrieval has lower projected API cost than paid decision-based methods as queries accumulate. Most QASPER articles already fit within the hybrid candidate pool, limiting the benefit of scanning. These results highlight evidence retention, answer quality, and reuse cost as complementary criteria for choosing a long-document retrieval strategy.
authors: Juan Terven, Diana-Margarita C\'ordova-Esparza, Julio-Alejandro Romero-Gonz\'alez, Edgar Chavez-Urbiola, Juan Irving Vasquez, Julian Andres Ramirez-Bautista, Silvia L. Chaparro-C\'ardenas, Gendry Alfonso-Francia
bullets: Compares 11 lexical, dense, hybrid, and full-document retrieval configurations across QASPER articles and textbook questions.
On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), exceeding Jev full scanning (88.7%).
Hybrid + Decisions produces the highest observed book answer accuracy among retrieval methods (0.892), despite recovering less reference evidence.
Full scans examine all passages but can lose relevant evidence during later reduction and incur substantially higher book latency.
Reusable dense retrieval has lower projected API cost than paid decision-based methods as query volume grows; most QASPER articles fit the hybrid candidate pool.

papers.title: Scan or Index? large Evidence Coverage, Answer Quality, and Cost in Long-Document RAG
papers.tldr: For long-document RAG, hybrid retrieval can retain more useful evidence than full scanning while delivering better latency and reuse economics, though evidence coverage does not guarantee answer quality.

papers.abstract: Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints. Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats. Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge. Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources. To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness. The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment. We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm. Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B-14B planners to 70.5-76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85-26.41 W of average power. Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.
authors: Weizhe Xu, Jialiang Fan, Essien Taylor, Zijun Wang, Russell Joseph, Fanxin Kong
bullets: Addresses the deployment and safety limitations of large language models and the rigidity and computational cost of classical planners.
Builds a safety-aware dataset from classical planners, a teacher LLM, and formal verifiers.
Uses supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning guided by a verification-based reward machine.
Evaluated across PDDL domains, household simulators, edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm.
Compact 4B–14B planners achieve 70.5–76.0% success on PDDL tasks; INT4 deployment on Jetson Orin uses 17.85–26.41 W average power.

papers.abstract: Coarse-to-real (C2R) video generation converts coarse animation, simulation, or game-rendered videos into photorealistic videos while preserving scene layout, camera motion, and dynamics. Training such models requires aligned (coarse, realistic) video pairs, which are expensive to create and confine prior systems to narrow synthetic domains. We exploit a simple asymmetry: paired videos are hard to obtain, but paired real-to-coarse images are easy to construct with existing editing and 3D reconstruction tools. Using these image pairs, we train the DINO-R2C model to transfer realistic images to coarse images in DINO feature space, and apply it frame-wise to ordinary real videos to synthesize pseudo-coarse videos. The C2R# model then learns to generate each real video from its pseudo-coarse counterpart, free from needing (coarse, realistic) video pairs. At inference, the DINO-R2C model is discarded and actual coarse videos drive the C2R# model directly. Thus, our pair-free training scales with any real-video corpora rather than with paired synthetic videos. We will release the model and project webpage at https://gonzalognogales.github.io/coarse2real-sharp/.
authors: Gonzalo G\'omez-Nogales, Daohan Lu, Peiye Zhuang, Tinghui Zhou, Yi Zhou
bullets: Addresses the high cost and limited domain coverage of paired coarse–real video data.

At inference, C2R# directly uses actual coarse videos; DINO-R2C is discarded.
The approach can leverage broad real-video corpora without paired synthetic videos.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots require spatial representations that capture geometry and semantics while staying sparse enough for planning in large, unknown environments. Graphs provide a natural representation for this purpose and underpin both classical planning methods and a growing class of reinforcement-learning (RL) policies. However, RL training needs hundreds to thousands of parallel environments, each constructing and updating its own graph. Existing graph libraries are typically designed for either single-robot deployment or fixed graphs, and CPU-based graph construction limits scalable training to only a few dozen environments. We introduce GGraph, an open-source GPU-accelerated graph library for both robot deployment and large-scale learning. GGraph supports real robots through ROS 2 interfaces and vectorized GPU-based policy training, with built-in support for tasks including 3-D navigation, exploration, and loop-closure integration. For single-robot operation, GGraph updates graphs in milliseconds. At scale, it enables graph-based exploration policies to train across hundreds of parallel robots, reducing wall-clock training time by one order of magnitude. Across simulation and real-world experiments, these results establish GGraph as a unified graph infrastructure for both large-scale robot learning and deployment.
authors: Yash Rampuria, Rohan Garg, Daniele Gammelli, Marco Pavone
bullets: Addresses the challenge of constructing and updating sparse geometric-semantic graphs across many parallel robot environments.

papers.abstract: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that supports Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan, Apple Metal and WebGPU backends that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs while rendering realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.
bullets: Targets the computational cost of high-fidelity, batch-rendered quadrotor simulation for vision-based control.
Combines GPU-optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a cross-platform ray-tracing engine.
Renders RGB, depth, segmentation, normals, and optical flow with configurable realism, including PBR, reflections, motion blur, and anti-aliasing.
Reports over 20× higher speed than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators, reaching millions of FPS even at high fidelity on consumer GPUs.
Validates the simulator by transferring a simulation-trained yaw-control policy to a camera-equipped Crazyflie running fully onboard.

papers.abstract: Conventional wafer defect analysis relies on offline, closed-world classifiers that fail to detect novel, unseen defect signatures emerging during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.
authors: Quanling Zhao, Ava Emami, Tsuyoshi Id\'e, Rajiv Joshi, Steven Holmes, Michael Passow, Tajana Rosing
bullets: Addresses the limitations of offline, closed-world wafer defect classifiers in continuously changing manufacturing environments.
Uses hyperdimensional computing with a memory-centric architecture for rapid anomaly detection and compact defect representations.
Models normal spatial patterns, then dynamically groups recurring failures without predefined class counts.
On WM-811K, it improves adjusted Rand index by 13.3 percentage points and normalized mutual information by 10.5 points over the strongest online baseline.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators must adapt not only to objects, but also to the spatial context in which they appear: where to position the base, how to manipulate, and where to look while navigating surrounding scene geometry. To address this, we present COWBOY, a scalable sim-to-real framework for learning such contextual whole-body manipulation. On whole-body dexterous grasping, COWBOY transfers zero-shot to hundreds of objects and diverse in-the-wild scenes, spanning cluttered tabletops, shelves, drawers, and other unstructured settings. Rather than learning scene adaptation directly with RL in simulation, a vectorized environment-aware whole-body controller (WBC) handles reaching in thousands of scenes by coordinating base-arm motion, collision avoidance, and active vision. Then, local RL experts are trained in local scenes for object interaction and can be reused across thousands of full-scene layouts. We distill these composed WBC-RL teachers into a single vision policy that controls the mobile base, arm, dexterous hand, and actuated camera from point-cloud observations. The resulting policy exhibits contextual whole-body behavior, automatically adapting base placement, camera viewpoint, arm trajectory, and grasp strategy to observed scene and object geometry. Videos are available at https://cowboy-manip.com
authors: Jiahui Yang, Jason Jingzhou Liu, Ray Muxin Liu, Andrew E. Wang, Kenneth Shaw, Deepak Pathak, Ruslan Salakhutdinov
bullets: Targets whole-body manipulation in cluttered, unstructured environments such as tabletops, shelves, and drawers.

The resulting policy transfers zero-shot to hundreds of objects and diverse in-the-wild scenes.
Controls the base, arm, dexterous hand, and actuated camera from point-cloud observations.

papers.abstract: NVIDIA tensor cores have supported 2:4 semi-structured sparsity since Ampere, and the pattern composes with quantization. When the two are combined, the practical question is which step to take next: from a given precision, add 2:4 sparsity or drop to the next lower precision? We compare the two at equal bits, with sparsity metadata counted, and at equal nominal tensor-core tiers, over all six GEMM operands of a transformer layer, with kernels measured on three GPU generations and online pruning and quantization included. Our results show that as long as a lower precision is available, adding 2:4 is the worse step, both less accurate and slower, because the energy that 2:4 discards from each group of four along the hardware-forced axis does not shrink with bits, while quantization error does. Once quantization reaches the lowest precision the hardware supports, 2:4 still speeds up linear layers by 1.3--1.7\x{}, and on an H100 a retrained 2:4 model served in FP8 by vLLM reaches 27\% higher prefill throughput than the dense FP8 model, with GSM8K accuracy on par. Its quality has to be won back by retraining, however, which restores perplexity long before reasoning; on Blackwell, whose sparse FP4 uses a pairwise 4:8 pattern, the loss is larger and our retraining budget did not recover it.
bullets: The study compares 2:4 sparsity and lower-bit quantization at equal bits and nominal tensor-core tiers, counting sparsity metadata.
It evaluates all six GEMM operands in transformer layers across three GPU generations, including online pruning and quantization overheads.
Adding 2:4 sparsity is both less accurate and slower than lowering precision when another precision level is available.
At minimum supported precision, 2:4 sparsity speeds up linear layers by 1.3–1.7×; on H100, retrained sparse FP8 reaches 27% higher prefill throughput with GSM8K accuracy on par with dense FP8.
Retraining recovers perplexity before reasoning quality; the loss is larger for Blackwell’s pairwise 4:8 sparse FP4 and was not recovered within the reported retraining budget.

papers.title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.
authors: Haori Lu, Tianyu Gao, Yaoyao Liu, Yingying Li

Employs dual-branch experience memory to improve both candidate planning and next-observation prediction.
Shows strong overall performance on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three LLM backbones.

papers.abstract: Modern robotic agents are increasingly expected to support steerable control, where a single policy can adjust its behavioral style at runtime under changing user preferences. Preference-conditioned reinforcement learning provides this interface, but conditioning alone does not ensure that a requested behavior change is strong, does not leak into unrelated behaviors, and does not compromise task performance. Our evaluation combines Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR) with coverage and utility metrics. We use these measures to compare reward-level, advantage-level, loss-level, and PCGrad-based aggregation across two humanoid-control frameworks. No aggregation level performs best across all environments and criteria. Experiments show that aggregating objectives early produces a wider range of behavioral responses but greater unintended changes in other objectives, while aggregating them later improves control precision at some cost to responsiveness.
authors: Ziqian Huang, Yuzhuo Chen, Shimin Zhang, Junyang He, Xinyue Annie Yang, Animesh Garg
bullets: Preference conditioning alone may not produce strong, isolated, or task-preserving behavior changes.
The study compares reward-, advantage-, loss-, and PCGrad-based aggregation across two humanoid-control frameworks.
Evaluation uses Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR), coverage, and utility metrics.
Early aggregation broadens behavioral responses but causes more unintended changes; later aggregation improves precision but reduces responsiveness.

papers.abstract: Blind and visually impaired individuals face uncertainty when navigating unfamiliar areas. Whether a cane or a guide dog is used for navigation, this may prove to be challenging. To mitigate this challenge, we present the Context-Aware Navigation Explanation framework that explains guide dog movements for obstacle avoidance and navigation using a large language model. This system integrates perceptual context with planned future trajectories to generate natural-language explanations of robot movement. We deploy the system on a Unitree Go2 platform in indoor navigation scenarios and evaluate how different explanation context configurations affect user trust and explanation satisfaction. Results show a strong positive relationship between explanation satisfaction and trust, and suggest that combining obstacle information with future trajectory leads to the most effective explanations. These findings highlight the potential of context-aware language explanations to improve transparency and trust in assistive robot navigation.

bullets: Addresses uncertainty faced by blind and visually impaired people navigating unfamiliar environments.
Introduces a framework that combines perceptual context with future trajectories to explain obstacle avoidance and movement.
