papers.abstract: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.
authors: Chaorui Yao, Yuming Paul Zhang, Lin Yang, Yuhua Zhu
bullets: Addresses vanishing action-value differences in standard Q-learning as the sampling interval becomes small.
Introduces PhiBE policy iteration using a single state-action critic that preserves continuous-time action-ranking information.
Learns critics directly from sampled increments, reuses one batch across iterations, and does not estimate drift or diffusion.
Provides a local suboptimality guarantee under linear function approximation, tracking discretization, approximation, and finite-sample errors.
Shows a bias-variance trade-off: finer sampling improves continuous-time approximation but may worsen statistical error at fixed sample size.

papers.abstract: Flow matching learns a generative velocity field by regression, but under distribution drift a field must be deployed before the current data arrive. We study this predictive problem for a fixed, possibly nonconvex, neural class, with dynamic regret against the best represented field of each round. We propose DyProd-FM, which refits flow matching on dyadic historical prefixes and selects among the fits with a sleeping Prod master. Without knowing any drift budget, it attains regret $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\omega+1,1+\sqrt{T\Omega}\})$ in the relative velocity risk variation $\Omega$ and $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\mu+1,1+T^{1/3}V_\mu^{2/3}\})$ in the target-law variation $V_\mu=\sum_t W_2(\mu_{t+1},\mu_t)$, up to approximation and fitting costs. Matching lower bounds for fixed classes show that both rates are optimal in $T$ and in the budgets up to logarithmic factors. Prior optimal dynamic-regret guarantees rely on a convex decision set with strongly convex or exp-concave losses, whereas our class may be nonconvex and no curvature in its parameters is assumed. The target-law rate rests on a second-order link between the two variations, which the base noise of flow matching provides.
bullets: Addresses deployment before current data arrive by minimizing dynamic regret against the best represented flow field at each round.
Refits flow matching on dyadic historical prefixes and uses a sleeping Prod master to select among models without knowing the drift budget.
Achieves near-optimal rates in both relative velocity-risk variation and target-law Wasserstein variation, up to approximation, fitting, and logarithmic costs.
Matching lower bounds establish optimal dependence on time and variation budgets for fixed classes.
The target-law guarantee relies on a second-order relationship between distribution and velocity-risk variation induced by flow-matching noise.

papers.title: Minimax-Optimal Predictive Flow Matching under Distribution Drift
papers.tldr: DyProd-FM achieves minimax-optimal predictive flow matching under distribution drift, even for fixed nonconvex neural classes without curvature assumptions.

papers.abstract: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation enables knowledge transfer across model families, allowing students to learn from stronger or more specialized teachers. However, differences in vocabulary and segmentation make teacher and student next-token distributions difficult to align. Existing logits-based methods are easy to integrate into standard distillation pipelines, but often rely on restrictive heuristics or tokenizer-pair-specific choices. They may restrict supervision to shared vocabulary subsets, require manually selecting different objectives for different tokenizer pairs, or match only the observed chunk and its complement rather than individual alternative continuations. We introduce Common-Support Distillation (CSD), a unified logits-based framework that constructs a shared support between the teacher and student at each aligned input chunk and matches the induced distributions with a single objective. For one-to-one alignments, CSD uses explicit common-token pairs as the shared support. For other alignments, it constructs a virtual support whose probabilities are computed using the autoregressive chain rule. A residual event captures probability mass outside the explicit support, ensuring that both induced distributions remain normalized. Across four teacher-student settings comprising Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B-PT students with Qwen and Phi teachers, CSD consistently achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated cross-tokenizer methods, outperforming the strongest alternative by up to 1.8 points and surpassing both continued pretraining and same-tokenizer distillation. For Llama-3.1-8B, CSD improves average accuracy over the strongest evaluated baseline by up to 4.2 points for the base student and 1.6 points for the instruction-tuned student.
authors: Mingyu Yang, Sharath Turuvekere Sreenivas, Adithyakrishna Venkatesh Hanasoge, Nima Tajbakhsh, Ashwath Aithal, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Addresses vocabulary and segmentation mismatches that make next-token logits difficult to align across tokenizers.
Uses explicit common-token pairs for one-to-one alignments and autoregressive chain-rule probabilities for other alignments.
Adds a residual event for probability mass outside the explicit support, preserving normalization.
Across evaluated teacher–student settings, CSD achieved the best average performance, with gains of up to 1.8 points and up to 4.2 points for Llama-3.1-8B base students.
The method is evaluated across multiple Llama, Gemma, Qwen, and Phi teacher–student combinations.

papers.abstract: Trajectory demonstrations show robots how to behave but not why, leaving them to guess which features of the task actually matter. Incorrect guesses produce misaligned internal representations and lead to incorrect robot behaviors. Because task features are often semantically defined, we argue that natural language is better suited for specifying features rather than relying on demonstrations. Although existing representation editing methods have proposed using language to specify new features, only allowing additive edits produces feature sets that are often over-specified or too narrowly scoped, especially in sequential editing tasks. We propose the Flexible Feature Editing Pipeline (FLEX), which uses language models to iteratively refine a robot's internal representation of task features from natural language corrections via three complementary operations: Add missing features, Generalize existing specific features, and Mask irrelevant features. We evaluate FLEX on 2D navigation scenarios, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation tasks, and a real-world study using naturalistic human language corrections and real-robot demonstrations. Comparisons against single-operation and unscaffolded baselines show that all three operations are necessary in interactive scenarios, and that FLEX achieves consistently higher normalized reward compared to other feature editing approaches while maintaining compact, transferable representations. Project available at https://mit-clear-lab.github.io/FLEX/
authors: Audrey Lee, Nathaniel Dennler, Ilia Sucholutsky, Andreea Bobu
bullets: Robot demonstrations show what to do but may not clarify which task features matter, causing misaligned representations.
FLEX iteratively edits representations using three operations: add missing features, generalize overly specific ones, and mask irrelevant ones.
Evaluated on 2D navigation, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation, and real-robot demonstrations with naturalistic language corrections.
All three editing operations are needed for interactive scenarios; FLEX achieves higher normalized reward than compared editing baselines while preserving compact, transferable representations.

papers.abstract: Adapting language models to new domains during post-training risks degrading previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon commonly known as catastrophic forgetting. Existing mitigation methods largely treat forgetting as a consequence of excessive model drift. They therefore constrain updates by preserving old outputs, replaying old data, or regularizing changes to parameters and representations so that the updated model remains close to its previous state. We take a different view: Rather than pulling the updated model back toward its old state, we translate the new domain into the model's pre-existing knowledge space, making unfamiliar knowledge learnable through familiar procedures. Therefore, we propose Skill Schema Transport (SST), a post-training framework that transports new knowledge into the model's existing skill space. SST abstracts each example type into a skill schema, preserving its essential operations, dependencies, and verification steps while removing domain-specific surface forms. By recasting new examples as instances of reusable procedures, SST turns knowledge update from trajectory memorization into procedural reuse. In continual domain adaptation settings, SST consistently reduces forgetting while improving generalization to related tasks. Across two 3B instruction-tuned backbones, SST improves average final performance on streamed domains by 2.53 to 5.75 points over sequential post-training. It also lowers max-drop forgetting in all evaluated settings, with the largest reduction from 42.41 to 7.10 points on the Qwen-3B MATH stream, while substantially recovering the OOD degradation induced by sequential updates.
authors: Zijie Liu, Zhen Tan, Charles Fleming, Tianlong Chen
bullets: Motivation: Continual domain adaptation can degrade previously acquired capabilities.
Method: SST abstracts examples into domain-agnostic skill schemas containing essential operations, dependencies, and verification steps.
Key idea: It promotes procedural reuse instead of memorizing update trajectories or constraining model drift.
Results: Across two 3B instruction-tuned backbones, SST improves final streamed-domain performance by 2.53–5.75 points over sequential post-training.
Scope/result: SST lowers forgetting in all evaluated settings and recovers substantial out-of-domain degradation, including a Qwen-3B MATH-stream max-drop reduction from 42.41 to 7.10 points.

papers.abstract: Selecting intermediate features from a frozen diffusion model for discriminative tasks is non-trivial because the useful signal is distributed across the denoising trajectory, network depth, and channels. In practice, this requires choosing a timestep, a block, and a channel subset. Existing methods either fix these choices by hand or optimize only a few extraction hyperparameters, most often the timestep, then reuse the same rule across inputs and budgets. We introduce Policy-Mask, a budget-conditioned policy trained on the downstream objective that jointly selects all three under a prescribed channel budget. Without normalization, the channel-score contribution grows with the number of selected channels and dominates the timestep and block updates. We normalize it by subset cardinality, keeping the three policy heads on comparable scales and stabilizing joint training. At matched budgets, Policy-Mask improves over fixed extraction and feature-filter baselines across segmentation, classification, and semantic correspondence, reaching 38.9 mIoU on ADE20K, 75.4% top-1 on CIFAR-100 at 128 dimensions, and 76.3 PCK@0.1 on SPair-71k. Component-wise ablations show that block selection materially affects downstream accuracy, and the highest recorded channel-budget score occurs at 256 retained channels, identifying a practical operating point for compact diffusion representations. We further adapt Policy-Mask to diffusion transformers, including PixArt-$\Sigma$ and SD3.5 MMDiT, by replacing U-Net channels with image-token hidden dimensions.
authors: Ivan Listopadov, Maksim Nakhodnov, Aibek Alanov
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of extracting task-relevant features distributed across diffusion trajectories, depths, and channels.
Trains three coordinated policy heads under a prescribed channel budget, with channel-score normalization to stabilize joint optimization.
Improves over fixed-extraction and feature-filter baselines across segmentation, classification, and semantic correspondence.
Reports 38.9 mIoU on ADE20K, 75.4% top-1 on CIFAR-100 at 128 dimensions, and 76.3 PCK@0.1 on SPair-71k.
Finds block selection materially affects accuracy; 256 retained channels is the highest-scoring recorded budget, and the approach extends to diffusion transformers.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success in decision-making tasks, but modern online RL remains highly sensitive to the quality of training experience. Understanding the contribution of individual training instances is therefore central to data-centric RL, with applications ranging from experience selection to policy interpretation. Existing data attribution methods for online RL primarily focus on local influence within a single training round, overlooking the non-local data influence across multiple training rounds. In this work, we formalize data attribution in online RL through a trajectory-level leave-one-out quantity, RL-LOO, which measures how one training sample influences a downstream target after subsequent online updates have taken place. We then derive RL-IF, a first-order estimator that propagates data influence through both optimization effects and policy-induced sampling effects, and provide theoretical guarantees on its approximation accuracy under smoothness assumptions. Our analysis further disentangles these two effects and shows both theoretically and empirically that the full RL-IF estimator can often be well approximated using the optimization effect alone. Building on this observation, we develop RINSE, a practical data filtering method for online RL. Experiments on standard control benchmarks and an RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation setting show that RINSE improves training efficiency and final performance over standard PPO and local attribution baselines. These results suggest that RL-IF provides a practical and principled framework for understanding and improving online RL.
authors: Shixuan Liu, Cheng Tang, Yuzheng Hu, Fan Wu, Han Zhao, Jiaqi W. Ma
bullets: Defines RL-LOO as a trajectory-level measure of a sample’s non-local influence on downstream targets.
Develops RL-IF, a first-order estimator capturing both optimization and policy-induced sampling effects.
Provides approximation guarantees under smoothness assumptions and finds optimization effects often suffice in practice.
Introduces RINSE, a practical filtering method that improves efficiency and final performance in control and RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation experiments.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic operation requires memory that scales with essential information rather than execution time. We present a parameter-space memory framework where each episode is stored as a separable object. A neural implicit representation is fitted to episode video from a shared, meta-learned initialization; the resulting weight delta constitutes the memory. Crucially, this delta remains a fixed size regardless of whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames. A learned projector maps the weight delta into token embeddings, conditioning a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint command regression, without frame retrieval at query time. On RoboMME, the language model exceeds chance across all question types, and the decoder achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.51. Replacing the delta with matched noise drops performance by 11.4 points, while random-origin weights are non-decodable, proving the meta-learned initialization is essential for embedding episode content. By representing individual experiences as fixed-size weight deltas in a common parameter space, this approach decouples memory cost from time horizon and provides a basis for scalable streaming memory.
authors: Leann Alhashishi, Christos Margadji, Sebastian William Pattinson
bullets: Addresses the challenge of scaling long-horizon robotic memory with episode duration.
Fits a neural implicit representation to episode video from a shared meta-learned initialization; the weight delta becomes the memory.
Projects each delta into tokens for language-model question answering and a decoder for joint-command regression.
On RoboMME, the language model performs above chance across question types, while action decoding reaches mean R² = 0.51.
Noise replacement reduces performance by 11.4 points, and random-origin weights are non-decodable, highlighting the importance of meta-learned initialization.

papers.abstract: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine's tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.
authors: Matthew Strong, Ankush K. Dhawan, Julien Poffet, Giuse Pham, Jinho So, Monroe Kennedy III
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable robot-learning data without depth sensors, robot hardware, or restricting augmentation to demonstrated objects.
Tracks object 3D poses using DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats and aligns photograph-based digital object “cousins” to demonstrated objects and functional regions.
Maps the human hand motion to feasible robot grasps and generates demonstrations in IsaacSim or MuJoCo.
Generates over 2,000 episodes in about two hours and supports training from one human video per task.
Across two real robots and four tasks, policies trained on generated data match or exceed teleoperation-trained policies across diverse object instances.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly take part in extended conversations where they can both shape and be shaped by another party's views, yet most persuasion research measures only one side of that exchange. We introduce a controlled LLM-LLM debate framework in which two language-model roles repeatedly discuss a contested topic (climate-change attribution): one is given an assigned stance and, in some conditions, an explicit instruction to persuade, while the other receives no assigned position. Across four ordered model combinations involving GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, we track both each role's explicitly reported position and a separate measure of its turn-by-turn behavior inside the conversation. Opinion dynamics differ substantially across model combinations: same-model interactions narrow the opinion gap on average, clearly for only one of the two models, while cross-model interactions widen it. Explicit reports and in-dialogue behavior capture distinct aspects of opinion dynamics, and a blanket instruction to persuade does not reliably increase influence. These findings suggest that conversational influence depends not only on assigned roles and initial positions but also on the participating models, with implications for how opinion change is measured in extended LLM interactions.
authors: Mohammad Siahkamari, Phuoc Dat Nguyen, Stephen MacNeil
bullets: Examines repeated debates about climate-change attribution between assigned-stance and unassigned LLM roles.
Tracks both explicitly reported opinions and turn-by-turn conversational behavior.
Same-model interactions generally narrow opinion gaps, while cross-model interactions widen them.
Reported opinions and in-dialogue behavior reflect distinct aspects of opinion dynamics.
Results indicate that assigned roles, initial positions, and model identity jointly shape conversational influence.

papers.abstract: The weights of a trained network do not have uniform sensitivity to model accuracy: the 1% most sensitive weights carry about a fifth of the damage a bit flip can do. This distribution decides the bit-flip tolerance of a model, the fraction of weights a code must cover and the bits each weight needs; existing schemes work with the distribution training leaves. We show that we can systematically modulate or alter the weight sensitivity distribution of a trained model, thereby shifting weights from one sensitivity bin to another. The sensitivity of a stored weight is the product of its gradient and the step a flip takes in the storage format, and LEAN adds a composite regularizer on both factors, a range term that bounds the flip step and a tail term that lowers the gradient of the most sensitive weights, with one coefficient {\lambda} setting how far the distribution moves. Ten epochs with the term, as a fine-tune or as the last epochs of training, shrink the sensitive tail 5 to 13 times on nine vision models (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet) within 0.5 points of accuracy; real flips confirm that the reshaped weights do less damage, a plain gradient-norm penalty does not reproduce the effect, and a preliminary extension to three small language models shows the same tail shaping. With a BCH code over 1% of the weights the model then survives 300 progressive bit-search flips in every training seed and 500 in two of three, where three of four published defenses with the same code fail by 300 and WCAT falls to 75% at 500. The reshaped distribution also cuts the parity for a fixed guarantee 3.7 times and makes a sensitivity-ordered 8/6/4/3-bit format affordable, which stores ImageNet ResNet-50 at a 3.29-bit weight payload, 2.4 times smaller than INT8, above the accuracy of LSQ at 3 bits.
bullets: Targets the uneven sensitivity of stored weights, where a small fraction can cause disproportionate bit-flip damage.
Adds a composite regularizer that limits storage-format flip steps and reduces gradients among the most sensitive weights; a single coefficient controls the reshaping strength.
Across nine vision models, ten epochs reduced the sensitive tail by 5–13× while staying within 0.5 accuracy points; real bit flips confirmed lower damage.
With BCH protection over 1% of weights, models survived hundreds of progressive bit-search flips, and the reshaped distribution reduced parity requirements by 3.7×.
Supports sensitivity-ordered mixed-precision storage, achieving a 3.29-bit weight payload for ImageNet ResNet-50 and preliminary tail shaping in three small language models.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview. Step 1: a normally trained network has a heavy-tailed weight-sensitivity distribution; the top 1% of weights (HIGH) carry about 20% of the first-order damage of sign-bit flips. Step 2: ten epochs with the extra term λPLEAN, as a fine-tune or as the last epochs of training, move weights out of HIGH and MID into LOW; λ sets how far, and accuracy changes by at most 0.5 points. Step 3: the deployed model needs 3.7 times less parity for the same guarantee, survives 300 to 500 progressive bit-search flips with a 1% BCH code, and stores at 3.3 bits per weight in a sensitivity-ordered format.

(b) HIGH weights per layer before and after LEAN, ResNet-18 CIFAR-10, λ = 40: the deep layers empty, the first convolution and first stage keep most of what remains. Figure 6 shows the same data as a cumulative distribution. The bulk of the distribution is unchanged; the HIGH tail moves left into the MID and LOW bands.

The shaded bands are the baseline LOW, MID and HIGH bins. The LEAN curve separates from the baseline at the MID boundary and stays about one decade lower across the HIGH band. The box in each panel gives the count above the HIGH threshold before and after.

Fig. 7. The knob. HIGH-bin share (bars, log scale) and clean accuracy (line) against λ for six models, at the values trained for the sweep. The HIGH bin falls monotonically and saturates near 0.1%; accuracy stays within 0.5 points up to λ = 40 and drops at λ = 100.

Fig. 9. LEAN inside training, λ = 40; ResNet-18 CIFAR-10 in the top row, VGG-16 CIFAR-10 below. (a, d) Test accuracy for epochs 180 to 200 of a 200-epoch run; at epoch 190 the run is forked into a plain control and a branch with the LEAN term on. (b, e) The penalty over the ten LEAN epochs inside training (learning rate 0.0005 to 0) and in the fine-tune (0.002, cosine). (c, f) HIGH share and accuracy of the control, the last-epochs model, the last-epochs model with the rate held at 0.002, and the fine-tune. (g) HIGH share per recipe on four more pairs, accuracy inside the bars.

Fig. 3. The LEAN procedure. The trained network is quantized and its sensitivity distribution is measured once, which fixes the HIGH and MID thresholds; ten epochs with the LEAN term follow, as a fine-tune or as the last epochs of training, with the tail T re-selected and the tail term applied, through double backpropagation, every fourth step; the model is then remeasured against the fixed thresholds and packed. λ is the only knob; the low-bit format uses a separate quantization-aware fine-tune (last paragraph of this section).

(b) The cumulative distribution, counted from the tail: the number of weights whose damage is at least a threshold s; one ten-epoch fine-tune leaves 9 times fewer weights above the baseline HIGH threshold at the same accuracy, while Hessian-aware training leaves the tail where normal training left it (1.01% against 1.00% above the threshold). (c) Accuracy under progressive bit search when the same 1% BCH code protects each model: the normally trained and the Hessian-aware model fall to chance by 300 flips, the LEAN model (λ = 40) keeps 94% after 500 in two of three training seeds and after 300 in all (Table V).

papers.title: LEAN: Loss-Engineered Modulation of the Model Weight-Sensitivity Distribution for Efficient, Error-Tolerant Neural Networks

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops. We measure how much of the weight gradient this throws away, exactly and for every k from one backward pass, on nine looped language models, and report three findings. First, on a trained model this lost gradient is set near the output: once the loop count is well above k, it barely changes with the loop count (within about 0.03 from 32 to 64 loops on the three models we tested, as a pre-registered test predicted for Parcae). Where the backward signal shrinks, $\rho^k$, with $\rho$ the signal's fitted shrink per loop, approximates it at moderate loop counts but overstates it at long ones, because the fitted $\rho$ drifts up as the fit takes in more loops. On Ouro the signal grows, and keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient. Second, the lost gradient falls during fine-tuning, by 0.07-0.22 within 300 steps on three of four models, on held-out problems too. The fall is not just the read-out's share of the gradient; training only the layers outside the loop reproduced up to half of it, and it also falls under truncated training. So a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. Third, we could not show that it predicts the training cost of truncation better than rules that need no measurement: on two new models it tied Parcae's cost at the same k, in a test too small to separate them.
bullets: The study exactly measures gradients omitted when backpropagating through only the last k loops in nine looped language models.

In trained models, the omitted-gradient fraction often stabilizes once total loops greatly exceed k, though behavior varies: on Ouro, retaining two of four loops loses 81% of the final output gradient.
The omitted-gradient fraction decreases by 0.07–0.22 within 300 fine-tuning steps on three of four models, including on held-out problems.
This decrease is not explained solely by the readout layer and also occurs under truncated training.
Gradient-loss measurements did not outperform simple measurement-free rules for predicting truncation cost in a small test on two new models.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes gradient behavior in looped language model architectures; relevant to architectural advances and training of foundation language models.
papers.title: How Much Gradient Does Truncated Backprop Lose in Looped Transformers?
papers.tldr: Truncated backpropagation can discard a large, loop-count-dependent portion of gradients, but the loss often shrinks during fine-tuning and does not yet reliably predict truncation’s training cost.

papers.abstract: Few-shot image classification (FSIC) frequently suffers from visual ambiguity, where background clutter and RGB appearance similarities hinder discriminative feature matching in data-scarce settings. To mitigate this, we propose DAFIC, a geometry-guided framework that incorporates monocular depth into representation learning, episodic adaptation, and dense support-query matching. DAFIC first learns geometry-aware token representations through RGB-D self-supervised pre-training. Subsequently, the Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation (DGA) module uses depth-derived geometry to refine patch representations with geometry-enriched class context while suppressing background interference. Spatial Bidirectional Patch Matching (SBiM) then performs bidirectional dense matching on the refined features, reducing sensitivity to spurious correspondences and background clutter. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks show that DAFIC achieves strong performance against existing methods, with ablation and robustness analyses supporting the effectiveness of coupling geometry-conditioned episodic adaptation with bidirectional matching for few-shot visual recognition.
authors: Zhiqi Miao, Estefan\'ia Talavera, Weichuan Zhang, Jiapan Guo
bullets: Addresses visual ambiguity from background clutter and similar RGB appearances in data-scarce classification.
Uses RGB-D self-supervised pre-training to learn geometry-aware token representations.
Applies Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation to refine patch features with class context while suppressing background interference.
Uses Spatial Bidirectional Patch Matching for more robust dense support-query correspondence.
Experiments on four benchmarks, including ablation and robustness analyses, support the framework’s effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our proposed DAFIC framework. The depth estimator first predicts a pixel-wise aligned depth map, which is concatenated with the RGB image to form an RGB-D input. The RGB-D pre-trained ViT backbone then extracts token embeddings, where the CLS token encodes geometry-enriched global semantic context. Next, the Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation (DGA) module refines the patch embeddings: Depth-guided Attention (DA) converts depth priors into geometry-salient patch attention (scaled by β); Geometryaware Adaptation (GA) then integrates the enriched CLS (class) embedding (scaled by λ). Finally, based on the refined patch embeddings, the non-parametric SBiM classifier performs query-to-support bidirectional dense matching, together with an auxiliary global similarity objective, for reliable FSIC.

Figure 7. More visualizations of patch-to-class semantic alignment between baseline CPEA [20] and DAFIC. Warmer colors (towards red) indicate stronger class relevance, whereas cooler colors (towards blue) denote weaker or non-relevant regions. As shown, the RGB-D ViT backbone alone already yields more classconsistent responses than the baseline. After applying the full DAFIC framework, the patch-to-class alignment is further improved and becomes more precise.

Figure 6. Comparison between our RGB-D and RGB-only self-supervised pre-training across four datasets, using six metrics to monitor the training dynamics. RGB-D pre-training generally achieves lower total and class-level losses, converges faster, and yields higher training accuracy than RGB-only pre-training, while its clustering metrics (NMI and F-score) are generally lower. The yellow and red curves denote the training phases before and after the selected checkpoint used for downstream few-shot classification.

papers.selection_reason: Depth-guided geometric adaptation for few-shot classification incorporates geometric priors into visual representations.
papers.title: Depth-guided Geometric Adaptation for Few-shot Image Classification
papers.tldr: DAFIC improves few-shot image classification by using monocular depth to make feature adaptation and dense patch matching more geometry-aware and less sensitive to clutter.

papers.abstract: Progress on foundation model pretraining is gated by who can afford a trial, and relational pretraining is no exception. Recipes are developed inside individual labs, reported under private protocols, and do not accumulate. Speedrun leaderboards remove that barrier by decentralizing the search rather than the training run. The problem is fixed, the stack is open, entries are ranked by wall-clock time to a quality target, and one GPU is enough to hold the record. We introduce modded-nanoRT, the first such leaderboard for Relational Transformers. Which database to hold out decides whether the benchmark can resolve improvements at all, so we fix it by calibration, ranking six candidates by how sharply a 45-minute learning curve separates improvement from seed noise. We open the leaderboard with typed trilinear attention, a relational operator that conditions attention scores and values on the foreign key traversed, together with Muon and SIGReg. The recipe reaches the target in 305.63 seconds on one NVIDIA H200, 8.11x faster than the reference implementation, and wins 13 of 15 pairs outside the development database. We will release the benchmark, its frozen artifacts, and the record runs. Our code is available at https://github.com/kunumi/nanoRT.
authors: Gabriel Wedson Mendon\c{c}a de Souza Veloso, Luan Borges Teodoro Reis Sena, Denis Oliveira Correa, Francisco Galuppo Azevedo
bullets: Addresses the lack of shared, affordable protocols for comparing relational pretraining recipes.
Calibrates and fixes the held-out database by ranking six candidates for sensitivity to improvement versus seed noise.
Uses typed trilinear attention with Muon and SIGReg in the opening recipe.
Wins 13 of 15 pairwise comparisons outside the development database.
Releases the benchmark, frozen artifacts, and record runs; code is publicly available.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a speedrunning leaderboard for relational foundation model pretraining to improve training efficiency and speed.
papers.title: Speedrunning Relational Foundation Model Pretraining

papers.abstract: Visual question answering requires models to assign attributes and relations to the correct objects, a problem known as visual binding. Structured prompts make these assignments explicit through labeled fields. Yet an improvement from the full prompt does not reveal which labels help or how they interact. First, we isolate field-label effects across ten models and six tasks by holding the image and claim fixed. These comparisons reveal differences that overall accuracy can hide. With a relation label present, adding object-role labels helps Qwen3 but hurts Qwen2 on Spatial. Second, we compare auxiliary hints that preserve or swap the question's role assignments against a no-hint baseline. Across two image sets, Qwen3's advantage with preserving hints mainly reflects errors caused by swapped hints. Preserving hints remain near baseline. Field order further affects the harm. Third, we test clearer hint wording and direct selection of the relation shown in the image. Clearer hints improve text matching but do not consistently improve visual judgments. In contrast, relation selection partly reduces errors for some hints in Qwen3 and GPT-4.1-mini.
authors: Xiaoyu Ma, Zheyuan Zhang, Kaiwen Shi, Yanfang Ye
bullets: Structured prompts expose visual-binding errors that overall accuracy can obscure.
Object-role labels interact differently with models: they help Qwen3 but hurt Qwen2 on Spatial when relation labels are present.
For Qwen3, preserving hints stays near the no-hint baseline, while swapped hints account for much of the apparent benefit of preserving hints.
Clearer hint wording improves text matching but does not consistently improve visual judgments.
Selecting the relation shown in the image partly reduces hint-related errors for some cases in Qwen3 and GPT-4.1-mini.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of compositional prompt cues in visual question answering directly concerns multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Beyond Correct Answers: How Compositional Cues Shape Visual Judgments
papers.tldr: Visual prompt structure can substantially alter visual judgments, but its effects depend on the model, task, hint correctness, and field order.

papers.abstract: Instruction-guided video generative models offer a scalable solution for stress-testing autonomous driving systems by simulating diverse environmental conditions. However, driving scenes operate within a dense Operational Design Domain (ODD) governed by strict traffic semantics. When applied to global driving-condition edits, general-purpose instruction-guided video editors frequently corrupt these semantics, leading to structural hallucinations and ``temporal shock.'' This work distills and protects traffic semantics during video editing at three levels. First, we construct a hybrid dataset by combining temporally aligned real-world videos with synthetic edits, balancing foundational scene structure with unambiguous appearance signals. Second, during training, we adapt advantage conditioning from offline reinforcement learning to align the model using dense rewards. We extract dense, pixel-level rewards from the hybrid data to serve as a localized signal and actively steer generation toward structurally reliable pixels. Finally, our model mitigates temporal shock by introducing thinking frames, a transition mechanism that seamlessly reconciles static image conditioning with dynamic video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method prevents the corruption of multi-actor dynamics, establishing state-of-the-art spatiotemporal consistency, yielding consistent user preference (39% relative improvement in content preservation and 12% in temporal consistency), and achieving a significant 5% gain in downstream road line segmentation and 7% gain in downstream multi-object detection.
authors: Mauricio Soroco, Yuqiu Liu, Zaid Tasneem, Francesco Pittaluga, Abhishek Aich, Wuyang Chen, Manmohan Chandraker, Ziyu Jiang
bullets: Targets structural hallucinations and “temporal shock” caused by general-purpose video editors in driving scenes.
Uses a hybrid dataset combining temporally aligned real videos with synthetic edits to preserve scene structure and clarify appearance changes.
Applies advantage conditioning with dense, pixel-level rewards to steer generation toward structurally reliable edits.
Introduces “thinking frames” to smoothly connect static image conditioning with dynamic video context.
Reports 39% relative improvement in content preservation, 12% in temporal consistency, 5% in road-line segmentation, and 7% in multi-object detection.

papers.abstract: We present WorldStream, an open-ended 3D world model with three simultaneous capabilities: it extends playable terrain beyond any pre-specified map, acts on open-ended language in the running world, and restores visited places with their edits. A hierarchical planner over a typed decision model emits structured decision state: Macro fixes settlement, ecology, transport, and hydrological structure across a group of tiles; Micro specializes that contract into tile semantics under measured terrain and accepted neighbor commitments. Deterministic local code compiles accepted plans into terrain, roads, settlements, vegetation, and entities. Streaming separates their reach: plans run ahead along the predicted corridor, compilation only where movement will soon need it, geometry behind the user released. One world record retains plans, seeds, object identities and mutable state, boundary commitments, and edits by attribute, revised as the user advances and edits; returning tiles recompile from it. The same record grounds interaction: the model acts on existing entities, including stateful NPCs that update as they act, edits the present region, or attaches intent to unplanned regions. Together they yield a world expanding under bounded budgets, connected across independently planned tiles, and interactive.

papers.abstract: Automated judges of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) outputs are necessary, but large language model (LLM) judges are costly and slow at scale. We compared Jev, a decision language model that returns structured judgments, with frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On 118 pediatric answers, Jev's agreement with physicians' ordinal quality ratings (Gwet's AC2 0.50; expected score 0.53) matched or exceeded that of seven of 12 LLM judges, including frontier models, Claude Opus 5.5 (0.49) and GPT-6 (0.38). On physician-graded binary HealthBench criteria, Jev matched or exceeded four of six LLM judges. On MedHELM's open-ended tasks, Jev's agreement with a three-LLM jury approached or exceeded the jurors' internal agreement. On HealthBench Professional, Jev matched the benchmark's reference judge, GPT-5.4, on 91% of criteria (other judges, 91-93%). Frontier judges cost 73-294 times more than Jev and took 7-57 times longer. Jev may enable efficient clinical AI evaluation at scale.

bullets: Addresses the high cost and latency of LLM-based clinical AI evaluation.
Compared Jev with frontier and open-weight LLM judges across four clinical evaluation settings.
Jev matched or exceeded several LLM judges on physician-aligned ordinal and binary assessments.
Its agreement with a multi-LLM jury on open-ended tasks was comparable to the jury’s internal agreement.
Frontier judges cost 73–294× more and took 7–57× longer than Jev; findings support scalable evaluation, with scope limited to the tested use cases.

papers.abstract: We present Register Anything Model (RAM), a unified model for generalizable 3D point cloud registration that robustly estimates 6-DoF transformations across diverse domains spanning sensors and environments. Existing registration methods are typically tailored to a single domain, with carefully tuned architectures and hyperparameters, and thus degrade markedly when applied to novel domains. We bridge this gap by training a single model on diverse data from indoor, outdoor, and object domains. A central challenge is the severe geometric discrepancy across domains, i.e., differences in scene scale, sensor noise, point density, and structural patterns, which hinders processing with a unified point-based model. To address this, we introduce a geometry-aware normalization strategy that jointly voxelizes and normalizes point clouds into a standardized geometric space, adaptively based on their geometric properties to preserve salient local structures while standardizing resolution. Built on this normalization, RAM follows a hierarchical coarse-to-fine paradigm, and employs an efficient geometric transformer that models local geometric consistency instead of globally over all points. This design mitigates discretization noise introduced by voxelization, and improves computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on 12 benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in terms of inlier ratio and registration recall. Notably, our method outperforms the counterparts trained on each separate domain, showing superior generalization capability.
authors: Zheng Qin, Junhua Xi, Yan Huang, Jiahong Lai, Anwen Huang, Qiong Li, Guangda Zhang, Kai Xu
bullets: Targets the poor cross-domain generalization of registration methods tuned to individual sensors or environments.

Outperforms models trained separately for each domain, demonstrating stronger generalization across domains.

papers.abstract: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.

bullets: Existing harness-evolution methods can degrade when more optimization tasks are added, due to poor evidence selection.

As the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR’s pass rate rises from 64.3% to 68.3%, while baselines decline.
Its racing mechanism reduces validation executions by 60% while identifying near-optimal candidates.

papers.abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real-robot manipulation tasks. Videos and code are available at https://anonymous-submission-20.github.io/T-WLA.github.io/.
authors: Kaichen Zhou, Yuzhen Chen, Hannah Yao, Chonghe Jiang, Rao Fu, Xihang Yu, Wei Dai, Bashar Kabbarah, Haoyu Chen, Ishita Goluguri, Zhiyang Dou, Haonan Chen, Fangneng Zhan, Mengyu Wang, Wojciech Matusik, Antonio Torralba, Paul Pu Liang

papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.
authors: Pedro H. Barcha Correia, Matheus Azevedo de S\'a, Paulo H. Gomes de Senna, Giovanni Mandel Martignago, Victor Takashi Hayashi, Charles Christian Miers, Marcos A. Simplicio Jr
bullets: Introduces a general threat model for memory injection in LLM-as-a-service platforms.
Shows that all evaluated services—ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash—can collectively achieve all NIST attack goals under this model.
Identifies attack vectors spanning personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and MCP-connected resources.
Finds persistent manipulation in fresh sessions, including disinformation, harmful content, and simulated unresponsiveness; Claude also enables organizational spread and prompt exfiltration.

papers.abstract: Most unified multimodal models treat images and text asymmetrically: a pretrained language model generates text, an attached diffusion head generates images, and outputs that contain both are produced in a fixed order, so the first output cannot adapt to the second. We ask whether both modalities can instead be generated by one process that is trained on them jointly from scratch. Pretrained encoder spaces hold both modalities in one continuous form and carry knowledge learned at scale, and recent work finds them effective as generative targets for vision and language. We therefore model the joint distribution directly in these spaces. We introduce JUICE (Joint Unified multimodal modeling In Continuous Encoder spaces), a single flow matching Transformer over frozen image and text representations, in which each modality has its own noise level. Which modalities are clean and which are generated then decides the task: image generation, captioning, visual question answering, or joint generation. Controlled pretraining runs test each design choice. At equal guidance, generating text as continuous states leaves image generation intact (48.41 GenEval, against 47.86 for a model trained only for text-to-image generation), while captions lose some exact wording. Training on joint and conditional denoising together beats either alone, and semantic encoder spaces beat VAE latents and raw pixels as targets. At 2.1B parameters, with no language model initialization and at 224x224, JUICE reaches up to 0.88 on GenEval and 73.1 on VQAv2. By sampling both modalities from the joint distribution (coupled sampling), it can also draw a route on a map while writing out the matching moves. On mazes with several valid solutions, joint success rises from 54.6% with independent sampling to 93.7%, and no modality has to go first. On visual spatial planning, JUICE solves 99.8% of maps at its training sizes.
authors: Jiahan Li, Huangyuan Su, Shengbang Tong, Shusheng Yang, Ruihan Guo, Suozhi Huang, Hexu Zhao, Pratyusha Sharma, Sherry Yang, Jiatao Gu, Rob Fergus, Kyunghyun Cho
bullets: Addresses the asymmetry of prior unified models, where one modality is generated first and cannot adapt to the other.
Uses frozen image and text representations, modality-specific noise levels, and a shared flow-matching Transformer.
Supports image generation, captioning, visual question answering, and joint generation by varying which modalities are clean or generated.
Joint and conditional denoising together improves performance; semantic encoder spaces outperform VAE latents and raw pixels as targets.
Coupled sampling greatly improves multimodal consistency on mazes, raising joint success from 54.6% to 93.7%; JUICE reaches up to 0.88 GenEval and 73.1 VQAv2.

papers.title: JUICE: Unified Multimodal Modeling in Pretrained Representation Spaces

papers.abstract: Flow-matching policies adjust inference cost through the number of solver steps, but reinforcement learning at a single fixed solver budget can hide degradation at cheaper deployment budgets and even erase useful one-step behavior present in a pretrained policy. We introduce Action-Ratio-Clip Flow (ArcFlow), a deployment-aware algorithm for training one flow policy across a specified range of solver budgets. ArcFlow combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection. For reconstruction objectives, its bridge aggregates temporal probes into one surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action, with a boundary residual exactly equal to deployed one-step reconstruction error. Cycling exposes the shared field to the deployment range, and selection optimizes its performance floor. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget endpoint supervision applies the same principle without replacing the native update. Both realizations preserve the architecture and deployment-time cost. Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow attains the highest mean one-step return among five flow-policy baselines on 25 of 30 tasks under each method's reported training settings. Component studies identify complementary improvements from boundary supervision, the fixed-grid bridge, budget exposure, and deployment selection. These results establish deployment-budget-aware training as an effective route to strong low-step control with one policy serving multiple inference costs.
bullets: Targets degradation at low solver budgets caused by training at only one fixed budget.

papers.abstract: Aggressive low-state weight quantization can substantially reduce neural-network representational flexibility, making predictive performance difficult to preserve when only a few discrete weight states are available. We investigate this regime for Transformer-based electricity-load forecasting using 3-, 5-, 7-, and 16-state weight quantization across feed-forward-only and attention-plus-feed-forward quantization. Two tasks predict either the next hour or the next 24 hours from the preceding 48 hours across two co-primary electricity-consumption datasets. Direct post-training quantization (PTQ) increased mean normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) relative to full precision by 6.25 and 7.04 percentage points in Datasets A and B, whereas quantization-aware fine-tuning (QAT-FT) recovered approximately 90.2% and 94.5% of these penalties. Quantization-aware training from random initialization (Scratch-QAT) also produced competitive low-state solutions, with particularly favorable behavior at three states. We further introduce accumulated-update thresholding, which accumulates optimizer-proposed weight changes before commitment. Relative to paired Scratch-QAT controls, this reduced committed shadow-weight updates by approximately 99.7% and discrete state transitions by approximately 77--80%, while mean NRMSE changed by only +0.042 and +0.197 percentage points. These results show that useful Transformer forecasting can be retained under highly discrete weight representations while strongly suppressing target-state activity, supporting a prospective route toward compact, low-activity edge forecasting using multilevel synaptic devices.

bullets: Studies 3-, 5-, 7-, and 16-state weight quantization for next-hour and next-24-hour forecasting from the previous 48 hours.
Direct post-training quantization worsened mean NRMSE, while quantization-aware fine-tuning recovered about 90.2%–94.5% of the added error.
Quantization-aware training from scratch produced competitive low-state models, with particularly favorable behavior at three states.
Accumulated-update thresholding reduced shadow-weight updates by about 99.7% and discrete state transitions by about 77–80%, with minimal NRMSE change.
Results support compact, low-activity edge forecasting with highly discrete or multilevel synaptic devices.

papers.abstract: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting alternatives to explore and safely accepting plans in world-model agents.
Compares imagined action sequences from the same model state and measures variability in repeated rollouts of the actor’s sequence.
Uses this reference to scale exploration signals and accept a plan only when its predicted advantage exceeds reference variability by a fixed factor.
Reuses the base world model, actor, and critic without an additional disagreement ensemble; evaluation runs the learned actor alone.
Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI has the highest task-average score among compared baselines in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline on 15 of 18 tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SDI. Imagine: candidate action sequences (siblings, blue) and repeated rollouts of the actor’s fixed sequence (dashed gray) start at the same latent state zt. The lower branch normalizes, clips, and weights the exploration bonus b to augment the first imagined reward r̃. The bonus anneals after the first training success. Exploration and gating use separate rollout settings; evaluation uses the actor alone.

papers.abstract: Conventional surgical segmentation relies on closed-set categories or explicit text queries, which cannot resolve implicit queries that require reasoning about workflows, instrument functions, and temporal relationships. To address these limitations, we propose SurgReasonSeg, a complexity-aware method that brings reasoning segmentation over digital twin (DT) representations to surgical video. Specifically, SurgReasonSeg constructs DT representations from surgical foundation models and trains two low-rank adapters (LoRA) of one large language model with reinforcement learning (RL), each specialized for a different query complexity. A lightweight router, also trained with RL, selects between the two adapters to balance latency against accuracy. SurgReasonSeg also sets the temporal context with an adaptive sliding window conditioned on query complexity and workflow phase, and retrieves relevant historical cases from a surgical context memory by workflow similarity and procedural relevance. We further introduce EndoVis-ReasonSeg, a surgical reasoning segmentation benchmark with 1,460 training and 961 test samples across semantic, spatial, and temporal categories. On EndoVis-ReasonSeg, SurgReasonSeg improves J&F over the strongest baseline, ReSurgSAM2, by 0.178, 0.237, and 0.297 on semantic, spatial, and temporal queries, and it also achieves the best results on the Ref-EndoVis17 and Ref-EndoVis18 referring segmentation benchmarks. A backbone-matched attribution protocol separates the contribution of the upstream segmenter from that of the reasoning modules. Our method runs at 18.8 FPS averaged over the query distribution, enabling real-time reasoning segmentation in surgical videos.
bullets: Addresses limitations of closed-set labels and explicit text queries that cannot capture workflow, instrument-function, and temporal reasoning.
Builds digital-twin representations and uses two reinforcement-learning-trained LoRA adapters, with a learned router balancing accuracy and latency by query complexity.
Adapts temporal context windows to query complexity and workflow phase, while retrieving relevant historical cases from a workflow-aware surgical memory.
Introduces the EndoVis-ReasonSeg benchmark with 1,460 training and 961 test samples across semantic, spatial, and temporal queries.
Reports higher J&F than ReSurgSAM2 across all three query types, best results on two referring-segmentation benchmarks, and 18.8 FPS average speed.

papers.abstract: Non-uniform allocation can improve post-training pruning of large language models, yet quality can still degrade sharply at high sparsity. To control degradation as sparsity increases, we introduce LADDER (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement), which allocates sparsity incrementally. At each step, it evaluates pruning an additional fraction of weights from each eligible layer and commits the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter. This process produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple budgets. We evaluate LADDER on five OPT, Llama, and Qwen models across 10-90% sparsity, using SparseGPT as its candidate-generation backend and comparing against uniform and adaptive allocation baselines. Results reveal a clear operating-regime trade-off: LADDER is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity but becomes substantially more robust from 70% onward. This high-sparsity advantage largely persists after posterior distillation across four of five models and translates into improved retention of aggregate zero-shot accuracy.
authors: Nicol\'as Mauricio Cuadrado \'Avila, Ivo Gollini Navarrete, Martin Tak\'a\v{c}, Samuel Horv\'ath
bullets: Targets sharp quality degradation in large language models under aggressive post-training pruning.
Evaluates candidate pruning steps per layer and selects the update with the smallest end-to-end degradation per removed parameter.
Produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple sparsity budgets.
Across OPT, Llama, and Qwen models, its main advantage emerges at 70% sparsity and above.
The high-sparsity benefit generally persists after posterior distillation, though performance is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity.

In our main experiments, the local backend is SparseGPT.

papers.abstract: Objects move, cameras pan, and weather drifts with the wind: much of what changes in sequential data is motion. Motion changes where things are, not what they are, and is therefore a symmetry of the data. Yet standard recurrent networks are not equivariant to it: their memory stays put while the input moves on. Flow equivariant recurrent networks first brought this symmetry into sequence models, for motions of constant velocity, or flows, by enumerating a bank of velocities. We extend this idea in three directions: from simple recurrent networks to convolutional LSTMs, from flows to motions whose velocity changes in time, and from enumerating velocities to estimating them. Treating a sequence as a field over time, we show that motion becomes a gauge symmetry: a global symmetry made local in time. Built on this view, our motion equivariant convolutional LSTM (MELSTM) uses its velocity model as the gauge field and is provably equivariant to every motion. Across future-frame prediction, classification of digits visible only through their motion, and action recognition under camera shake, MELSTM outperforms a convolutional LSTM and its flow equivariant counterpart with the same number of parameters: it is more accurate, generalizes to longer horizons and to unseen motions, and carries a fraction of the flow equivariant model's state.
authors: Vahid Hosseinzadeh, T. Anderson Keller, Michael Puthawala
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between moving inputs and stationary recurrent memory.
Extends motion-equivariant recurrence from simple RNNs to convolutional LSTMs and from constant-velocity flows to time-varying motion.
Estimates motion rather than enumerating a bank of velocities.
Demonstrates gains in future-frame prediction, motion-based digit classification, and action recognition under camera shake.
Outperforms parameter-matched convolutional LSTMs and flow-equivariant models while using substantially less state, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Hidden-state transport under RNN, Flow Equivariant RNN (FERNN), and Motion Equivariant RNN (MERNN) models. The first row shows the transformed input, ϕ ▷ Xt in the flow column and ψ ▷ Xt in the motion column. Here an MNIST digit undergoes two simultaneous changes: a geometric transformation along the group orbit (the motion, which differs across columns) and an intrinsic appearance change transverse to the group action (identical across columns). The second row shows the hidden state of an untrained leaky accumulator, ht+1 = λht + Xt (λ = 0.92), which can be viewed as a convolutional RNN, ht+1 = W⋆ht+U⋆Xt, with kernels W (x) = λδ(x) and U(x) = δ(x). The third row shows FERNN’s hidden state, which is lifted to velocity copies g ∈ {−3, . . . , 3}2 and evolves as hgt+1 = λ g ·hgt +Xt; we show the copy of maximum energy, i.e., the copy with the largest ∥hgt ∥2 2. The fourth row shows MERNN’s hidden state, ht+1 = λTvt ht + Xt, where Tvt is the transport operator and vt is the digit’s velocity at time t. Matched transport stacks evidence into a sharp digit at the true location, whereas mismatched transport leaves a decaying ghost trail along the residual motion.
Figure 4: Motion generalization sensitivity. Each model normalized by its own training error (1.0 = no degradation).

Figure 5: Motion-Only MNIST: Training efficiency and test accuracy. Right: five-seed mean ± s.d. of the best validation and the test accuracy and of the median time per epoch. Dotted lines: chance (10%).

Figure 3: Rollout stability and context-boundary sensitivity. Left: median rollout MSE. Middle: MSE at t = 16 of sequences whose last velocity change came 1–3 frames before the context boundary (boundary velocity age), relative to settled sequences (age ≥ 4). Right: the age-1 group over the rollout; the FELSTM penalty persists through mid-rollout before gradually decaying.
Figure 2: Training efficiency and test error. Right: test MSE over the trained horizon and at t = 100; mean ± s.d. over five seeds.

Figure 6: Motion generalization sensitivity in classification. Relative to their own training accuracy (far lower for LSTM), LSTM and FELSTM respond alike, except at speed 1, where LSTM improves because its 3 × 3 recurrence can move its memory with the digit.

Figure 7: KTH: training and generalization to camera shake. Left: validation accuracy under the training shake. Right: test accuracy under shakes of amplitude A and frequency f (A = 0: static camera); mean ± s.d. over three seeds.

Figure 9: The channel-handover penalty across the seven motion regimes. Top: kinematics of the seven evaluation regimes and the training baseline. The unpredictability ρ collapses the switching rate r and the jump magnitude |∆v| into a single number; net context displacement falls as ρ rises, because the trajectories become diffusive. Bottom: FELSTM’s architectural penalty (MSE normalised by the LSTM baseline) against ρ(1 − ρ). Because FELSTM allocates separate channels to discrete velocities, a velocity change forces a handover that strands accumulated temporal history; we model its cost as the product of the disruption (ρ) and the predictive value of what is stranded (1 − ρ). The penalty is negligible up to ρ(1 −ρ) ≈ 0.1, including under pure chaos (churn_max, ρ → 1), where the stranded history is worthless, and grows steeply above it. random_walk (frequent tiny jitters) and churn_half (less frequent but far larger jumps) are kinematically opposite, yet sit at nearly symmetric points of the parabola and show nearly equal penalties.

Figure 8: Length generalization beyond the trained horizon. Two held-out sequences; rows are the ground truth, LSTM, FELSTM, and MELSTM. The dashed box marks the 25 frames seen in training (15 context + 10 predicted); the rest is extrapolation, run out to t = 140, past the 85-step horizon scored in Figure 3. LSTM collapses almost immediately, FELSTM smears into high-frequency artifacts late in the rollout, and MELSTM stays sharp throughout.

Figure 12: Stochastic frame-pair velocities. In training, MELSTM uses frame-pair velocities with a probability that decays to 0 by epoch 25; validation uses slot tracking only. Losses (MSE + L1) are means over three seeds with the min–max range shaded; faint traces are recorded every 25 batches and circles once per epoch (Appendix B.1.2). Table: test MSE over the trained horizon and at t = 100; mean ± s.d.
Figure 13: Frame-pair curriculum. As Figure 12, but training uses frame-pair velocities on the first steps of the context, a window that shrinks from the whole context to none by epoch 25.

Figure 11: Velocity accuracy (one training run). The estimator is parameter-free and receives no gradient, so the rise from ≈ 66% at epoch 5 to above 99.5% by epoch 8 reflects the hidden-state template improving, not the estimator being fitted. Final values are means over the last five epochs. In the same run, the validation loss stays on a plateau near 7 × 10−2 until about epoch 6 and then falls by an order of magnitude while the accuracy climbs: the model leaves the plateau when the slots lock onto their digits. The five seeds of Figure 2 leave it at different times, which smooths their mean.

Figure 14: Hidden states on Motion-Only MNIST. Channel-averaged state of each MELSTM slot (a) and of the FELSTM copies at the velocities the digit takes during the context (b); the bottom rows show the input frames. The digit’s outline is drawn only for the reader: the frames themselves are pure noise. MELSTM’s slot s1 follows the digit and accumulates its shape, while s0 follows the background; because the digit’s velocity keeps changing, no FELSTM copy accumulates the shape for long.

Figure 10: Slot specialisation. Hidden-state evolution for a validation sequence (top) and a training sequence (bottom). Within each block the first two rows show the channel-averaged states H̄1, H̄2 of the K = 2 slots and the third the corresponding frame; column titles give t, in red once the decoder takes over. Each slot localises onto one digit and tracks it, and this is the template that Eq. (97) correlates against the incoming frame.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework integrating a robust wrench observer with a hybrid pose and force controller for physical Human-Robot Interaction (pHRI). In pHRI tasks, robots are expected to perform task-space motions robustly while remaining compliance with human disturbance, which proposes distinct control objectives. Most existing approaches focus mainly on either robustness or compliance and rely on force sensors for real-time tracking. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. Firstly, a neural network (NN) is trained to improve the observer performance by compensating for system friction and unmodeled dynamics. Secondly, a task-null-space decomposition is applied to separate the joint velocity and reduce the effect of the human disturbance on the observer. Finally, a hybrid pose and force controller is introduced to achieve the end-effector pose and force tracking. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides robust and accurate wrench estimation while maintaining reliable pose and force tracking performance. The proposed approach offers an effective solution and framework for pHRI without the need of force/torque sensor measurements which can be applied to many robotic manipulator platforms which do not have force/torque sensors.
authors: Nuo Chen, Ya-Jun Pan, Onur Toker
bullets: Targets pHRI tasks requiring both robust task-space motion and compliance to human disturbances.
Uses a neural network to compensate for friction and unmodeled dynamics in the wrench observer.

Employs hybrid pose and force control for simultaneous end-effector pose and force tracking.
Experiments report accurate wrench estimation and reliable tracking without force/torque sensors.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework. The observer estimates the end-effector force using a momentum observer and NN compensation. A task-null-space decomposition separates the joint velocity q̇ into the task-space velocity q̇t and null-space velocity q̇n. The task-space velocity q̇t is sent to the NN to reduce the effect of human disturbance on force estimation, while q̇n is used for null-space compliant control. The proposed hybrid pose and force controller provides reliable position, orientation, and force tracking while maintaining compliance in the null-space.

papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).
authors: Ming Zhong, Stacy Li, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski
bullets: Evaluates agents on 20 ML-for-science benchmarks spanning 11 domains under in-the-wild, long-horizon conditions.

Agents commonly miscalibrate novelty, underuse resources, and quickly narrow into local engineering sweeps.
Lightweight skills for ideation, experiment management, and checklists increased improvements to 20.1% for Claude Opus and 8.1% for Codex.
The testbed tracks progress toward agents capable of domain-level scientific reasoning, beyond routine ML engineering.
